content:
Among the greatest cinematic mysteries of our time, when it’s harder than ever to make movies, is the fact that David and NathanZellner continue to realize their uncompromisingly DIY, endearingly childlike vision through an indie filmography that only seems to grow in scale and purpose. It’s a welcome miracle that the duo who once captured the rhythms of childhood in their own idiosyncratic way (“Kid-Thing”), channeled compassion for those who might think the buried “Fargo” treasure is real (“Kumiko the Treasure Hunter”), and made a goofily unhinged groom out of Robert Pattinson nearly a decade before “The Drama” got there (“Damsel”), continue to play in their lovable sandbox.

For most audiences, the Zellners’ rhythms and textures are an acquired taste of sorts, like oysters or Marmite, that some would swear by, and others couldn’t fathom. Thankfully, many of the finest actors out there seem to revere them. In fact, quite a few of them — including Léa Seydoux, Cate Blanchett (also a producer), Chris Pine and Kelvin Harrison Jr. — turn up and gleefully let loose in the brothers’ latest indie oddity “Alpha Gang,” about a group of isolated, leather-clad space aliens aiming to conquer the earth while donned in ‘50s biker gear. Because, well, why not?

Popular on Variety

The story’s time period is purposely indistinct: We might be somewhere in the mid-20th century if the gang’s romantically fitted greaser outfits, meticulously sculpted hairdos, and disarming doo-wop musical tastes — played out of an old-timey jukebox — are any indication. Then again, who knows where and when any of this is happening, given that many earthlings also turn up throughout “Alpha Gang.” They represent figures of various real-world wars throughout history, tasked to eradicate the blue-blooded aliens: sometimes in tanks, with bazookas and hand grenades, sometimes in carriages and with vintage weapons. Still with me?

Trying to kill them first are the group of Alphas One to Six, played by Seydoux and Harrison Jr., as well as Doona Bae, Riley Keough, Dave Bautista and Lily-Rose Depp. Most of the time, they keep a straight, frozen face while dancing to ‘50s love songs with robotic moves. And they are all alarmed about this fast-spreading human disease called emotions. What if they catch it and regretfully display joy, sadness, anger and so on, slowly losing their powers? Late to the party, Keough’s Alpha Six, who appears on earth in a playful scene out of a vintage sci-fi, gets warned about these dangerous things called feelings by Seydoux’s Alpha One. But Six has bigger things to worry about, like the explosive diarrhea attack all Alphas have to endure when they enter Earth.

Yes, there are toilet jokes throughout “Alpha Gang,” and the funniest one is a running gag about the mystery Alpha who consistently leaves the seat up and pees all over it. Still, the most appealing quality of this film — directed jointly by the Zellners, but written by David only — is how much undeniable fun the cast seems to having delivering truly ridiculous lines with a straight face, like when a love-hungry Alpha Three (Harrison Jr.) asks a little bird to go steady with him.

He isn’t the only one losing himself in feelings. Alphas Two (Bautista), Four (Depp) and Five (Bae) also secretly harbor awakenings, with One and Six projecting anger and frustration in excess. While this construct, where emotions soften the aliens’ stiff edges, especially recalls Gary Ross’ “Pleasantville,” the already colorful Alphas don’t turn even more Technicolor. Instead, they tear up, they fear each other and they get blue periods. Again, why not?

A turning point arrives with Chris Pine’s entry as the latest Alpha, who is consistently the film’s funniest presence as soon as he joins it. The whole cast commits to the bit, having undoubtedly shown up to play— still, there is something about Pine’s overdone mannerisms that land with the most uproarious laughter. When a rival, ‘80s-style gang called Beta shows up with an eye-patched and hilarious Cate Blanchett in their ranks (wait until you hear her accent), the mayhem only escalates from there. It’s evident that the Zellners have conceived the Alphas and Betas with a “Terminator”-like logic: Betas are the more advanced aliens, refusing to join forces with the relatively naïve Alphas.

There will be body parts severed, much (blue) blood spilled, and extreme violence erupting in every corner of the Zellners’ brutalist designs and impressively immersive world-building that needs to be seen to be believed. And viewers’ mileage will certainly vary with this peculiar, fun little concoction on seclusion, connection and the need to belong that can’t hide its undercurrent of melancholy about the sorry state of a divided world. Shortly after it begins to overstay its welcome, yielding diminishing returns, the film thankfully concludes — reminding us that cinema can afford to make more room for uncompromising visions and kooky little artworks with something to say and some fun to spare.

title: ‘The Spiral’ Review: Paolo Strippoli’s Lurid Faustian Tragedy Shores Up His Reputation as Italy’s New Horror Virtuoso
summary: We don’t get a close enough look to see if the Devil actually wears Prada, but regardless, in Paolo Strippoli’s new horror romp “The Spiral,” she’s very chicly turned out indeed: Cool, crisp and collected in a tightly belted camel trenchcoat, hair pristinely bobbed and lips perfectly rouged, wielding a cigarette like a laser pointer. […]
content:
We don’t get a close enough look to see if the Devil actually wears Prada, but regardless, in Paolo Strippoli‘s new horror romp “The Spiral,” she’s very chicly turned out indeed: Cool, crisp and collected in a tightly belted camel trenchcoat, hair pristinely bobbed and lips perfectly rouged, wielding a cigarette like a laser pointer. As played with her signature husky-flutey delivery by Valeria Bruni Tedeschi, this film’s Lucifer has seemingly stepped straight out of a film noir, though she hardly needs to use her femme fatale wiles to seduce well-to-do fashionista and mother-of-two Anna (Jasmine Trinca) — she just needs to prey, with casual malice, on any parent’s worst fears regarding their families, and if that also means asking Anna to choose between her children, so much the better. Step on our necks, mother Mephistopheles, and let the kids suffer the consequences.

A faintly absurd Faustian fable blown up to grand guignol proportions through Strippoli’s brash formal command of his favorite genre, “The Spiral” doesn’t add up to an awful lot, but the sum of its parts is flashily entertaining enough. It’s the fourth feature from the 33-year-old Italian horror specialist, and his first to be programmed in the main competition at Venice — a status upgrade that, given the new film’s lurid but quite superficial pleasures, might strike some as premature.

Popular on Variety

In fact, it might be a year late. “The Spiral” arrives hot on the heels of Strippoli’s third feature “The Holy Boy,” a wickedly clever, creepy tale of small-town trauma, terror and faith that was a standout of Venice’s out-of-competition sidebar a year ago, and is an altogether more layered, probing and frankly frightening film than this one. Perhaps this year’s selection is the festival’s mea culpa; perhaps the star presence of veteran Euro-arthouse queen Bruni Tedeschi makes all the difference. Either way, this stylish hokum secures Strippoli’s claim to horror-auteur status, and should see him cross over into the international elevated-genre market. It would be no great surprise if Hollywood remake rights are negotiated before the film even makes it to U.S. screens, while major studios looking to zhuzh up their upcoming horror properties could do far worse than to take Strippoli’s card.

It certainly begins as it intends to continue, going straight in with the ear-splitting attack of Quentin Collette’s maximalist sound design — all manner of natural and unnatural phenomena shrieking in unison as the camera opens on a hand clutching a plane armrest for dear life, as extreme turbulence batters the aircraft hither and thither. Outside the window, a none-too-encouraging cyclone is forming in the clouds: the first of several spirals in the film’s image system, which, like many passing details in “The Spiral,” look cool and unnerving without leading anywhere in particular.

Cut to terra ferma, where the almighty rainstorm soaking the streets of Rome seems a comparatively trifling bit of weather. Anna, damp and frazzled, turns up unannounced at the door of her apprehensive adult daughter Alice (Romana Maggiora Vergano), insisting she has a terrible family secret to reveal, that can’t wait a minute longer. Her timing isn’t great; as it turns out, it never has been.

We rewind a quarter-century or so to the first of the film’s formally marked chapters, each titled after a different member of the family in question, though the story’s point of view doesn’t notably shift between them. In sunny Bari, Anna and husband Walter (Adriano Giannini) head up a picture-perfect model family — so very model, in fact, that seven-year-old Alice (Gabriella Telegrafo) has just been cast in a Barilla pasta ad. That goes out the window when, at a lush garden party on their luxury estate, Alice is brutally and unaccountably mauled by their bull terrier; ER doctors save her life, but as they bluntly inform her parents, they’re unlikely to save her leg.

With the threat of amputation looming, Anna heads to the church chapel — an ominous space merging gaudy Italo-modernism with aggressively Catholic candlelight, one of several coups here by production designer Marcello Di Carlo — to breathe, cry and pray. God doesn’t answer, but someone else does. Enter Bruni Tedeschi’s unnamed eavesdropper (“The Stranger,” to translate the film’s original Italian title), who at first gently commiserates with the distraught mother, before revealing some unsettling knowledge of the family’s situation, and proposing an even more unsettling solution: She can ensure that little Alice keeps her leg, but at some physical cost to her older brother Tobia (Alessandro Carbonara). Scarcely believing this outlandish offer and not in her right mind to begin with, Anna agrees.

Cue years of staggered, steadily worsening consequences, unboxed by Strippoli with gruesome relish. It’s for viewers to decide whether the streak of ableism and body-shaming that accompanies this fallout is the film’s failing or the work of the Devil herself, in what arguably amounts to a sick joke about Italian image-consciousness, Catholic guilt, or perhaps nothing all that deep. Mostly, Strippoli wants us to enjoy the loud, bumpy ride, and to a point, we do.

But his script winds up spiraling inwards rather than outwards. The belabored flashback structure saps some tension from the enterprise, while Anna’s dreadful secret (revealed rather early in proceedings) doesn’t really build in physical, moral or spiritual resonance, leaving it to Strippoli’s enjoyably vulgar, pedal-to-the-metal aesthetic to gee up the film’s narrative sputtering engine. He does, however, give Bruni Tedeschi’s very soigné Satan a few more opportunities to re-up the terms and conditions of her initial dastardly contract, giving the proceedings a welcome injection of camp energy each time. We all knew the Devil has all the best tunes — who knew she has all the best shoes too?

title: Luca Guadagnino on Casting Hollywood A-Listers in Subversive Roles: ‘I Have Worked With Some of the Finest’
summary: Luca Guadagnino discussed his warm rapport with Hollywood movie stars on Monday at the Venice Film Festival, one year after being on the Lido with his Julia Roberts-starrer “After the Hunt.” During a wide-ranging master class the Italian director, who was born in Palermo, Sicily, to an Algerian mother and a Sicilian father – and […]
content:
Luca Guadagnino discussed his warm rapport with Hollywood movie stars on Monday at the Venice Film Festival, one year after being on the Lido with his Julia Roberts-starrer “After the Hunt.”

During a wide-ranging master class the Italian director, who was born in Palermo, Sicily, to an Algerian mother and a Sicilian father – and whose career trajectory has been a long road full of twists and turns that have taken him to Hollywood – was asked about whether he likes casting top stars, such as Roberts, Daniel Craig, Tilda Swinton and Ralph Fiennes, in films that tend to subvert their conventional image with global audiences, as is the case with “Bond” star Craig in “Queer.”

“The truth, the banal truth, is that I am enamored with actors and definitely in love with my actors,” Guadagnino said. “So it’s a very tender emotion for me to work with them. We are like children playing on the beach, kind of creating these sandcastles. Finding ways to express what we want to express, and trying in a way to be truthful and not banal,” he explained.

Popular on Variety

“I’ve been lucky because, honestly, I have worked with some of the finest, most committed, bold performers I could have worked with. But I think they know that I love them,” Guadagnino added.

The feeling tends to be mutual.

That was clear when Julia Roberts arrived last year at the Venice Film Festival to promote “After the Hunt” wearing a cardigan emblazoned with Guadagnino’s face.

“Julia is fantastic,” Guadagnino told the packed room. “Every day of that shoot with her was quite inspiring.” Throughout the process of prepping and shooting “After The Hunt,” Roberts was knitting, he recounted. “And when I celebrated my birthday on the shoot of the movie, on Aug. 10 of that year, not only did Julia throw a party for me, but she gave me this present: It was the scarf she was knitting. It’s one of the most precious presents I have.”

Guadagnino kicked off his career thanks to his ability to charm movie stars.

In 1999, he made “The Protagonists,” a faux experimental doc in which Tilda Swinton and some pals try to reconstruct the motiveless murder of a London waiter. Guadagnino had become obsessed with Swinton after seeing her in Derek Jarman’s “Caravaggio” and cornered her at a Jarman retrospective in Rome, striking up a friendship that blossomed into a creative partnership.

Swinton eventually went on to play a restrained society dame who gradually bursts out of her loveless Milanese marriage in 2009’s “I Am Love.” “The idea of ‘I Am Love’ started with this image of a woman in a big, big mansion and feeling her feeling of displacement and loneliness,” Guadagnino said, adding: “I understand very well what it means to be estranged and strangled by being in a place where you don’t belong or you thought you belonged and you don’t. And in a way, it is fatal.”

One place where Guadagnino definitely doesn’t belong is swimming pools.

“I cannot swim,” he said, discussing “A Bigger Splash,” his 2015 sunshine, sex, food and rock-n-roll-filled remake of French thriller “La piscine,” starring Swinton and Ralph Fiennes.

“If you put me in the water where I can’t touch the ground, I will drown. So I’m quite terrified by water, by the sea. Totally terrified. And by pools, for sure,” he added.

In 2017, “Call Me By Your Name” bowed from Sundance, making a splash that reverberated with Italian critics and audiences after it scored Oscar nominations for best picture, actor – Timothée Chalamet’s role as Elio in the film launched his career – adapted screenplay and song. Guadagnino revealed that some of the shades of blue etched into that film “were just a big, big mistake made by the [processing] lab.”

“I have never been able to reshoot anything in my life because A: I’m very practical. And B: I never had the means to do that. So, I watched this thing, and I said: ‘This is miraculous, because those flashes of light, to me, are the butterflies in Elio’s stomach. And so we kept them in the movie.'”

Tomorrow Venice will unveil Guadagnino’s sprawling seven-hour Bernardo Bertolucci documentary “Joie de Vivre” in two parts, the first screening on Sept. 8, and the second on Sept. 9. Guadagnino will receive the festival’s Cartier Glory to the Filmmaker Award ahead of the first screening.

content:
“South Park” threw one final jab at President Donald Trump Sunday night as the show celebrated its Emmy win for Outstanding Animated Program.

The official “South Park” X account posted a graphic of Trump with his pants and underwear around his ankles, holding an Emmy award triumphantly in the air. The post was captioned, “Congratulations to Trey Parker, Matt Stone, and the entire South Park team on their Emmy win for Outstanding Animated Program!”

Congratulations to Trey Parker, Matt Stone, and the entire South Park team on their Emmy win for Outstanding Animated Program! pic.twitter.com/KlpvuhhWH2 — South Park (@SouthPark) September 7, 2026

In the photo, “You finally got your Emmy” is written above Trump’s head. This is most likely a knock at the president’s track record with the TV Academy honor. Trump was nominated twice at the Emmys for “The Apprentice,” receiving nods for Outstanding Reality-Competition Program in 2004 and 2005. He lost both times.

Popular on Variety

Trump was the main antagonist in “South Park” Season 27 and Season 28. After a two-year hiatus, Season 27 exploded onto Comedy Central with one of the most explicit and politically charged episodes in the series’ history. It showed Trump in bed with his lover and the future father of his child, Satan, and the grand finale was a PSA starring a deep-faked, naked Trump wandering through the desert. It ended with a scathing presidential slogan: “Trump: His penis is teeny-tiny, but his love for us is large.”

Series creator Trey Parker addressed the political angle in an interview with The New York Times. He explained that they put Trump in “South Park” not because “we got all political,” but instead because “politics became pop culture.”

“It’s like the government is just in your face everywhere you look,” Parker said. “Whether it’s the actual government or whether it is all the podcasters and the TikToks and the YouTubes and all of that, and it’s just all political and political because it’s more than political. It’s pop culture.”

title: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes Doc ‘You Can See Everything’ Detonates the Oscar Race — and Has A24 Chasing a 90-Year Record
summary: For three days, the Telluride Film Festival ran on a single unknown rumor. By Sunday night, the line outside the Werner Herzog Theatre had swelled into the longest of the weekend, phones were sealed in locked pouches, a security team worked the aisles in night-vision goggles and a Telluride programmer took the stage to warn […]
content:
For three days, the Telluride Film Festival ran on a single unknown rumor. By Sunday night, the line outside the Werner Herzog Theatre had swelled into the longest of the weekend, phones were sealed in locked pouches, a security team worked the aisles in night-vision goggles and a Telluride programmer took the stage to warn the crowd, only half-joking, that anyone who spoiled what came next was no longer loved. Then the mystery that had consumed the mountains finally broke. The secret screening was “You Can See Everything,” Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, and the room came apart.

A24 confirmed it the same night as the movie hit play, dropping a teaser and announcing an October theatrical release, which means the guessing game is over and the awards conversation has begun. With that release date, the studio has planted a 172-minute nonfiction epic squarely in this season’s documentary feature race — and it arrives as the rare title that critics and attendees started debating immediately after the credits finished.

Popular on Variety

Thirty-four days before she reported to prison, Holmes invited a skeptical crew inside her home to record her every move. What began as a portrait of a convicted felon became a three-year descent that A24’s own logline calls a journey “into the abyss.” Hollywood has chased the Theranos saga for years — Alex Gibney’s “The Inventor” got there in 2019, Hulu’s “The Dropout” won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy and a Jennifer Lawrence vehicle from Adam McKay collapsed before it could even start shooting — but no one has approached Holmes the way these two filmmakers do.

That is the first reason to take this seriously as a contender. Fielder is the most restlessly inventive nonfiction mind in television, coming off a second season of “The Rehearsal” that earned Peabody recognition and an Emmy nomination for writing. “You Can See Everything” is his feature directing debut. Oppenheim, meanwhile, is having the festival run of his life — his first scripted feature, the Robert Pattinson thriller “Primetime,” bowed in Venice to a rapturous response — and his nonfiction pedigree (“Some Kind of Heaven,” “Ren Faire,” “Spermworld”) gives the project a formal rigor that Fielder’s persona-driven work does not always foreground.

The pairing is the story. Two artists obsessed with how the camera warps the thing it records, turned loose on the most studied liar of the century.

The craft is what builds an awards case, and this one is stacked. Shot by David Bolen — the “Some Kind of Heaven” and “Thelma” cinematographer who also lensed Oppenheim’s “Primetime” — the film trades the filmmakers’ usual anamorphic gloss for a boxed-in 4:3 frame and long zoom lenses that let two operators drift through a family home like ghosts, but ones the families clearly acknowledge and want as part of their story. Editor Adam Locke-Norton, Fielder’s collaborator of two decades, sustains conversations well past the point of comfort, letting non-answers hang in the air. And Ari Balouzian, the composer and one-third of the soul trio Gabriels, threads a noir score through the domestic footage that turns a beach house into a crime scene of the mind.

In a documentary field where craft branches increasingly reward ambition, all three are legitimate below-the-line conversation starters.

You Can See Everything Courtesy of A24

Then there is the thing itself, which plays less like a true-crime doc than a controlled experiment in whether a viewer can tell honesty from performance. Fielder does not stay behind the lens for long. Drawn into the frame by his subjects and by his own need to interject, he becomes the film’s destabilized center — a filmmaker visibly struggling, in real time, to work out whether he is being played.

The result is a movie that keeps escalating in strangeness across its three-year span and lands a final movement that had Telluride’s most seasoned attendees walking out shell-shocked. “Wild” and “WTF?” were the words circulating on the gondola line, and they were compliments.

Which brings us to the hurdles, because they are significant. The documentary branch has never fully made peace with participatory, comedy-adjacent nonfiction and voters who prize the observational and the earnest may recoil from a film in which the director is this present and this implicated.

There are obviously lingering questions about how much of it is “scripted” — which will spark debates over whether an acting nomination can come from such a movie, because the central performance that surprises in the film is, in fact, eligible for Oscar recognition, Variety has confirmed, although not for SAG.

A24 insiders see hurdles in the documentary branch, which is why they’re eyeing this film as a — wait for it — best picture play. And why the hell not?

With A24’s arsenal of contenders this year — which could include the summer hit “The Invite,” the Cannes breakout “Club Kid” and the Telluride debut smash “The Debut” — is there a real path for the indie studio to challenge the record for the most best picture nominations by a single studio in one year?

That record belongs to Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer, which landed five at the ninth Academy Awards in 1937. A24 still has Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” to come out of Toronto, and it just dropped the aforementioned “Primetime” at Venice.

MGM achieved the feat when the Academy was nominating 10 films in the best picture category. “The Great Ziegfeld” was the big winner, taking home three statues. It was joined by four other MGM releases from 1936: “Libeled Lady,” “Romeo and Juliet,” “San Francisco” and “A Tale of Two Cities.”

At the time, MGM was the undisputed heavyweight in Hollywood, home to top talents such as Clark Gable, Judy Garland, Spencer Tracy, Greta Garbo, Joan Crawford, Jean Harlow and Norma Shearer. So expansive was the A-list roster that the studio famously boasted it had “more stars than there are in heaven.”

But the bigger record is hidden inside all of this.

A documentary has never been nominated for best picture across 98 ceremonies. When the Academy expanded the field to as many as 10 nominees in 2009, it pointed to exactly this kind of nonfiction (and animated) filmmaking as newly able to compete. Seventeen years later, it still hasn’t happened for documentaries; only three animated films have ever cracked the category.

A best picture nomination for “You Can See Everything” wouldn’t merely pad A24’s tally — it would make history as the first documentary ever nominated for the Academy’s top prize.

The 172-minute runtime is a genuine ask. And there is the subject herself: Platforming a convicted fraudster, even to interrogate her, invites the accusation of handing Holmes a stage and any campaign will have to make the case — loudly — that the film indicts rather than rehabilitates.

The smartest defense is baked into the movie’s DNA. This is not a redemption tour. It is a study of the impossibility of ever knowing what is real, which is either the perfect subject for a branch that fetishizes authenticity or a provocation aimed straight at it.

A24 has the muscle to fight that fight. The studio has run documentary campaigns before and knows how to convert festival heat into a shortlist slot, and the fall precursor calendar gives it a runway — the Gotham Awards, the IDA Documentary Awards, Critics Choice Documentary, Cinema Eye Honors and the DGA’s documentary prize all feed the Oscar shortlist and a film this discussed will not want for coverage.

The October release is early enough to build, and the Fielder factor guarantees a level of press attention most nonfiction contenders would kill for.

The bottom line is that the documentary race, whatever shape it was taking a week ago, now has to reckon with this. A movie about the impossibility of trust, made with the person least equipped to earn it, dropped without warning into a festival built on the honor system — the metaphors write themselves, and so, most likely, will the ballots of a lot of voters who cannot stop thinking about it.

“I’m not that person,” Holmes insists in the teaser. “I can promise you that.”

By the time the lights came up in Telluride, nobody in the room was sure whether to believe her.

title: Summer U.S. Box Office Hits All-Time $4.76B Record: How Audiences Surrendered To Moviegoing
summary: No one ever imagined this would be a record $4.76 billion summer. When we started off, we knew Universal’s The Odyssey was destined to be huge given that the 70MM Imax tickets sold out a year in advance. Sony/Marvel Studio’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was also bound to be big, but the biggest movie of […]
content:
No one ever imagined this would be a record $4.76 billion summer.

When we started off, we knew Universal’s The Odyssey was destined to be huge given that the 70MM Imax tickets sold out a year in advance. Sony/Marvel Studio’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day was also bound to be big, but the biggest movie of all-time at the domestic box office? No way! No one knew what the hell Backrooms was, but tracking knew that there was a there, there. But A24’s biggest opening of all-time at $81.4M U.S. and highest grossing title ever at $197.5? Stop it!

More impressive, admissions were also high. There’s misinformation out in the media that while the box office surged due to the inflation in ticket prices (the uptick wasn’t that melodramatic), the number of people in seats fell. According to box office stat firm EntTelligence, that’s absolutely not true with admission well above 322 million versus summer 2025’s final tally of 275 million.

Rentrak tells us that this summer was the first on record to see each of its four core calendar months generate more than $1B apiece domestically, read May ($1.07B), June ($1.08B), July ($1.18B) and August ($1.276B).

Watch on Deadline

How did we get here? And are moviegoers back, for real?

Many would like to credit the success of summer 2026 on the resurgence of the Gen Z crowd (roughly ages 14-29, or for the sake of a clean movie demographic stat — those under 25), who shook off their cloistered Covid ways, stepped away from iPads and mobile phones and literally came to the cinema for movies like Obsession (38% under 25 per Screen Engine/Rentrak’s Postrak), Backrooms (55% under 25) and Spider-Man: Brand New Day (51% under 25). And that’s very true. Before the start of the summer in early April, Fandango’s moviegoing study found that Gen Z and Millennials were among the most active moviegoers, with 92% of those surveyed saying they prefer going with others.

But you don’t get to record box office figures without the resurgence of non-frequent movies.

“There were a huge number of non-frequent moviegoers. We don’t see the momentum stopping, the top 15 films we’re tracking for the fall are running an average of 3.5 points ahead the average from the top 15 at the same point in time from last year. We see no signs of this slowing down,” said Bill Skelly, Head of Greenlight Analytics.

“We saw non-frequent moviegoers buying multiple tickets over the summer,” Skelly emphasizes.

Also, you can’t ignore the age old truisms including the power of premium format screens (clearly whatever the current supply is, there’s a demand for more) and product, product, product.

MICHAEL, Jaafar Jackson as Michael Jackson, 2026. ph: Glen Wilson / © Lionsgate / Courtesy Everett Collection

Lionsgate gets full credit for lighting the wick on the hot season with Michael, which wound up becoming their highest grossing movie ever at $372.3M domestic, and over $1 billion worldwide. And they went early during the last weekend of April. Michael reached a diverse crowd of 30% Black, 30% Caucasian, and 29% Hispanic and Latino. It was an every person movie with 46% over 35, and 54% under. And most of all, it was the first movie to pull in a crowd of non-frequent moviegoers with 45% combined saying they went to the movies a few times a year or every other month per Screen Engine/Rentrak’s PostTrak. From that point on, the occasional moviegoer made moviegoing a habit.

THE DEVIL WEARS PRADA 2, Anne Hathaway, 2026. © Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures /Courtesy Everett Collection

Now when it came to dating event films this summer, it was like all the majors were working together like instruments in a fine-tuned London Philharmonic performance of Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 22 in E flat, each pulling in their own chief demographic. Michael gave way 20th Century Studio’s The Devil Wears Prada 2 which brought in 75% women. That sequel also pulled in even more non-frequent moviegoers at 56%.

OBSESSION, from left: Inde Navarrette, Michael Johnston, 2025. © Focus Features /Courtesy Everett Collection

Focus Features’ TIFF Midnight acquisition, Obsession, arrived on May 15, and while overperforming its first weekend forecast, came in with an alright $17.1M but wound up being the Fatal Attraction of the summer, speaking to both sexes of the 18-34 demographic (75% turnout) who left cinemas debating who was the better: Bear or Nikki. Get this, the movie’s first weekend pulled in mostly frequent moviegoers (75% combined went once a week or once/twice a month to movies). Obsession ultimately made older 40-something demos obsessed to watch the Curry Barker directed movie. Barker together with Backrooms filmmaker Kane Parsons created a new big screen want for content from YouTube creators.

Renate Reinsve in ‘Backrooms’ A24

Disney/Lucasfilm’s Star Wars: Mandalorian and Grogu wound up being the lowest grossing of all the Star Wars live-action titles and an overall bomb in the summer (at $177.7M domestic, $345.3M WW off a $165M production cost), but it’s $98M 4-day opening alone was enough of a bridge along with Obsession‘s amazing near $32M 4-day second weekend hold to make the Memorial Day frame rich enough with more than $220M, and not a bust like the holiday’s 2024 ($132.2M) when Furiosa and Garfield failed to create a stampede.

‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Sony/Marvel

Sums up Joseph M. Singer, film financier and Elixir Media co-founder on the majors’ symphonic approach to dating: “The marketplace featured Spider-Man: Brand New Day, The Odyssey, Toy Story 5, The Devil Wears Prada 2, Obsession, Backrooms, and other successful films. They are not aimed at the same audience. There are tentpole films, animation, horror, those aimed at adults, and original or less conventional movies. A 20-year-old may want Backrooms. A family goes to Toy Story 5. A couple picks The Devil Wears Prada 2. A Christopher Nolan film brings several generations together, and Spider-Man draws an enormous mainstream audience. Multi-quadrant films have always driven the box office, but a film need not appeal to everyone if the calendar consistently offers something for everyone.”

“Moviegoing runs on habit. When people go regularly, they see trailers, talk about movies with friends, and start thinking about the next one. Moviegoing begets moviegoing. COVID-19 broke that cycle, and the strikes made it harder to rebuild because habits require frequent opportunities. One interesting movie every month or two does not make habitual moviegoers. A steady stream of varied, decent films does,” adds Singer.

Another thread woven into this summer says Skelly, “In our data, we saw that women were engaged. A few films were ‘made for women’, but not nearly enough. Instead, what happened is they made films that women were interested in.”

Aside from The Devil Wears Prada 2, movies which women were interested in were Michael (58% female draw), Obsession (41% women), Backrooms (women under 25, a challenging demo to consistently pull in, were the second biggest demo at 24%), and The Odyssey (women over 25 were the second biggest crowd at 31%).

Yes, there were upsets, in addition to Mandalorian and Grogu this summer, there was Supergirl ($72.3M domestic off $186M production cost), Moana ($126.2M off $250M cost before P&A), The End of Oak Street ($51.3M domestic off $80M-$92M cost), and Universal/Illumination’s Minions & Monsters, the lowest grossing in the Gru/Minions franchise at $183M domestic, $518M worldwide (still at an $85M cost, plus merchandising downstream, the nth sequel will be profitable, we understand). Anyone wondering whether momentum alone can rise all boats, here were examples of a returned audience making discerning choices on where to spend an average general adult ticket price of $13.46, child’s of $11.51, and/or adult PLF of $18.39 (all according to EntTelligence). If a movie had any sheen of similarity to any tentpole predecessor, then it failed to find any traction. In regards to the clever conceit of End of Oak Street (Jurassic Park in your cul-de-sac), that movie was a feathered fish in its confused sell of whether or not it was an action thriller or horror thriller.

Further compounding challenges for these movies, largely released in the late June to early July corridor was the World Cup per sources. Historically, it has never been a major draw for Americans. But with games taking place in our time zones, it became a major cultural event that people prioritized with stadiums and bars filled.

But the biggest catalyst fueling a record summer, which has triggered the Gen Z and non-frequents out of the house, per one studio boss, is that “Generations are shrugging off streaming as a destination of preference. Netflix’s stock is sinking, and if you look at the latest findings of their viewership report and how that company is handling that, streaming is bound to be the basic cable of home entertainment. The novelty has worn off.”

“Streaming is convenient. A theater is an outing. You leave home, meet friends, and sit with hundreds of strangers to share an experience. Gen Z spends more time with friends than any other generation and is especially likely to treat a movie as a social event. For a generation that lives much of its social life on a phone, that may be worth more than the doomsayers expected,” says Singer.

“Streaming, meanwhile, no longer feels special. People cook, text, talk, and scroll while a show plays,” he adds, “It has become a version of cable television.”

‘The Rivals of Amziah King’ Black Bear

Despite the pom poms that it was the best of summers, smaller and mid-sized movies have it hard, and that’s because it’s the survival of the fittest when it comes to holding screens, a difficult feat when specialty houses are also booking Spider-Man: Brand New Day and Odyssey. Distribution sources acknowledge that Covid has certainly damaged the theatrical landscape for these films with a multitude of cinema closures. It doesn’t matter if you’re a critically acclaimed novel auteur movie such as Black Bear’s Matthew McConaughey big-screen return ($2M domestic), The Rivals of Amziah King at 89% Rotten Tomatoes critical score and 80% with audiences, or Paramount’s Mark Wahlberg-looks-like-I-can-see-it on streaming period thriller, By Any Means (opened to $9.3M over Labor Day), which had so-so reviews, but a better audience score at 88%. It takes an incredible amount of oomph to turn a smaller film into an event for a specific crowd, and persuade adults that what they’re bound to see something completely different from what’s on a streaming menu. Just ask A24 about their starry adult sex comedy The Invite which made close to $26M domestic, and over $55M worldwide. The movie was a mini-destination for couples at 44% as well as adults (25-34 were the biggest demo at 33%, but 18-24, 35-44, and the over 55 set each pulled in 19% apiece with 45-54 accounting for 10% of attendees per PostTrak).

Lionsgate Motion Picture Chair Adam Fogelson, who was behind the success of the studio’s biggest film ever in Michael, told us earlier this summer that when it comes to harnessing the latest generation of moviegoers, “Marketers are having to learn a completely different language.”

“All of the things when I was growing up in marketing that were sort of held to be certain and true about how you reach an audience, those things, especially for the generations we’re talking about, have changed,” he added.

For example, “Don’t overshare too much in a trailer; if you do, “you’re going to get flat-out rejected,” the Lionsgate exec says.

“Some of the movies that are succeeding that are coming from this generation, they’re telling story in a very different way,” he adds.

So, is this just an anomaly summer? It’s clear that 2026 is bound to be the biggest domestic box office post Covid with $10 billion within reach. We’re certainly on the heels of another Barbenheimer, or Spider-Man: Brand New Odyssey at Christmas with Disney/Marvel Studios’ Avengers: Doomsday and Warner Bros/Legendary’s Dune: Part Three. The trick is for development executives to make unique, emotionally event movies that specific audiences designate as completely their own, a nuance that’s easier said then done.

For now, moviegoing is in a great place.

“Audiences appreciate that they have to work a little harder to make an appointment and see what’s made for them. Having everything at your fingertips on a streaming menu is what a child wants, “says another studio boss about the rebirth of moviegoing this summer, “They’ve surrendered to theatrical.”

Leaders of summer at the domestic box office for the period of May 1-Sept. 7:

Universal, $1.23 billion, +63% vs. summer 2025 Disney, $1.034 billion, -2% Sony, $1 billion, +459% Lionsgate, $270M, +296% Warner Bros, $239.3M, -76% Paramount, $219.8M, -21% Amazon MGM Studios $170.1M, +400%

title: ‘South Park’ Trolls Donald Trump After Winning First Animated Program Emmy In 13 Years
summary: Don’t call it a comeback — Comedy Central’s South Park, which returned to the Outstanding Animated Program category with its first nomination in five years, landed its first win in 13 years. On stage, South Park co-creator Trey Parker thanked fans. On social media, the show celebrated by taunting the Emmy-winning episodes’ frequent target, President […]
content:
Don’t call it a comeback — Comedy Central’s South Park, which returned to the Outstanding Animated Program category with its first nomination in five years, landed its first win in 13 years.

On stage, South Park co-creator Trey Parker thanked fans. On social media, the show celebrated by taunting the Emmy-winning episodes’ frequent target, President Donald Trump. Surrounded by the South Park characters, including Satan, who delivered Parker a character voice-over nomination this year, the cartoon version of the President is holding an Emmy statuette with his pants and underwear down.

The slogan, “You finally got your Emmy,” likely refers to Trump’s penchant for trophies and his status of a two-time Emmy nominee. As an executive producer of NBC’s The Apprentice, Trump shared in two Outstanding Reality-Competition Program nominations, in 2004 and 2005. The Apprentice lost to CBS’ The Amazing Race both times.

Watch on Deadline

Trump, depicted on South Park with real photographs pasted on an animated body, was relentlessly mocked during the 10 episodes that aired during the eligibility window for the 2026 Emmys Awards, split into two five-episode seasons, 27 and 28. The satire led to the White House clapping back with a statement that “the show has been irrelevant for 20 years, relying on uninspired ideas for attention.”

The lampooning of Trump is part of South Park’ storied high-wire act tradition of courting controversy with provocative, ripped-from-the headlines stories skewering pop culture. Which explains Parker’s aknowledgement accepting the Animated Program Emmy on stage Sunday, the show’s sixth win out of 19 nominations in the category.

“A big thank you to the greatest fans in the world. It’s only because of you guys that we haven’t been canceled in 30 years,” he said.

Created by Parker and Matt Stone, South Park, which premiered in 1997, scored a record three Emmy nominations this year in addition to a Television Academy Honor.

As promoted in the Emmy celebration collage with Trump, the series returns with new episodes Sept. 16.

title: Renate Reinsve, Johnny Flynn & Vicky Krieps Set For Mia Hansen-Løve’s Mary Wollstonecraft Picture ‘If Love Should Die’ As Goodfellas Boards Sales – TIFF
summary: EXCLUSIVE: Renate Reinsve has been officially confirmed for the role of Mary Wollstonecraft in Mia Hansen-Løve’s epic and intimate period drama If Love Should Die as Goodfellas boards sales for a script-backed TIFF launch where it will be one of the buzziest European productions on the market.   In fresh casting news, Reinsve is being joined by Johnny Flynn and Vicky Krieps […]
content:
EXCLUSIVE: Renate Reinsve has been officially confirmed for the role of Mary Wollstonecraft in Mia Hansen-Løve’s epic and intimate period drama If Love Should Die as Goodfellas boards sales for a script-backed TIFF launch where it will be one of the buzziest European productions on the market.

In fresh casting news, Reinsve is being joined by Johnny Flynn and Vicky Krieps in key roles, with Charlie Kelly, Will Keen, Tom Sturridge and Jane Beever also featuring in the cast.

The film is a European co-production between Ireland, France, Norway, Spain and UK, backed by Anonymous Content and RT Features, with Anonymous Content co-repping domestic rights with CAA Media Finance.

Norwegian actress Renate Reinsve arrives on the film fresh from her performance opposite Sebastian Stan in Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes 2026 Palme d’Or winner and awards season frontrunner Fjord, following a buzzy run on last year’s award trail with Best International Feature Film winner Sentimental Value.

Watch on Deadline

Equally in demand actors Johnny Flynn and Vicky Krieps recently appeared together in Malgorzata Szumowska and Michal Englert’s The Idiot(s) which received a buzzy world premiere in Telluride over the weekend.

Other recent credits for Flynn include A Prayer for the Dying and another raved about Telluride title, Elsinore, while Phantom Thread breakout Krieps was seen over the past year in Jim Jarmusch’s Venice 2025 Golden Lion winner feature, Father, Mother, Brother, Sister and Cannes 2025-selected drama Love Me Tender

First announced in 2024, If Love Should Die will focus on the remarkable last 12 years in the life of 18th century English writer, philosopher and women’s rights advocate Wollstonecraft, who also is famed for being the mother of Frankenstein creator Mary Shelley.

Set in England on the eve of the French Revolution, it follows Wollstonecraft, a then young, poor, solitary woman, as she carves a daring path through the ideals of the Enlightenment. Dismissed from her post as a governess, she resolves to live by her pen, against all odds.

If Love Should Die will be Hansen-Løve’s first English-language feature since Cannes 2021-selected drama Bergman Island, starring Vicky Krieps and Mia Wasikowska. To date, she has directed eight feature films with other highlights including Things to Come, starring Isabelle Huppert, which won the Berlin Film Festival’s Silver Bear for Best Director in 2016.

The film is set in the UK as well as multiple other European territories including France, Portugal, Norway, and Sweden.

Hansen-Løve will be joined on the shoot by multi-award-winning cinematographer Claire Mathon (Portrait of a Lady on Fire, Spencer, Saint Omer) and her regular editor Marion Monnier as well as production designer Mela Melak (A Real Pain, High Life) and Louise Stanton as costume designer (The Quiet Girl).

“I’m thrilled that I’m finally able to make the film I’ve been preparing for a long time and that is particularly close to my heart. It’s a huge challenge: bringing Mary Wollstonecraft to the screen for the very first time. I’m also very happy to be supported by such a talented, committed team and above all, to share this adventure with the wonderful Renate Reinsve,” said Hansen-Løve.

The production brings together a cohort of top award-winning European producers spanning Mia Hansen-Løve’s long-time producer David Thion at Paris-based Les Films Pelleas (Anatomy of a Fall); Ireland’s Patrick O’Neill and Conor Barry for Wildcard (Kneecap); María Zamora for Spain’s Elastica Films (Alcarràs); Norway’s Maria Ekerhovd at Mer Film (Sentimental Value) as well as the UK’s Joshua Horsfield and Saskia Duff at Intake Films (The Brutalist, The Testament of Ann Lee) and Thembisa Cochrane and Georgie Paget at Caspian Films (Frank & Louis).

Production is financed by Rodrigo Teixeira for RT Features (Paper Tiger, Bergman Island, Call Me By Your Name) Nick Shumaker and David Levine for Anonymous Content (Possible Love, In Waves, Nickel Boys); Raffaella Leone for Leone Film Group (Paper Tiger, Love Me Love Me, A Beautiful Day); Marco Perego for Artists Haven (Paper Tiger, Minotaur, Fjord, Butterfly Jam) and Nightjar Films (How to Shoot a Ghost), while MUBI financed development.

Coproducers are Sweden’s Marie at Kjellson and Wik (Gentle Monster), Lars Thomas Skare for Mer Film and Kristina Börjeson for Film i Väst (Sentimental Value, The Testament of Ann Lee, The Apprentice). Phillippe Martin at Les Films Pelleas, who produced Palme d’Or winner It Was Just an Accident, is an associate producer.

The production is also coming together in association with executive producers: Franklin Laviola and Nicholas Laviola (The Man I Love), Francesca Mormanni (Cut Your Teeth) Pio & Co (It Was Just an Accident), La Femme qui Aaimait les films (A Woman’s Life), Tempio (In-I in Motion ), Mikino (Drôles d’oiseaux), Bobby Allen of MUBI and Seona Bell.

Additionally, it is co-produced by Film i Väst, Arte France Cinema (Olivier Père, Rémi Burah, Mathilde Hersant), and The Match Factory in co-production with Bayerischer Rundfunk (Commissioning Editor: Harald Steinwender, Bettina Ricklefs), in collaboration with ARTE (Commissioning Editor: Barbara Häbe).

The film is supported by Eurimages, Les Films du Losange, Elastica Distribution, Leone Distribution, Norwegian Film Institute, Screen Ireland, Mediafondet Zefyr, Vestnorsk Filmsenter, ICAA, Arte France, Canal+, Cine+/OCS, Filmin, HBO (Spain), Région Île-de-France, Région Normandie, UK Global Screen Fund, with support from BFI and National Lottery.

Mia Hansen-Love is repped by Gersh Agency and Intertalent; Reinsve, by CAA and Narrative PR; Flynn, by CAA, United Agents and Public Eye Communications and Krieps is repped by United Agents, CAA, Agence Adequat and Tapestry London. Will Keen and Charlie Kelly are repped by Independent Talent Group, and Tom Sturridge is repped by WME and Independent Talent Group.

title: ‘Look Back’ Director Hirokazu Koreeda On Adapting Manga And Learning To Live With The Ghosts Of The Past – Venice Film Festival
summary: Hirokazu Koreeda is not the world’s most prolific director or even Japan’s (that honor goes to Takashi Miike, who passed the 100-film milestone years ago). But he is certainly one of the most versatile and unpredictable; there are few directors who could follow the heart-wrenching poignancy of Still Walking (2008), a film about a family […]
content:
Hirokazu Koreeda is not the world’s most prolific director or even Japan’s (that honor goes to Takashi Miike, who passed the 100-film milestone years ago). But he is certainly one of the most versatile and unpredictable; there are few directors who could follow the heart-wrenching poignancy of Still Walking (2008), a film about a family grieving for the death of a son, with Air Doll (2009), in which a wide-eyed inflatable sex doll comes magically to life.

Koreeda is frequently compared to Yasujirō Ozu, who still casts a long shadow over world cinema even though he died in 1963, aged 60, with next to no international profile. Like Ozu, Koreeda explores the dynamics of family, with a special interest in fathers and sons, and it’s a recipe that landed him the highest honor in Cannes 2018 for Shoplifters, putting him on a footing with fellow Palme d’Or winners and countrymen Akira Kurosawa and Shohei Imamura.

Despite the serenity of Koreeda’s shooting style, there is a restlessness to the artist that nevertheless makes his work hard to categorize. Though he frequently returns to his pet themes, he does so in many different ways, shooting in foreign places (France for 2019’s The Truth and Korea for 2022’s Broker), and dabbling in genre, as he did with 2017’s The Third Murder, a courtroom drama, and this year’s sci-fi-tinged AI fantasy Sheep in the Box.

Watch on Deadline

His Venice entry Look Back recalls his 2015 film Our Little Sister, a bittersweet study of the female friendships that develop when three grown-up sisters discover they have a 15-year-old step-sibling. Look Back, based on a manga by Tatsuki Fujimoto, tells the story of Fujino, a fourth-grade student who is fast becoming something of a star at school with her expertly drawn cartoon strips. Fujino then discovers that she has serious competition from Kyomoto, an agoraphobic student so talented that Fujino loses the will to continue, binning all her reference books.

Fujino soon realizes that Kyomoto is really not a threat — her skills as a background artist perfectly match Fujino’s — and together they work as Fujimoto, seamlessly switching from young girls to teenagers, with superb work from the film’s matching pairs of actresses. Working as a team gives Kyomoto the confidence she needs to leave home and go to art school. There, the film takes a surprisingly dark turn, separating the two girls forever and resulting in a touching Sliding Doors twist that may take viewers a minute or two to catch up with as Fujino finds a way to process her overwhelming sense of loss.

Deadline sat down with the director to discuss this latest chapter in his storied career…

DEADLINE: How long ago did you start with Look Back?

KOREEDA: It was in 2023 that I met the author of the original manga, Fujimoto Tatsuki. So, the project must have started quite a bit before that, maybe in 2022.

DEADLINE: What was it about this story that appealed to you? Do you read a lot of manga?

KOREEDA: I wouldn’t say that I read a ton of manga, but there are a few authors that I really like and continue to follow. One thing is that I’m not of the generation that really grew up reading Shonen Jump, which is the weekly published magazine of manga. And Fujimoto is of that generation. So, it’s not as if I’d encounter his work unless it was published as a collected book. And when I did see his book, it wasn’t like, “Wow, that’s Fujimoto Tatsuki.” It was actually the cover that I was really drawn to.

I picked it up and read it, and I was really drawn into the story. This would’ve been around the period of the pandemic, when work had slowed down significantly for me, and it seemed to tell a story about what happens when artists encounter situations of despair that are kind of out of their control and how artists can start creating again after those types of periods. So, I could really relate to it, and I felt encouraged by the work.

DEADLINE: What does the word “shonen” mean, by the way?

TRANSLATOR: I’ll answer this. Shonen just means “young boy”.

DEADLINE: Is Shonen Jump the market leader?

KOREEDA: In Japan, as far as the weekly magazines that are produced for young people to read, there’s Shonen Jump, there’s Shōnen Sunday, and then there’s Shōnen Magazine, so there are these three. When I was growing up, I always read Shōnen Magazine, and there’s kind of a division between young people, whether they prefer Jump or Magazine. And that’s why I said I wasn’t familiar with his work. But today, I would say Shonen Jump is the most powerful of the three, in that it continues to be really popular.

DEADLINE: Was it daunting to adapt something that is already visual? You’re adapting a comic book with frames. How did it affect your filmmaking?

KOREEDA: I do understand that, in manga, the frame is already decided, but I would say that the cels of manga or comic books and the framing of a film are very different, in the sense that with a film, the size and ratio of your frame is set. But with manga, depending on the size and shape of the cel, it’s a way to create a kind of rhythm and speed in the reading experience, and that’s something, of course, that you can’t really recreate in the filmic medium. So, there is the key visual of the manga, what I saw on the cover — the image of the back of the protagonist as they’re drawing the manga.

But, of course, just recreating that doesn’t make a film. And it was when I met Fujimoto — and I also met a professional assistant to manga artists — that I learned about the importance of sound in the process of writing manga. So, when you’re listening to someone draw out a cel, the way that they might draw out the line and the speed and confidence with which they draw the line is really what tells you how professional and how skilled they are as a manga artist. And that’s where I thought the sound is going to be very important to the film. I thought that the core of the film would revolve around this idea of watching the back of the protagonist. When they first put pen to paper, there’s a sense of hesitation in the sound. Slowly, it builds up speed and becomes more positive. Then, by meeting their friend, one sound becomes two, and that sound then turns into a digital process. I knew that if I could build a film around this idea, it would be very simple yet powerful.

Furi Nanasa and Rokka Okada in ‘Look Back’ K2 Pictures

DEADLINE: Why did you decide to stick with two female protagonists when you could have so easily made it two boys, two guys? What was it about exploring two female manga artists, both very different personalities from very different worlds?

KOREEDA: It’s a very simple source material, so I had decided very early on that I wasn’t going to add anything that wasn’t already there. So, when you see scenes with the protagonist’s mother, or the teacher, or even the editor of the magazine, those might only be represented in the manga as one cel in the story. But just by expanding upon, for instance, those characters, it was a way to add this idea that there are these adults around these two children that are encouragingly gazing over them and watching their back, in a sense. I wanted the audience to be able to overlap their own perspective on the two girls with the adults around them.

But the idea of changing the gender of the characters never crossed my mind, because it really was about being faithful to the source material. Because when we think about the two characters, Fujino and Kyomoto, two parts of Fujimoto’s name are in each of the characters, right? The Fuji from Fujimoto and the Moto in Kyomoto. And that’s because Fujimoto said to me that both those characters dwell inside him, in a way. And I imagine that maybe he was only able to write those characters because they’re girls, and if they had been boys, that they would be too close to his own identity and that he needed a kind of distance in order to flesh out the characters.

DEADLINE: It’s fascinating to see the way they seem to grow up in front of us. What’s the secret? Were there any visual effects? The two pairs of actresses work together so seamlessly, and we get a sense of these girls getting older without ever really seeming to.

KOREEDA: Right. Having a character grow up is probably the most difficult thing to try to depict in live-action film, because viewers can easily get caught up in the change that happens. And with manga, obviously, you can draw that in a very seamless way. And it’s not something that you can solve by casting people with similar faces. I needed to make sure that they had a kind of rapport. So, before we even started shooting, I made sure that the four actors met up with each other and we were able to forge a relationship.

And then during the casting process, something that I kept in mind is that to me there’s this idea that in a dynamic of actors working in a scene together, someone is always the catcher and the other is the pitcher, if we’re going to use a baseball analogy. And in this sense [referring to the older actresses], Natsuki Deguchi is a pitcher and Aju Makita is a catcher. And I knew that those roles needed to be played in similar ways by the younger actors as well. So, if anything, that’s something that I was thinking about in the casting process — “How are they going to match that catcher-pitcher sensibility?”

DEADLINE: A lot of your films deal with regret, but I don’t think I’ve ever seen regret in your films portrayed quite like it is in this movie. What made you decide to use the rewriting of reality to express remorse?

KOREEDA: This is quite difficult to explain, but I think that as a person who makes things, who creates, that process can’t be sustained if it’s just fun. At some point, you need to really reconsider and rethink this idea of, “Why am I continuing to make things? Why am I continuing to create?” And I think that this is one way in which I related to the original manga. But when I think of all of the people that have pulled me through this journey and encouraged me to make films, half of those people no longer are on this earth.

These include people that were very early in recognizing my work. I think of critics and writers such as Donald Richie and Roger Ebert or Tony Rayns. All these people are no longer living. And I think of their presence and this desire to continue to make work that they would be happy to watch and I wouldn’t feel embarrassed to show them. So, as the years go on, this feeling that I’m being watched over by these people that were important to me in the past has gotten stronger and stronger. This also includes actors that I’ve worked with, like Kirin Kiki, or producers that I’ve also worked with that have passed away.

And in a sense, I carry them with me as I make my work. And that is by no means a burden. It’s something that I feel is, organically, a kind of responsibility that I’ve started to take on in my creative process. So, when we look at the two characters in Look Back, Fujino decides that she’s going to continue to make manga with the idea that Kyomoto is there watching her and pushing her along and encouraging her. And in that sense, she’s carrying that legacy with her. That was something that I found truly relatable and was so very moved by.

DEADLINE: In the second half, there’s quite a jolt when the film seems to rewind and Kyomoto takes over the story from Fujino…

KOREEDA: Yeah, that last section when Fujino is thinking about an alternate life, an alternate possibility for how their story could have continued, when I was reading the manga, I definitely was confused for a second: What’s reality and what is a fantasy? And in a sense, it resolves in this kind of transcending of space-time. And I recognized it as a very complex depiction. I knew it would be hard to translate into live action because in manga and in drawing, sure, you can change the style up a little bit, and it’s easier to convey those things. It was definitely a challenge to think about how to distinguish between that reality and fantasy.

DEADLINE: How do you work so quickly? Do you ever take time off? I don’t understand how you made these last two films so quickly, back-to-back.

KOREEDA: So, as I mentioned, with Look Back, I started the project maybe about three years ago. And then as for filming, there are different sequences that go along with different seasons. So winter, spring, summer, fall, and then winter and spring again. We had to film in these sections that matched up with the seasons. And then, in between those shoots, I was shooting Sheep in the Box. They weren’t completely on top of each other, I was shooting in parallel.

But I’ve done that before — with, for instance, Our Little Sister. As we were filming in the different seasons, I was also filming it alongside After the Storm. So, it wasn’t my first time working on two movies in a single year. If anything, I find the process quite healthy because, especially with these two films; one was an original script and the other was an adaptation. So, there are two different approaches, and I found it easy to switch in between the two.

DEADLINE: It follows on neatly from Sheep in the Box, because that also had a slightly fantastical element. Are you taking a new direction in your work?

KOREEDA: No, I wouldn’t say that it’s an intentional thing. It just happens to be that I’ve made a couple of films that have these elements of fantasy.

DEADLINE: What was the reaction to Sheep in the Box in Japan? It was a slight departure for you.

KOREEDA: [Laughs.] As you said, I think that people though it was a little different from the work that I usually make.

DEADLINE: Things threaten to take a very dark turn in Look Back, but you don’t go there. What would a Koreeda horror movie look like?

KOREEDA: Horror film? Is that something you’d like to see?

DEADLINE: I’m just curious. I think you could make something very dark.

KOREEDA: I hope to give it a try someday. When I say horror, I’m thinking more in the vein of Kobayashi Masaki’s Kwaidan (1964). As a child watching television with my mother, in the summertime, they would often air Yotsuya Kaidan, which is a series about ghosts. It’s kind of a thing in Japan. In the summertime, there are these ghost stories, and then in December they would always air this program called Chushingura, which is more of a period piece. So, these are two things that I’m interested in and something that I hope to make films about one day.

DEADLINE: What’s going to be next?

KOREEDA: I’m currently in the process of writing a script, and I can’t say I know where exactly it’s headed. I don’t know if this script is going to become my next film or when I can plan on shooting the film, but I do have a desire to work on another film abroad, in a language that’s not Japanese. And then perhaps after that, I’ll be return to Japan and challenge myself by making a work that engages in history — specifically Japan’s experiences during the war — and try to understand that in a new way myself. These are the two things that I hope to be working on.

title: Elon Musk Documentary Teaser Asks If Billionaire Is the ‘Greatest Living Inventor’ or a ‘Fascist’ Who ‘Has Lost His Mind’
summary: The first teaser trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated Elon Musk documentary “Musk” has been released. The film will world premiere out of competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 8 before continuing to the Toronto International Film Festival. content:
The first teaser trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated Elon Musk documentary “Musk” has been released.

The film will world premiere out of competition at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on Sept. 8 before continuing to the Toronto International Film Festival.

In the 48-second teaser, montages of spacecrafts and astronautical devices fill the screen while voices giving varied commentary about Musk play in the background. The snippet does not give away much about the plot, but illustrates Musk’s polarizing character.

“He’s possibly the greatest living inventor. He is the real-life Iron Man. He is one of the greatest builders of all time,” the background voices say. As the montage progresses, the tone of the statements changes. “He is the greatest capitalist in history. He’s chaotic, random, capricious, manifestly cruel and selfish. He’s a fascist,” the backtrack continues.

Popular on Variety

“Elon is a nuke,” the voice in the teaser concludes as a spacecraft hits the ground and implodes, bursting into flames.

Gibney first revealed in March 2023 that he had begun work on the documentary and was “many months” into production. Musk responded to news of the project on his X/Twitter account by predicting it would be “a hit piece.” Gibney fired back on the same platform, asking “how would you know?”

The film, with a nearly four-hour running time, will feature an original song from Talking Heads frontman David Byrne, who wrote and performed the new track entitled “Let Me Sell You a Dream.”

Gibney directs and produces “Musk,” joined by Jessie Deeter and Erin Edeiken for Jigsaw Productions, Dana O’Keefe for Double Agent, Joey Marra and Zhang Xin for Closer Media and Anonymous Content’s Nick Shumaker and Jessica Grimshaw. Ronan Farrow and Lawrence Wright round out the producing team.
