title: ‘Elsinore’ Director Simon Stone, Basking in Telluride’s Glow, on Making a Movie About Love of the Theater, the Peak AIDS Era, and Being ‘100% in the Service of Andrew Scott’
summary: The Telluride Film Festival casts a wide net, as almost all festivals of its ilk do, but if it has had any speciality that stands out among many, it might be the well-earned tearjerker. There is as much crying at Telluride every year as there isn’t in baseball, but with the festival’s emphasis on top-line […]
content:
The Telluride Film Festival casts a wide net, as almost all festivals of its ilk do, but if it has had any speciality that stands out among many, it might be the well-earned tearjerker. There is as much crying at Telluride every year as there isn’t in baseball, but with the festival’s emphasis on top-line prestige fare, returning patrons look forward to going through some emotional catharsis in the mountains every Labor Day weekend. Among the 2026 lineup, probably no film got passholders any deeper in their feels than “Elsinore,” starring Andrew Scott and directed by Simon Stone. Their remarkable film dramatizes the true-life story of a well-known British actor — Ian Charleson, of “Chariots of Fire” fame — who died at the peak of the AIDS crisis in 1990, but who spent his last months and weeks staying alive long enough to achieve the life goal of playing Hamlet at the National Theatre.

There won’t be a dry eye in the house when this goes wide, as the cliche goes, but there also won’t be an untickled funny bone, given a performance by Scott that’s almost as drolly funny as it is passionate and heartrending (with no small help from writer Stephen Beresford). And there won’t be any un-warmed hearts among any viewers with a deep love for the life of the theater, since the movie serves as a love letter to stagecraft and community, on top of of most obviously being an ode to the seeming indomitability of Charleson as he bravely forestalled his final bow.

Popular on Variety

Stone’s long history as an actor before he became a premier stage director in Australia and then London — before finally moving into film — deeply informs every legit-loving moment of “Elsinore.” Variety spoke with him the day after his new film unspooled in Telluride, where he enjoyed a crowd waiting to give him and Scott yet another ovation in the lobby, some time after the credits rolled. Under his direction, Scott is an instant contender in the best actor face, and Stone may be up for some contending himself.

You told the crowd at the premiere that “Elsinore” was hot off the presses. How recent was it?

We finished on Wednesday of last week, so it’s a week and a half old. It’s very fresh. I think we were very lucky. Focus happened to have a slot that was unoccupied in their fall slate. And I think of course they recognized what Andrew’s doing in the movie is kind of undeniable (for awards consideration), and also that it’s a film that really resonates with audiences. I think that when you’re dealing with studios who still believe in watching movies in the theater, a film like this is like catnip. It’s specially made as an advocate for the theater-going experience. And I think all that catapulted us into a schedule that meant that we had to go fast, because we had to get to here (Telluride). We’re releasing in November, and when we release the movie, it will have been about 10 months from when we shot it. That’s lightning.

I’m not sure of comparable stories about how quickly a film turns around, and that is a testament to the work of everyone who told that story, and how prepared Andrew was. I guess we were all. I’d directed “Hamlet” on stage; Andrew had played Hamlet on stage; I had directed at the National Theatre. We knew all of these environments and this community. When you live that life for a long time, you want to be true to it, so there was an insistence on veracity and honesty that held true.

‘Elsinore’ director Simon Stone at the Telluride Film Festival Chris Willman/Variety

We all probably could have guessed that Andrew had done “Hamlet” on stage.

He had to relearn all the soliloquies, and I dadidn’t know exactly what scenes what bits were from, so I had to remind myself. But I essentially directed that production of “Hamlet” live, and we shot a documentary of me directing it, essentially, but I had an avatar of Johnny Flynn pretending to be me. But nobody knew when they walked into that rehearsal room on those days how it was gonna be staged. I staged it live, the way you would in a rehearsal room. What you’re watching in all of those rehearsal sequences is Andrew genuinely improvising. I mean, he knew his lines, but the idea of how he does it and where he does it, how it… That thing where Johnny (as the director) goes, “Don’t be afraid of intimacy. Hold each other,” those are all lines that I, a minute before we rolled, had fed into Johnny’s ear. Because I direct plays all the time, so I was like, “Well, this is the easiest way of us shooting this — for me to just direct this play.”

What were the other actors in the “Hamlet” scenes told about the story or about what to do?

They knew the backstory because in London, Ian’s story is one of those myths that is really meaningful, and a lot of his friends were in the film. And it’s a love letter to what theater is — it’s right there. They all wanted to do that, and to make it genuine, as opposed to like… You see so many depictions of theater as this over-the-top, self-centered, performative thing, and I wanted to show it as a crucible, as a shelter, as a safe place.

Andrew Scott stars as Ian Charleson, who was dying of AIDS while playing Hamlet, in ELSINORE.

Credit: Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC Anthony Dickenson

There is a scene when Ian starts coming clean about his illness with the rest of the “Hamlet” cast, and a viewer might wonder if, in a scene like that, there will be one token person who seems uncomfortable after learning he has AIDS, but they appear uniformly supportive. It does show what theater buffs hope the inner theater community is really like.

That’s right. I also think the theater community is a group of outsiders. It’s a bunch of freaks and geeks, and the reason we got into it was to share a common humanity, despite not being an average human being. There are a lot of parallels with the gay community at that time, and there is a distinct overlap, obviously. There are a lot of gay kids that ended up in theater because it was a place to express things that they felt that they couldn’t express elsewhere. So I think it’s a kind of rallying cry for acceptance and truth. And when we screened it last night, so many people were so heartfelt in really trying to express how moved they were by having felt seen or having felt someone in their life was seen by this film. That’s worth a million reviews or a million articles. It’s just a single person saying “That meant so much to me,” and I think Ian would feel really happy that that’s his legacy.

You must know what you’ve got on your hands. Did you expect the kind of reaction you’ve gotten in Telluride?

I would never have the hubris to assume that my reaction to something is gonna be someone else’s reaction to something. But I do know that I’ve made it in the spirit of heartfelt positivity about the joy we can find in life in the face of adversity. I think we’re living in a time in history where things feel so insecure geopolitically, socially — so divisive, so much difference. We’re focused on difference all the time in the media or in politics, like what separates us. I knew that people would really appreciate a film which is about no matter how different we are, we have to be together, otherwise all is lost…. The final scene seems like a triumph of an individual, but it’s not. It’s a group of people saying, “You are one of us.” The final scene is a flashback, because by the time you see the final scene, he’s already passed. So what you know is that you’re being let into what might have been his last memory as he disappeared, and it’s a memory of being with a group of people who said “We love you.”

Where do you think we’re at now in terms of people doing stories about “the AIDS era”? In terms of major films, it’s receded a bit.

Well, like all of these things, I think they need to recede. You know, thank God people aren’t making so many World War II movies. Every second movie in the ’50s was about the Second World War, and it had to be, because it was the big reckoning. When I was growing up, most multiplexes had one Second World War film in it at any point. And if you chart the history of Hollywood, you realize that becomes less and less and less and less. And, and there, of course, is the danger because at the end of the day, it was an important kind of reckoning, and it was an important catharsis. Then, of course, people go, “Well, that can’t be the only thing we’re focusing on,” because at a certain point it becomes fetishistic. I do think that that’s the same thing with any cataclysmic event: It needs a real analysis, but then it also needs the catharsis, which is we’ve explored — what it was about us that we got wrong. In the AIDS epidemic, it was very much a marginalization of a group of people that we thought that that was their problem rather than ours. I hope that we have learnt the lesson from that.

I also think that it’s because unless you’re in certain parts of the Third World, you’re not dealing with the idea of fatality if you get an HIV diagnosis. So all of these things mean that it kind of becomes less immediately relevant or immediately urgent. But that doesn’t mean that it doesn’t represent all sorts of lessons that we can learn about ourselves now. And I think that what’s great about this film is that AIDS is a context in the film. It’s a situation. In the same way that Martin’s film (Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine,” also showing in Telluride) is (set) in the ’70s…. The idea of American intervention in overseas political environments, that’s a context. But at the same time, (“Wild Horse Nine”) is a conversation about what happens when arrogant white men think that they can tell other people how to live, and that then suddenly feels relevant to now.

And I think that we found an equivalent thing with this. AIDS is a context, but it’s a conversation about divisiveness in communities, about the endless attempts to separate ourselves from each other and to create taboos in minority communities about what’s acceptable and what’s not acceptable. And I think that this film is is about: stop looking for everything that’s different about you and find something that’s similar. Find the common ground. Ian did that so beautifully in his life.

So I think it’s a very long-winded answer to your question about the relevance of the AIDS movie. But I think that the great triumph is that when “Philadelphia” was made, it had to be the only topic of that film, and we’ve got to a point where it’s one of five strands. And that’s an achievement. That’s a triumph.

Dealing with a terminal illness is closer to universal than not. People die unexpectedly, of course, too, but for the most part…

Yeah facing the end of life is a pretty common thing. The beauty of what he does in the movie is that he looks into the abyss and he finds hope. And weirdly, I was talking to some people where it was like, “Last night I was crying my eyes out, but today I feel really good.” I was like, that’s a common response to people who watch the film, because it’s true catharsis. It’s like a good session with your therapist. It’s like, yeah, it was painful to witness for a second, but at the end of the day, what it gave you was hope, and that’s a great thing to have. Because he faced the end willingly and with beauty, and that grace is extraordinary.

You said it was Andrew’s performance that put Focus into a hurry in wanting to get this out at a premium time this fall. What does his work on this mean to you, as his director?

Well, I mean, Andrew is one of those actors that I think we took for granted for a long time, thinking that he’ll always turn up and he’ll always be amazing. And I think this is one of the first projects where we had to be as amazing as he was — that he wasn’t just in the service of what we were doing. I think we as an industry have done that a lot. We’ve hired him to be in the service of what we need to do, and he’s always turned up, he’s delivered, he’s been brilliant. But this is the first one that’s been really 100% about what can we do to be in the service of you, Andrew, and he deserves the movie in the same way that Ian deserves this portrait of him. And I feel so honored to have kind of been a priest of that temple.

title: MPA Signs Two Lumiere Summit Declarations, Joins Roundtables With Presidents Macron and Lee
summary: The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit on Monday, adding its name alongside those of governments and private sector organizations worldwide to the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation in the Fight Against Film and Audiovisual Piracy. The summit […]
content:
The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit on Monday, adding its name alongside those of governments and private sector organizations worldwide to the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation in the Fight Against Film and Audiovisual Piracy.

The summit was co-chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

MPA chair and CEO Charles Rivkin participated in two separate business roundtables – one with President Lee focused on the industry’s engagement with Korea’s creative sector, and one with President Macron on the future of the industry and opportunities to strengthen ties with France’s creative sector. Both sessions included MPA member studio CEOs.

Popular on Variety

“Our industry is fueled by a simple proposition: audiences love great stories, well told. … From the U.S. to France to Korea and beyond, we each have a stake in ensuring that our industry remains a force for openness, a source of investment, and a driver of jobs, growth, and opportunity. This summit proved a vital forum to translate that common ground into greater cooperation,” Rivkin said.

Emilie Anthonis, president and managing director of the MPA’s Europe, Middle East and Africa region, took part in a session on Korea’s expanding role in the worldwide film and television industry, which also featured President Lee. She also appeared in a session titled “The Race Against Piracy: A Global Challenge,” where she highlighted the work of the MPA and the Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment (ACE) – the world’s leading anti-piracy coalition – in addressing the cross-border scale of content theft. Anthonis welcomed the summit’s recognition that protecting intellectual property and fighting piracy are fundamental to sustaining the creative economy.

The MPA’s member studios are Netflix, Paramount Pictures, Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, Sony Pictures, Universal Studios, The Walt Disney Studios and Warner Bros. Discovery.

title: ‘Look Back’ Review: Once Past the Over- Preciousness of a Child’s World, Hirokazu Kore-eda’s Manga Adaptation Becomes a Moving Tribute to Friendship
summary: There’s barely an adult in sight in Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” where anyone out of school age is marginalized practically to the point of superfluidity. Like much in the first half of this sweet — at times too sweet — adaptation from Tatsuki Fujimoto’s manga of the same title, also made into an animated film […]
content:
There’s barely an adult in sight in Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back,” where anyone out of school age is marginalized practically to the point of superfluidity. Like much in the first half of this sweet — at times too sweet — adaptation from Tatsuki Fujimoto’s manga of the same title, also made into an animated film in 2024, the preciousness of a child’s world can create a barrier for those who don’t automatically melt at the sight of a youngster’s smile. But then, as often happens in Kore-eda’s child-focused body of work, there’s a moment when, unexpectedly, what’s on screen suddenly hits a point of transcendence and resistance falls away. That moment can take a bit of time to come, but the payoff is worth the wait.

Fujino (Furi Nanase) is the undisputed star of fourth grade, encouraged by her teacher Mr. Tamai (Kankuro Kudo) and exalted by her peers for the manga strips she draws and shares at school. She thrives on being the queen, so when impressively advanced manga strips appear in school drawn by Kyomoto (Rokka Okada), a reclusive classmate no one has seen, Fujino is not pleased. In response, she redoubles her efforts, neglecting her friends and family in order to once again be the best.

Popular on Variety

Two years later it’s elementary school graduation time and Mr. Tamai asks Fujino to deliver Kyomoto’s diploma to her home. Though not thrilled with the assignment, she enters the girl’s home, down a corridor piled high with notebooks, looks at the “do not enter” sign and turns away, but not before one of her manga strips gets blown under the door. Just when Fujino leaves, out runs Kyomoto in a tizzy — because she recognizes the girl as the creator of the school’s beloved manga strips, a true master, or “sensei.” This adulation is all Fujino needs to take Kyomoto under her wing, and soon the two are inseparable, collaborating on strips where Fujino writes the stories and draws the figures while Kyomoto does the backgrounds.

Clearly more advanced than the average schoolgirls, the two enter a competition sponsored by the Shueisha publishing house, whose editor (Masaki Suda) recognizes their talents and publishes their first story. Success comes rapidly to the teens, now played by Natsuki Deguchi (Fujino) and Aju Makita (Kyomoto), but their roles remain the same, which suits Fujino just fine. When high school ends the Shueisha editor offers them a series, but Kyomoto wants to go to art school instead. Fujino sees it as a betrayal and determines to be a manga star with or without Kyomoto’s help.

For all of Fujino’s rather full-on sunniness, the truth is she’s a prima donna who lashes out if she doesn’t get her own way. What happens next at first feels like a dreadful narrative misstep, seemingly reinforcing the idea that cutting oneself off from others can save them from life’s travails. Those already familiar with the original manga know better, but so should audiences acquainted with Kore-eda’s humanistic approach to characters: who we are and how we experience the world together, rather than our achievements, is our real saving grace.

As long as audiences accept that this is basically a two-hander, the absence of any other characters with more than stick-figure attributes becomes less problematic. Fujino’s mother exists solely to feed her family and clean house, while Kyomoto’s mother is barely glimpsed — at times it’s difficult to be sure whether the withdrawn girl is real or just a figment of Fujino’s imagination, since for some time that’s the only place she seems to legitimately inhabit.

Sound design is a key element of this world, from the sounds of graphite on paper acting like a musical accompaniment in tandem with Yuta Bandoh’s pleasant score, to the more mechanically produced noise of digital pencils on computer screens. The director’s partiality for seasonal changes is on full display, from brightly colored, sun-tinged summers to autumnal glows and winter’s snowy pleasures. Each season is given major prominence in the children’s world, though why Kore-eda chose a generally pale palette of diffused light isn’t clear. Unless, that is, it’s designed as a contrast to the later saturations of the girls’ more elaborate designs, and the manga animation insert that stirringly helps to bring things to a bittersweet, though deeply satisfying, close.

title: Summer Box Office Breaks All-Time Record With $4.67 Billion
summary: Need proof the movies are really, truly back? The summer box office was already the biggest since COVID upended the industry in 2020 — and now the season has become the highest-grossing of all time. Domestic ticket sales from May 1 through Labor Day on Sept. 7 stand at $4.76 billion, according to Rentrak. Revenues […]
content:
Need proof the movies are really, truly back? The summer box office was already the biggest since COVID upended the industry in 2020 — and now the season has become the highest-grossing of all time. Domestic ticket sales from May 1 through Labor Day on Sept. 7 stand at $4.76 billion, according to Rentrak. Revenues surpassed the long-held record set in 2013 with $4.755 billion, anchored by “Iron Man 3,” “Despicable Me 2” and “Man of Steel.”

This summer’s benchmark comes with two major caveats: Ticket sales from more than a decade ago weren’t adjusted for inflation, and popcorn season was slightly longer (running at 130 days compared to 123 days in 2013) because of Labor Day’s placement on the calendar. Still, it’s a significant milestone because it signals that after five years of uncertainty about the movie business, people have fallen back in love with the silver screen.

While the summer box office record marks an important turning point for movie theaters, the numbers are only part of the story,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “What makes this summer uniquely important and potentially pivotal is that, for many people, it may have been the season that reminded them just how much fun it is to go to the movies. That can inspire future moviegoing, create a new generation of theatergoers and, with so many great films still ahead, keep that momentum going.”

Popular on Variety

This summer is also notable as the first in history where each of the four months generated above $1 billion, with May bringing in $1.07 billion, June powering to $1.08 billion, July earning $1.18 billion and August soaring to $1.27 billion, according to Rentrak. Popcorn season, which runs from early May through Labor Day, is crucial because revenues for those months represent 40% of the annual box office. This summer is only the second since the pandemic in which ticket sales surpassed $4 billion. The first time was in 2023, when “Barbenheimer” fever buoyed grosses to $4.09 billion. In 2019, the last “normal” period at the box office, summer revenues climbed to $4.3 billion, thanks to “Avengers: Endgame” and several other billion-dollar blockbusters. In 2018, popcorn season reached $4.42 billion with “Avengers: Infinity War” and “Incredibles 2” among the highest-grossing movies.

This season, studios succeeded with time-tested franchise sequels like “Toy Story 5” and “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” as well as Gen Z-fueled sleeper hits like “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” Much of the credit for the potential milestone belongs to Sony’s Marvel adventure “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” which has been a behemoth with $923 million domestically and $2.4 billion globally to date. Universal’s Christopher Nolan epic “The Odyssey” also shattered expectations with $589 million in North America and $1.62 billion worldwide. Those triumphs helped offset some major bombs, including Disney’s live-action “Moana,” Warner Bros. and DC’s “Supergirl” and Amazon MGM’s “Masters of the Universe.”

Over Labor Day weekend, Sony’s Marvel juggernaut “Spider-Man: Brand New Home” was No. 1 for the sixth consecutive frame with $23.5 million during the four-day holiday frame. With unprecedented staying power, “Brand New Day” will soon surpass 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” ($936 million, not adjusted for inflation) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the domestic box office. Meanwhile, it’s already the third-biggest release ever globally behind 2009’s “Avatar” ($2.9 billion) and “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.7 billion).

“The Odyssey” secured second place with $17.3 million over the holiday after eight weekends on the big screen. Imax has contributed $486 million globally, representing a massive 30% of the film’s total box office tally.

Third place went to another holdover, “Coyote vs. Acme,” with $15.8 million from 3,727 venues over the four days. With great reviews and positive audience scores, “Looney Tunes” spinoff has been a hit with $38.3 million domestically after two weekends of release. It was originally set at Warner Bros. before the studio shelved the completed film as a $30 million tax write-off. That prompted outrage from the creative community, leading Warner Bros. to allow the filmmaking team to shop “Coyote vs. Acme” around town before selling it to indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment.

Newcomer “By Any Means,” an R-rated thriller from Paramount, stumbled at No. 4 with 9.3 million from 2,903 theaters from Friday to Monday. Directed by Elegance Bratton, “By Any Means” centers around the unlikely partnership between a young Black FBI agent (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) and a notorious mafia hitman (Mark Wahlberg) as they investigate a wave of brutal killings targeting civil rights leaders. It carries a $30 million production budget, funded by Hammerstone Studios.

Two other new holiday releases, Lionsgate’s anxiety-inducing sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and A24’s action thriller “Onslaught,” failed to even crack the top 10.

“Fall 2: Deadpoint” crash-landed at No. 12 with $2.8 million at 1,704 venues over the holiday weekend. Those ticket sales are similar to its predecessor, 2022’s survival thriller “Fall,” which opened to $2.5 million. That film managed to climb to $7.2 million domestically and $18 million globally by the end of its run, becoming a modest success against a mere $3 million budget. The sequel follows two friends who travel to Thailand and get trapped at 4,000 feet after a sudden rockslide.

“Onslaught” fared even worse, debuting in 13th place with $2.2 million from 1,918 theaters through its first four days. Directed by Adam Wingard (“Godzilla vs. Kong”), “Onslaught” stars Adria Arjona as an army sniper who struggles to protect her young daughter from an army of genetically engineered super soldiers.

title: ‘Musk’ Teaser-Trailer: World’s Richest Man Called “Chaotic, Capricious,” “Manifestly Cruel And Selfish” In Damning Alex Gibney Doc
summary: Bleecker Street has released a teaser-trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated documentary Musk, and it’s not a flattering portrait of the SpaceX, Tesla, Starlink honcho and X owner. content:
Bleecker Street has released a teaser-trailer for Alex Gibney’s highly anticipated documentary Musk, and it’s not a flattering portrait of the SpaceX, Tesla, Starlink honcho and X owner.

Yes, the teaser begins with voices of some people heaping praise on Elon Musk – one idolator roaring he’s “the greatest capitalist in history!” But those encomiums are quickly followed by harsher appraisals from Musk observers: “He’s chaotic, random, capricious,” says one. Another offers, “He is manifestly cruel and selfish.” Yet another observes, “In a science fiction novel, he would not be a hero.”

Watch the teaser-trailer above.

Watch on Deadline

‘Musk’ Courtesy Bleecker Street

Gibney’s film, which premieres Tuesday at the Venice Film Festival, clocks in at just under 4 hours. He and Musk have already tangled on the X/Twitter platform, with the mega-billionaire branding him a “douche.” (To which Gibney amusingly retorted, “Douché.”). Leaving epithets aside, what can be said about Gibney is that he is one of documentary’s most respected figures, and the Oscar-winning director of Taxi to the Dark Side, Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Belief, Steve Jobs: The Man in the Machine, Zero Days and many other documentaries.

RELATED: Telluride Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews

It’s perhaps worth noting that Gibney enjoys the backing of a multi-billionaire too – Wendy Schmidt, who bought a controlling interest in Gibney’s production company, Jigsaw Productions in 2025.

After Venice, Musk heads to the Toronto Film Festival. Bleecker Street plans to release it theatrically on October 16, with HBO debuting the film on premium cable and the HBO Max streaming platform after that. The documentary is expected to make a strong bid for Academy Award recognition.

RELATED: Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews

In 2024, Gibney appeared on Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast and gave us something of a preview of the film.

Director Alex Gibney Courtesy of DOC NYC

“He is a larger-than-life figure,” he said of Musk. “People have their opinions about him, but I think the challenge… is to bring something that people don’t expect to find, something in the material that’s hiding, some stuff that’s hiding in plain sight, which is what I’d say we are finding that I think will be surprising for folks. And it’s not just like, is it Elon thumbs up or Elon thumbs down? I’m not really interested in that kind of formula, douche or not. But it’s more like, what do we really think about how he operates? And I’m pretty confident that what we’re coming up with will be illuminating and also kind of formally innovative. We’re really going to have fun with this.”

Watch the teaser-trailer for Musk above.

title: MPA Signs Two Declarations At Lumière Summit, Attends Roundtables With Macron & Lee Jae Myung
summary: The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit, aimed at deepening international collaboration and investment in audiovisual sector, protecting intellectual property and strengthening the creative economy. The MPA joined government and private sector partners in signing the Lumiere Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation […]
content:
The Motion Picture Association signed two declarations at the Lumière Summit, aimed at deepening international collaboration and investment in audiovisual sector, protecting intellectual property and strengthening the creative economy.

The MPA joined government and private sector partners in signing the Lumiere Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image and the Declaration on Strengthened International Cooperation in the Fight Against Film and Audiovisual Piracy at the conclusion of the Summit.

MPA Chairman and CEO Charlies Rivkin also attended roundtables with Summit co-chairs, French President Emmanuel Macron and South Korean President Lee Jae Myung.

Rivkin joined President Lee and MPA member CEOs for a business roundtable focused on the industry’s commitment to partnering with Korea’s creative sector. He also participated alongside MPA member CEOs in a separate business roundtable with President Macron on the future of the industry and opportunities to deepen collaboration with France’s creative sector.

Watch on Deadline

“Our industry is fueled by a simple proposition: audiences love great stories, well told. The Lumière Summit was an opportunity to write the next chapter for a creative sector that empowers creators, protects consumers, and connects audiences around the world,” said Rivkin. “From the U.S. to France to Korea and beyond, we each have a stake in ensuring that our industry remains a force for openness, a source of investment, and a driver of jobs, growth, and opportunity. This Summit proved a vital forum to translate that common ground into greater cooperation.”

title: The Business of Lucy Darling: How Carisa Hendrix Went From Performing At Haunted Houses To Touring Globally As Her Old Hollywood-Inspired Character – Comedy Means Business Podcast
summary: Carisa Hendrix, the Canadian-born comedian, magician and variety artist, has a business mind as unusual as her career origin story. It’s a story that took Hendrix from performing at haunted houses for $50 a night as a teenager to building a global touring business around Lucy Darling, an original character she introduced at the Melbourne […]
content:
Carisa Hendrix, the Canadian-born comedian, magician and variety artist, has a business mind as unusual as her career origin story.

It’s a story that took Hendrix from performing at haunted houses for $50 a night as a teenager to building a global touring business around Lucy Darling, an original character she introduced at the Melbourne Magic Festival in 2017.

Inspired by the Old Hollywood bon vivants Hendrix grew up admiring —Zsa Zsa Gabor, among them — Lucy is a wickedly sharp and glamorous 1940s socialite whose shows blend crowd work, magic and vaudevillian stunts. Already this year, Hendrix has sold hundreds of thousands of tickets as she concurrently tours six different shows revolving around the character.

Hendrix came to performing through arts programs for at-risk youth, where she acquired an eclectic set of skills — from stilt-walking and balloon artistry to fire-eating and sleight of hand — initially with no greater ambition than “to not starve to death.” She imagined performing as something she could do on the side while pursuing a career in education, thinking that it would be “just be a cute thing I did in my teens.”

Watch on Deadline

But after years of teaching and working in youth programs, a conversation about her five-year plan forced Hendrix to acknowledge how deeply she’d fallen in love with performing — and that she could no longer treat it as a hobby.

After leaving teaching, Hendrix launched the entertainment agency Ballyhoo Entertainment, as a means of booking herself and other performers for corporate events. And the company quickly grew. But in the summer of 2017, Hendrix put its broader booking business on hold to focus on a character she had created as a lark: Lucy Darling.

The response in Melbourne was strong enough that Hendrix decided to give Lucy a year on the road as an experiment — and nearly a decade later, she’s still living out of a suitcase. A testament to the character’s unique appeal came in 2024, when one of Hendrix’s crowd work clips as Darling went viral with some 21 million views.

While WME has worked with Hendrix to scale her touring business, she’s overseen most of the machinery herself from the very beginning, from creative and production infrastructure to routing and ticket pricing. She even built her own ticketing algorithm to determine where Lucy’s audience was and what size venues would make sense to headline in different markets.

When data suggested that Lucy could go from playing to audiences in the hundreds to theaters with a capacity in the thousands, Hendrix put her own money behind the theory to get promoters behind her, absorbing tens of thousands of dollars in expenses to book venues in the Pacific Northwest through four-wall rental arrangements. It was a nerve-wracking decision, but Hendrix needn’t have worried, as she was able to begin moving large quantities of tickets almost immediately when they went on sale.

Hendrix breaks down the story in full today on Comedy Means Business, unveiling the business mechanics behind her rapid rise. Explaining the community values behind the Lucy Darling experience, which she says has become something like a themed party, she also talks finding “green flags” in collaborators and business partners, the wild experience that is the Las Vegas residency, and much more.

Check out the full episode by clicking above.

title: 20th Century’s ‘Whalefall’ Producers Reflect On Shooting In California: “The Best Creative Teams Are Here”
summary: In a time when many film and television productions shoot in other states or countries despite having their roots of development in Hollywood, 20th Century Studios has taken a big swing with its upcoming feature Whalefall, which arrives in theaters October 16. Starring Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily […]
content:
In a time when many film and television productions shoot in other states or countries despite having their roots of development in Hollywood, 20th Century Studios has taken a big swing with its upcoming feature Whalefall, which arrives in theaters October 16.

Starring Austin Abrams, Josh Brolin, Elisabeth Shue, John Ortiz, Jane Levy and Emily Rudd, the film adaptation of Daniel Kraus’ book shot in a couple California locations — from Monterey to San Pedro — before finishing up at Radford Studios, where Deadline visited set during production last September.

Executive producer Doug Merrifield, whose credits stretch from 2023’s Candy Cane Lane and The Shallows (2016) all the way back to associate producer on 1993’s Free Willy, revealed that he compared schedules and budgets in both California and Louisiana as shooting locations side by side before production began.

Watch on Deadline

“On paper, Louisiana was a little cheaper — six figures cheaper, not seven figures cheaper — but at the end of the day, we were able to convince 20th Century that the best creative teams are here for this kind of picture,” Merrifield told Deadline a little over a year ago. “To their credit, even though it was a little more expensive to make the movie in California, they agreed to do that.”

Merrifeld added that — at the end of the day —should the film have shot in New Orleans, the cost comparison would have been a wash if not more expensive, once specialists were brought in.

RELATED: California Lawmakers Officially Carve Out Compromises For Film Industry On Corporate Tax Credit Cap

“We had the ratio between the cost above the line, below the line, and then visual effects with Guillaume [Rocheron]. In California, you don’t get an incentive on above the line, but we had enough in post and visual effects to offset the loss of what we didn’t get from above the line,” Merrifield continued.

The visual effects, set design and other “specialty skills” in Merrifield’s words were important in a story with a premise like Whalefall’s, where Austin Abrams’ character spends an hour in a whale’s stomach after diving deep in the ocean looking for his father’s (Josh Brolin) remains. Said whale stomach models were built by the Wētā Workshop in New Zealand, but the head, throat, esophagus and larynx were constructed in California because they were too big to ship to set in time. The 12-foot-tall 18-foot-long whale head was manufactured by StudioArt & Technology.

“It’s so unfortunately rare to have the opportunity to shoot here, that when people know that a movie’s shooting in L.A., that is their first choice,” said producer on the Imagine Entertainment side of things, Allen Mendelbaum. “They can come home at night, see their families and everything. Why not? I think we’re really punching above our weight in this movie, because the crew is as good as it gets.”

RELATED: California Lawmakers Officially Secure $750M Annually For Film & TV Tax Credit Program With Final Budget Vote

For 50 days — which later turned into 62 — of filming, with a cast of 11 and a crew of 180 plus 409 background players, the film received nearly $11 million in tax credits on $50M total qualified expenditures. For the crew members living in the valley, including director Brian Duffield, production at Radford Studios was a huge plus, especially with stacked stage levels for easy access when shifting between shooting environments like the tank that simulates the ocean Jay (Abrams) dives in and then the whale’s head, throat and stomach, where he spends most of his time in the story.

“We originally were looking at L.A. Center, which was sort of a split [geographically]. [Radford] made us a great deal. And the fact that we had all these four stages [during production.] The tank [was] on 17, we had all the [whale] stomachs on 16, and then we had our special lead throat, and the 360 rigs on 12 across the way,” Merrifield said. “We were fortunate that it is at this time we were able to make such a good deal. But unfortunately, it is because it’s so slow right now.”

Whalefall benefited from a $330 million round of funding that preceded the newly approved expansion of the California Film & TV Tax Credit program, which included a total of $750 million in incentive funding.

RELATED: ‘The Pitt’ S3, Kimmel EP’d Game Show, ‘High Potential’ S3, & ‘Stewie’ Score California Tax Credits

“I’ve seen, where it’s started [to] already help the increase to television. For features. ultimately, if we want more feature work here, we’re going to have to have some sort of ATL (above the line) incentive credit, which you don’t get here right now. So if you have a big above the line, it doesn’t make sense to shoot here,” Merrifield who worked on the Free Willy films in Mexico City, shared.

With a smaller cast, Whalefall could make production in California work, but for other major projects with heavy-hitting stars attached, above-the-line costs are a different story.

“Things take time to trickle down, but I think in a year, we’ll have a much better idea how the new, increased incentive here has helped, not only television, but I’m hoping, in features,” Merrifield added.

RELATED: Big Money! Jobs! Newsom Boasts Big Bucks Film/TV Tax Credits “Delivering Results”; Eddie Murphy’s ‘Donkey,’ Disney & Ben Affleck Flicks Get Incentives

California is currently in the middle of both film and television application cycles for the state’s tax credit program. Applications close in September for feature films and independent productions, while the window for television series runs into October. Though production in California remains low, several other projects that have benefited from the California Film Commission’s incentive will release this fall alongside Whalefall.

On the anniversary of the program’s funding rising to $750 million in July, projects like Ben Affleck’s upcoming Gingerbread Men produced with Matt Damon and their Artists Equity banner as well as Disney’s Hexed coming this fall were among 41 films that received $187 million in incentives over the summer.

Recent developments around efforts to shift production back to the heart of Hollywood have involved a 35% incentive for postproduction to move to the Golden State. President Donald Trump has also voiced vague intentions to back a federal film and tv tax credit as well.

Last July, the California Film Commission allocated its $40 million of funding since the increase went into play to Dan Fogelman ($20.8M) and Ryan Murphy ($17.9M) for their upcoming television projects. Mid-March 2026, The Pitt, High Potential and Season 2 of Bill Lawrence’s Rooster comedy were among 14 small-screen projects to receive tax credits.

RELATED: California Lawmakers Introduce Compromise For Film Industry On Corporate Tax Credit Cap

December 2024’s round of distributed funding, which totaled to $108.6 million awarded to 10 film and TV projects including Whalefall, also saw Season 2 of Bill Lawrence’s Bad Monkey, which returns this December, get part of that funding for 93 filming days in California with the production generating $82 million in qualified expenditures and employing 460 cast and crew members and 4,290 background performers.

Whalefall joins such big studio projects shooting in Callifornia as the multi-Oscar winning Paul Thomas Anderson $140M feature production, One Battle After Another, Netflix’s The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth (which had $105.9M in qualified tax expenditures), as well as this year’s 13 Going on 30 reboot at Netflix ($10.9M for $31.2M in qualified expenditures) and the It Follows (2014) sequel They Follow ( $7M for $20M in qualified expenditures).

Last April, 38 features were given California state credits. Back in October 2025, there were over 50 films approved for such tax incentives including Amazon MGM Studios’ Heat 2 ($104.1M in qualified expenditures) and the upcoming Jumanji: Open World sequel ($161.5M in qualified expenditures).

title: Venice Film Festival 2026: Read All Of Deadline’s Reviews
summary: The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John […]
content:
The 2026 Venice Film Festival got underway on Wednesday, September 2, with Oscar-winning English director Danny Boyle’s Ink — starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy — kicking off an 83rd edition that includes films starring the likes of Robert Pattinson, Penelope Cruz & Javier Bardem, Jack Huston & Sofia Boutella, Dakota Johnson, John Malkovich & Sam Rockwell, Alicia Vikander & Susan Sarandon, Nick Nolte and Kate & Rooney Mara in their first movie together.

Along with Ink, this year’s competition lineup includes such buzzy titles seeking awards-season glory as Florian Zeller’s Bunker, Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love, Andrea Pallaoro’s The Echo Chamber, Casey Affleck’s Company and Warner Herzog’s Bucking Fastard.

Studio titles largely are absent this year, but the overall lineup also includes new films by Luca Guadagnino, Paul Schrader and Wim Wenders along with Laura Poitras’ short about ICE protests in Minnesota, and Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace’s doc on the comeback of rock band Oasis.

Watch on Deadline

Check out Deadline’s reviews out of Venice, and keep checking back as we add more. Click on each headline to read our full review.

‘The Basics of Philosophy’ Noora Films

Section: Out of Competition

Director: Paul Schrader

Cast: Jack Huston, Sofia Boutella, Daniel Zovalto, Bill Pullman, Dana Delany, Shiloh Fernandez, Karl Glusman, Elizabeth Petruso, Santiago Cabrera, Trevor Dolden, Richard Gere

Deadline’s takeaway: With this introspective character study, Schrader continues to making the kind of grownup films we rarely get to see anymore, outside of Europe at least. He never presents easy answers in his movies — same with this deep dive into the philosophy of life and the key question we can ask of many Schrader characters, “Can we change?” — PH

‘Bucking Fastard’ Lena Herzog

Section: Competition

Director-screenwriter: Werner Herzog

Cast: Kate Mara, Rooney Mara, Orlando Bloom, Domhnall Gleeson

Deadline’s takeaway: Although it appears to start with a tone of gentle mockery, there’s something quite sweet and generous at work beneath the stylized strangeness of the tale of two sisters played by Rooney and Kate Mara, a tone that Werner Herzog has never really struck before in his fiction work, with the possible exception of 2019’s Family Romance LLC. — DW

Section: Venice Open – Out Of Competition

Director: Barthélémy Grossmann

Cast: Kiefer Sutherland, Ever Anderson, Al Pacino, Michael Rispoli

Deadline’s takeaway: Amazingly, Al Pacino is about the only thing that isn’t over the top here, generously giving center stage to Kiefer Sutherland in a role that’s fun, unbelievable — and sometimes unbelievably funny. Is it any good? Who knows. It’s certainly the most balls-out, no-f*cks-given rock ’n’ roll phenomenon to hit the Lido this year — DW

‘The Girl with the Leica’ Manuel Alberto Claro

Section: Orizzonti

Director: Alina Marazzi

Cast: Emilia Schüle, Aaron Altaras, Luna Wedler, Lucas Englander, Thomas Schubert, Sebastian Schneider, Idan Weiss, Lia von Blarer, Hans-Christian Hegewald, Jeremy Mockridge, Joel Basman

Deadline’s takeaway: The jazzed-up, unconventional biopic of the late photojournalist Gerda Taro asks questions about the the fine line between bravery and ego in the process of bringing back dispatches from the front line, but its structure over-complicates a simple yet quite profound meditation on an artist’s identity and legacy. — DW

‘Ink’ Netflix

Section: Competition

Director: Danny Boyle

Cast: Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce, Claire Foy, Jonathan Hyde, Lucy Russell, Abigail Amin, Bertie Carvel, Brian Gleeson, Christopher Fulford, Patrick Kennedy, Blake Harrison, Georgie Henley

Deadline’s takeaway: Danny Boyle with his whip-smart, in-your-face stye is the perfect filmmaker to bring this world set in 1969 London to life as the brash if trash visionary Rupert Murdoch and his hand-picked editor-in-chief launch what would become a new era of tabloid journalism, changing the media world for better or worse in the process. Here all the cylinders are firing, and it is thrilling stuff indeed. — PH

Section: Venice Open – Out of Competition

Directors: Dylan Southern, Will Lovelace

With: Liam Gallagher, Noah Gallagher

Deadline’s takeaway: The great mystery about why Noel and Liam Gallagher put aside their differences for a heavily promoted multimillion-dollar world stadium tour is never really addressed in this more-than-feature-length documentary. Instead, the directors look at what came out of it for the estranged brothers, offering an insider’s view one of the most crazily oversubscribed reunion tours of all time. — DW

Section: Competition

Director: Lee Chang-dong

Cast: Jeon Do-Yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-Jeung

Deadline’s takeaway: As you might expect from this master filmmaker, the story takes time to develop, and at nearly three hours it takes a little too long here. But the cast of top South Korean actors here is well chosen, and they deliver Lee Chang-dong’s vision on the screen in this handsomely filmed and pertinent film. — PH

‘Primetime’ A24

Section: Competition

Director: Lance Oppenheim

Cast: Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever, Skyler Gisondo, Phoebe Bridgers, Anna Faris

Deadline’s takeaway: Primetime is a film about the way populism fuels moral decadence — but in such a subtle way that its proponents don’t realize it. They usually do, however, when what goes around comes around, which is very much the moral of the story here. Delivering a performance described as a mixture of Jerry Maguire and Count Dracula, Robert Pattinson may finally be entering the Christian Bale period of his career. — DW

‘The Spiral’ Venice Film Festival

Section: Competition

Director: Paolo Strippoli

Cast: Jasmine Trinca, Romana Maggiora Vergano, Adriano Giannini, Valeria Bruni Tedeschi

Deadline’s takeaway: Does Paolo Strippoli’s unashamedly commercial horror-thriller reinvent the wheel? No, it doesn’t. But instead of lecturing us about the parlous state of the world today, he is happy to give us a grand guignol morality play that tells us not so much that we’re doomed but reminds us that it’s the things that we might yet do that may throw our lives off-track. — DW



‘Wild Horse Nine’ Searchlight Pictures

Section: Competition

Director: Martin McDonagh

Cast: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi, Mariana di Girolamo, Ailín Salas, Tom Waits, Parker Posey

Deadline’s takeaway: John Malkovich gives a career performance in a perfect if unexpected casting. This so-called “buddy movie” of a wildly different stripe easily is one of the year’s best films, and in its own peculiar way the most spiritual. Martin McDonagh now is 5-for-5 as a writer-director. — PH

title: French President Emmanuel Macron Calls on YouTube to Finance Content and Warns of Growing Threat to Cultural Model (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: French President Emmanuel Macron said the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, which he co-chaired with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Monday, was deliberately held at a moment of dramatic upheaval for the entertainment business, from the growing dominance of YouTube and TikTok to AI and media consolidation. Speaking to Variety at the event, he […]
content:
French President Emmanuel Macron said the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, which he co-chaired with South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Monday, was deliberately held at a moment of dramatic upheaval for the entertainment business, from the growing dominance of YouTube and TikTok to AI and media consolidation.

Speaking to Variety at the event, he pointed to the growing power of YouTube, TikTok and other social platforms as one of the reasons the timing was right for the landmark gathering devoted to the future of cinema and the moving image.

“YouTube is very efficient. It’s de facto the default platform in a lot of countries for a lot of people. And it’s quite clear that today they divert a lot of people from these platforms or the big channels where a lot of money is invested in creation,” said Macron at the Fondation Maeght, a French art foundation showcasing works of art from Georges Braque to Joan Miró, nestled amid a luxuriant forest.

Popular on Variety

French President Emmanuel Macron on the growing global reach of YouTube: pic.twitter.com/NM9yWRf6i3 — Variety (@Variety) September 7, 2026

He argued that YouTube, which is currently outtalking Netflix in over 20 international markets, should increasingly be brought into the same ecosystem as other global platforms such as Netflix, Amazon and Disney, that have been required to invest in local production.

France and other countries need to “engage with them” in a multilateral way, he said, to try to change the platform’s approach so that it helps finance “local content,” while supporting “more creativity, more creations, more respect of the authors.”

Macron, who’s been a driving force behind the rise of French AI companies, including Mistral, as well as the creation of the EU’s AI Act and the international summit on AI that was held last year, also said France wanted to compete aggressively in AI by expanding computing capacity, data centers and European models. But he insisted that technological ambition must be accompanied by protections for intellectual property and much greater transparency.

Asked about his discussions about EU regulations with companies such as Google or OpenAI, Macron said that while France is eager to compete in the AI race, it’s also pushing for greater transparency and protections for creators in Europe.

“When you have content produced by AI, you just have to know it. So transparency for us is key,” he said. “We want to flag when the content is produced with AI. Because we think it’s fair.”

Without that, Macron warned, AI could “totally transform the relationship to truth,” feeding distrust not only in creative content but in science and democracy.

Macron also addressed the increasing consolidation of the entertainment business and his discussions surrounding the greenlighting of the Paramount-Warner Bros. deal by the EU regulators. He said he didn’t have an active role in lobbying for the merger, but admitted that he supported “the commitments made to invest more in Europe and to create more content and to provide guarantees and commitments vis-à-vis our theaters.” Paramount Skydance boss David Ellison traveled to Paris (as well as London and Germany) in January and met with Macron, among other high-level political and industry figures.

The French President described the merger case as fundamentally “a U.S. M&A story,” saying his priority was ensuring that a major company like Paramount Skydance maintained a strong footprint in France and Europe. While Ellison wasn’t present at the Lumiere Summit, Paramount Skydance’s Andy Gordon was there and sat at Macron’s table at lunch, alongside The Walt Disney Company’s Dana Walden, Netflix’s Ted Sarandos, NBCUniversal Entertainment’s Donna Langley, Mediawan’s Pierre-Antoine Capton and Sony’s Tom Rothman, among others.

“What is important to us is to make sure that you will still finance creation, that you will still work with us, that you will still make more movies in France and in Europe,” he said.

The Summit is also being held on the last stretch of his second mandate as he is due to leave office in May. With the far-right and far-left parties dominating polls ahead of the next presidential election, the French film and TV industry has shared deep concerns over the future of France’s prized cultural model that could come under threat.

Asked what would survive beyond 2027, Macron pointed first to France’s international tax credit for international movies and TV series, which was recently strengthened with the inclusion of above-the-line costs and has helped draw a growing number of major U.S. and international productions to the country.

“We improved tax credits, international tax credits. If somebody wants to withdraw this tax credit, it will just kill the industry and a lot of opportunities,” said Macron, who had told Variety in a cover interview in 2024 that he would fight for “Emily in Paris” Season 5 to remain in the French capital, prompting a comedic feud with the Rome mayor. Besides the sixth and final season of “Emily in Paris,” “The White Lotus” season 4 is also currently shooting in France.

He also pointed to the investment made during his presidency in studios and production infrastructure as part of his France 2030 plan, which he said has turned France into a leading international shooting destination.

“We want more of them to make new movies in our country. Why? Because it’s good for our ecosystem,” he said. “It will hire a lot of technicians and actors and so on. It will show our landscapes, and it will create jobs during the movie is made and it will attract a lot of people in our landscapes and our cities and so on.”

Yet, Macron suggested the bigger battle after his departure could be over the foundations of France’s cultural policy itself.

“Some extremes are fighting very hard against the CNC (National Film Board) and what we call this exception culturelle and the DNA of the French model,” Macron said. France’s system, developed over decades, uses levies on cinema admissions that are collected by the National Film Board and re-injected into local production, alongside other schemes supporting independent producers, filmmakers and theaters.

“We have to be ready to resist because this model has been created during decades by a lot of artists, by the state and the different governments and it’s extremely important,” he said.

Ultimately, Macron tied the defense of the French model not only to jobs and filmmaking but also to the country’s soft power.

“Culture and art is part of what France is, but it’s part as well of our soft power outside,” he said. “Recognizing that art is an exception which requires specific investment of the government, diversity of people, players, authors, protection of their rights and a specific effort in terms of multilateralism is crucial.”

title: Macklemore Says His Call to ‘Free Palestine’ Is Not a ‘Criticism’ of Jewish People: ‘None of Us Will Be Free Until We Are All Free’
summary: Macklemore is speaking out about his call to “Free Palestine,” which the rapper made while opening for Ed Sheeran on Friday night at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. “To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you,” Macklemore said on […]
content:
Macklemore is speaking out about his call to “Free Palestine,” which the rapper made while opening for Ed Sheeran on Friday night at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium.

“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters: criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you,” Macklemore said on Saturday night (via Newsweek). “My message is for peace; love for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect, and equality.”

He added, “So I say free Palestine, I say free Lebanon, I say free Cuba, I say free Congo, free Sudan, I say free all people in America living in fear of this terrorist organization, ICE. None of us will be free until we are all free.”

Popular on Variety

During his Friday night set, Macklemore told the audience that he wanted the people in Gaza and the West Bank to know that he had not forgotten them: “I believe that every human being walking on this earth deserves exactly the same freedom.” The statement caused the Israeli American Council to release a petition that demands that the four-time Grammy winner be removed from the rest of Sheeran’s Loop tour.

The petition reads, “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

title: ‘No Paradise If You Are Killed by a Woman’ Review: Iraq’s Oscar Submission Offers a Patriotic Anthem to the Kurdish Peshmerga’s Fight Against Islamic State
summary: The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impressive drama about a resourceful female Peshmerga sniper. Although selected as Iraq’s submission for the Best International Feature Oscar, the third fiction feature from Norwegian-Kurdish helmer Halkawt Mustafa (“Red […]
content:
The trope of the lone action hero with near-superhuman strength gets a gender switch in “No Paradise If You Are Killed By A Woman,” a visually impressive drama about a resourceful female Peshmerga sniper. Although selected as Iraq’s submission for the Best International Feature Oscar, the third fiction feature from Norwegian-Kurdish helmer Halkawt Mustafa (“Red Heart,” “El Clásico”) may fall between two stools for Western viewers: There’s not enough action for genre fans and the narrative’s blend of melodrama and earnestness may turn off highbrow arthouse viewers. But it’s a different story in MENA territories where Sony/Empire has already nabbed distribution rights. Regional and Kurdish diaspora audiences should appreciate the strong visual and technical craftmanship used in this harrowing tale.

The narrative centers on Vyan (striking London-based Kurdish thesp Avan Jamal, impressive), a 24-year-old Kurdish émigré to Norway who is visiting Iraqi Kurdistan with her parents and younger sister Helin in 2014, when Islamic State (IS) launches an attack. Their parents are murdered and Vyan and Helin are sold as IS sex slaves. Ever resilient, Vyan manages to kill the man who bought her and make her way to Peshmerga territory. There, she joins an elite unit of female fighters as a sniper.

Popular on Variety

As Vyan’s poetic voiceover narration states, Peshmerga means “before death” and its fighters enter combat out of strength, not out of fear. Certainly, Vyan is fearless. She reckons that she has killed more than 100 of the enemy in three years. Given that, as the title notes, IS fighters believe that there is “No Paradise If You Are Killed by A Woman,” it’s no wonder they have placed a million-dollar bounty on her head.

After heroically preventing an IS suicide truck bomber in an armored vehicle from attacking her unit’s base, the heavily wounded Vyan returns to Norway to recover. There, a government official (Thorbjørn Harr) offers her a difficult choice: accept a new identity and government protection (they fear the fact that she is an IS target could endanger other Norwegian citizens) or be prosecuted for fighting for another country. Luckily, Norwegian civilians don’t have to worry. A phone call to the family’s old landline confirms that Helin remains trapped in Mosul, in the clutches of an IS fighter known as the Swedish sniper. Loyal Vyan prepares for what may be her final mission: to singlehandedly rescue her sister.

The last half of the film feels as if it could easily be adapted into a tense video game as it follows Vyan silently creeping through tunnels and crawling through the aftermath of IS carnage. It certainly gives a more detailed picture of how a sniper operates, and the lonely patience required for the job, than Clint Eastwood’s “American Sniper” ever did. Vyan uses logic and the help of friendly Kurdish commander from the Iraqi government forces in Mosul to locate the IS snipers preventing civilians from leaving the devastated city.

Research for multi-hyphenate Mustafa’s 2015 TV project “The Women ISIS Fears” and his time as a war photographer seeing strong female fighters inspired “No Paradise,” which he dedicates to his daughters. Like the helmer’s previous features, it proudly incorporates Kurdish customs and traditions, from the “singing” that Vyan’s rifle performs to the traditional tunes sung by her Peshmerga captain and the Kurdish commander in Mosul.

Highlights of a polished technical package include the prowling camerawork of Norwegian DP John Erling H. Fredriksen and the film’s use of actual Mosul locations. The shocking ruins of what was once a thriving population center attest to a brutal military campaign to liberate the ancient city from IS. Also worthy of special mention in a film where the main character spends much of her time in silence is the tension-building sound design by Mattias Eklund and Jan Kasskawo.

title: Andrew Garfield Hopes ‘The Uprising’ Makes Billionaires “Scared Sh*tless”: “They’re The Most Soul Sick”
summary: As Andrew Garfield portrays the ultimate folk hero in The Uprising, he hopes it serves as a warning for the kings of our time. The 2x Oscar nominee, whose character Ploughman is inspired by the legend of Robin Hood in Paul Greengrass-helmed film, noted that billionaires should be “scared shitless” by the movie that premieres […]
content:
As Andrew Garfield portrays the ultimate folk hero in The Uprising, he hopes it serves as a warning for the kings of our time.

The 2x Oscar nominee, whose character Ploughman is inspired by the legend of Robin Hood in Paul Greengrass-helmed film, noted that billionaires should be “scared shitless” by the movie that premieres Sept. 10 in the United States.

“Well first, I hope they come and see it, for first thing,” said Garfield of his hope for audiences at a recent screening. “But secondly, I hope it’s galvanizing. I hope there’s some awakening that people feel, that they feel that their own, that we all feel like our own struggles are being reflected in the struggles of these characters from a distant time and place, and that it could be directive. And I hope that if any billionaires watch it, they’re scared shitless.”

Later in the Q&A, the moderator quoted one line in the movie, “There will be no peace until we are healed.” Greengrass considers that phrase “true of today as it is 600 years ago, for sure.”

Watch on Deadline

Garfield added, “I’m going to include the billionaires in that as well, because they’re the ones that might be the most soul sick. They’re the ones that might need the healing the most in a way.”

Written and directed by Greengrass, The Uprising is a retelling of the true events that inspired the legend of Robin Hood, starring Garfield as a farmer in 1831 England, who leads a rebellion against King Richard II (Woody Norman) over a brutal tax, in the wake of a devastating plague.

Malik Elassal, who stars as Samir in the Queens-set Gen Z sitcom, nominated NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani to make a cameo, noting “I feel like we could make this happen” to get the Democratic Socialist politician in a future episode.

Watch on Deadline

In Adults, a group of five 20-somethings in New York City attempt to master adulthood while sharing their friend Samir’s (Elassal) family home in Queens, which he has to himself. The show also stars Lucy Freyer, Owen Thiele, Amita Rao and Jack Innanen.

title: Macklemore Emphasizes “Free Palestine” Pleas Are “In No Way A Criticism” Of Jewish People: “My Message Is For Peace”
summary: Macklemore is making his stance clear as he doubles down on his onstage “Free Palestine” pleas during Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour. While opening for night two of Sheeran’s New Jersey stop at MetLife Stadium on Saturday, the 4x Grammy winner responded to the outcry around his onstage words the night before, emphasizing that his support […]
content:
Macklemore is making his stance clear as he doubles down on his onstage “Free Palestine” pleas during Ed Sheeran‘s Loop Tour.

While opening for night two of Sheeran’s New Jersey stop at MetLife Stadium on Saturday, the 4x Grammy winner responded to the outcry around his onstage words the night before, emphasizing that his support for Palestinians is “in no way a criticism” of Jewish people.

“To all of my Jewish brothers and sisters; criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, in no way is a criticism of you,” he said on stage. “My message is for peace, love, for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.

Introducing his pro-Palestine protest song “Hind’s Hall”, Macklemore continued, “So, I say Free Palestine, I say free Lebanon, I say free Cuba, I say free Congo, I say free Sudan, free all people in America living in fear over this terrorist organization ICE. None of us will be free until we all are free.”

Watch on Deadline

“Wanting all humans to be treated equal should never be controversial,” wrote Macklemore with the video on Instagram.

The post comes after the Israeli-American Council started a petition urging Sheeran to “remove Macklemore” from the remainder of the tour.

“This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event,” the petition reads. “The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.”

Macklemore wrote his 2024 protest anthem “Hind’s Hall” in support of pro-Palestinian protests on college campuses, named for Columbia students’ renaming of academic building Hamilton Hall to Hind’s Hall, in honor of 5-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who was killed in the Gaza Strip by IDF forces.

title: Space Force Uniform Is Inspired By Quasi-Satirical Film ‘Starship Troopers’
summary: Among a flurry of posts this weekend, Donald Trump revealed the service dress uniform designs for his Space Force. Without additional comment, the president shared photos and an overview of the uniforms on Truth Social, which include in their color palette “space gray” and “midnight black” as well as knee high leather boots and snazzy […]
content:
Among a flurry of posts this weekend, Donald Trump revealed the service dress uniform designs for his Space Force.

Without additional comment, the president shared photos and an overview of the uniforms on Truth Social, which include in their color palette “space gray” and “midnight black” as well as knee high leather boots and snazzy epaulettes. The overview indicated the ensemble was “inspired by the discipline and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform.”

The admission is a bit of a shocker, not just because Trump loves winners and the critically-panned 1997 Paul Verhoeven film was a flop, but also because it was a satire of fascism. In his review at the time, Roger Ebert noted the picture’s “quasi-fascist militarism,” while admitting that those aspects were leavened a bit by “an element of sly satire.” But, for Ebert, that was not enough. “We smile at the satirical asides, but where’s the warmth of human nature? The spark of genius or rebellion? If Star Wars is humanist, Starship Troopers is totalitarian.”

As for the costumes themselves, Ebert was only slightly less critical. He calls them “a cross between Buck Rogers and the Archie comic books.”

Watch on Deadline

Trump has seemingly drawn inspiration from movies and television before for his newest branch of the United States Armed Forces, which he created in 2019. When the president unveiled the logo, science fiction fans almost immediately called out the similarity to that worn by Captain Kirk and other Starfleet officers in Gene Roddenberry’s enduring, space faring sci-fi franchise. Star Trek legend George Takei even weighed in, telling Trump to give the source material its due.

In 2020, then-Vice President Mike Pence celebrated the one year anniversary of Trump’s new branch by announcing that — as those serving in the Navy are known as sailors and those in the army are known as soldiers — “henceforth, the members of the United States Space Force will be known as ‘guardians.’”

The announcement drew a quick reaction from Guardians of the Galaxy fans, who thought there might be an unacknowledged connection between the film series and the new name.

title: Venice Horizons Winner Anuparna Roy Returns to Lido With Mumbai Story of Migrants, Desire and Belonging ‘Lovers in the Blue Night’
summary: Indian filmmaker Anuparna Roy has been carrying Ameena’s story since childhood. Ameena was a bonded laborer in Roy’s hometown, and something she once said about her marriage stayed with the director long after she grew up and moved away. That memory became the seed for “Lovers in the Blue Night,” which premieres in the Horizons […]
content:
Indian filmmaker Anuparna Roy has been carrying Ameena’s story since childhood.

Ameena was a bonded laborer in Roy’s hometown, and something she once said about her marriage stayed with the director long after she grew up and moved away. That memory became the seed for “Lovers in the Blue Night,” which premieres in the Horizons competition at the Venice Film Festival a year after Roy’s debut feature, “Songs of Forgotten Trees,” made her the first Indian filmmaker to win the section’s best director prize.

International sales on the new film are being handled by Parallax.

Popular on Variety

Roy says “Songs of Forgotten Trees” was a personal story made under difficult funding conditions, built around two women who barely leave a single house. “Lovers in the Blue Night” widens that frame to four migrants moving through Mumbai; she also describes the production itself as far more professional this time, with deadlines and limitations she is still learning to work inside.

Asked whether she expected the new film to move into Venice’s main competition rather in Horizons, Roy says she dreamed of it rather than expected it, and that landing in the section again is no disappointment. She still considers herself a new director learning her craft alongside filmmakers she admires.

Ameena’s arc did not stay fixed to the facts that Roy remembered. She says her early instinct was rebellious, imagining the character finding real love and leaving her marriage behind. But that path stopped looking like simple freedom as the script developed. “That is also another loop — another loop of patriarchy,” Roy says, describing what looks from the outside like an escape into a happy ending.

That refusal to let escape read as simple freedom extends to how Roy treats her characters’ circumstances more broadly. She wanted the migrants’ hardship to shape them without defining them entirely, resisting the idea that displacement should crowd out their ordinary desires for intimacy, jealousy or tenderness. Karim, a closeted gay man married to Ameena, and his lover Sukka, a man trying to break free of caste, sit at the center of that approach. Roy says she wanted a neutral, empathetic language for both men rather than exaggerating poverty or turning their struggle into ideology.

Roy frames love itself as a form of resistance for characters, who are punished for wanting things. “When you are lonely or displaced, even a small gesture of intimacy can begin to feel enormous,” she says, describing what she calls the illusion of love: a space where affection, longing, isolation, need and fantasy start to blur together, so that people fall for the possibility of a person as much as the person themselves.

One choice stands out. Karim produces rat poison and kills rats in wealthy Mumbai housing societies, a job Roy based on someone she saw doing the same work in the city’s Andheri East suburb. She calls the image of him coming home from that job to kiss another man “no less than revolutionary,” and says placing the two things side by side felt deeply political to her.

Displacement links this film to Roy’s debut. Both stories draw on floods Roy experienced growing up in a coastal region near the Bangladesh border, close to the Bay of Bengal, and both send their characters into exile from a destroyed home. Where her first film explored two women, this one turns to two men and the duality of bisexuality.

Upcoming stories include “In the Shadow in the Light,” a romantic feature about a dysfunctional marriage modeled partly on her parents, and an untitled project about a woman’s sexual transit.

APC Studios’ boutique distributor About Premium Content (APC) has signed a number of key international broadcast deals ahead of this year’s Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre on French-language scripted and unscripted series “Blue Gold,” “Seasons” and “An Artful Imbrolio.”

The eight-part crime drama and family saga “Blue Gold” has been licensed to Walter Presents for the U.K. and Ireland, RTP in Portugal and Blue Play in Switzerland, joining U.S. streamer MHz Choice.

Produced by Authentic Prod (“Sam,” “Montmartre”) for France Télévisions the series is written by Marie-Anne Le Pezennec (“Dolmen”) and Ludovix Lacroix and directed by Hippolyte Dard.

Popular on Variety

Barbara Probst stars in ‘Blue Gold’ Courtesy of About Premium Content

Set in the 1980s in Provence, “Blue Gold” chronicles the saga of three women from three generations, Marie, Alice and Flore, and one decades-old buried secret. When a body is found and murders start piling up, Flore will have to solve the family puzzle by revealing the truth. Barbara Probst, Sylvie Granotier and Déborah Krey star.

The four-part “Seasons,” a French-language drama series produced by Windy Production for Arte, has been picked up by RTP in Portugal and RTBF Auvio for French-speaking Belgium. It previously sold to Radio Canada’s Ici Tou.TV Extra for French-speaking Canada.

‘Seasons’ Courtesy of About Premium Content

Beginning in August 1991 at the seaside resort of Les-Sables-d’Olonne, it follows Camille, 15, as she first meets the two best friends Martin and Alexandre on the beach and crashes into their lives like a comet. Perpetually torn between the two men, Camille will live a crazy love story with them over more than 30 years.

Nicolas Maury (“Call My Agent”) directed, co-wrote and stars in the show, co-written by Hélène Duchateau (“The Forest,” “Unfaithful,” “The Eclipse”).
