APC Stories’ three-part art investigation documentary “An Artful Imbroglio” went to Filmin in Spain and RTP in Portugal. Produced for Arte, the unscripted series, which is set in Paris, Rome, London and New York, sheds light on one of the art world’s greatest mysteries.

In the spring of 2014, a mysterious, anonymous letter triggered one of the biggest scandals in the art world: the alleged trafficking of fake old master paintings on an unprecedented scale. At the heart of this imbroglio unfolds a gallery of colorful characters, all revolving around an ultra-charismatic art dealer.

title: Lumiere Declaration Sets 15 Principles for Global Film Governance, Calling Audience Attention ‘a Trust to Be Honored, Not a Resource to Be Captured’
summary: Representatives of countries, international organizations, film, television and gaming industry leaders, creators, festivals and cultural institutions from across the world adopted the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image on Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence. Jointly presented by France and the Republic of Korea and convened under the co-chairship […]
content:
Representatives of countries, international organizations, film, television and gaming industry leaders, creators, festivals and cultural institutions from across the world adopted the Lumière Declaration on the Future of Cinema and the Moving Image on Monday at the Lumière Summit in Saint-Paul-de-Vence.

Jointly presented by France and the Republic of Korea and convened under the co-chairship of their respective presidents, the declaration sets out 15 principles and remains open for further signatures. “We lay here the foundations of a multilateralism of the moving image,” it states – a framework adopted 200 years after the first photograph and 130 years after the Lumière brothers’ first public screening of the Cinématographe, and one the declaration describes as the beginning of something new: “the moving image now has the beginnings of a global governance – a multilateralism meant to grow, through new initiatives, new partners and future gatherings.”

What the declaration argues, at its core, is that moving images exist for more than the capture of attention. They are, it states, “a common good: a vehicle for emotion, memory and knowledge, for individual emancipation and collective transformation.” Ambitious, intentional works “remain irreplaceable,” and “the future of our industries will be defined by the works we choose to create and support.”

Popular on Variety

The sharpest line in the document draws a direct contrast with algorithmic platforms: “The attention of an audience is not a resource to be captured, but a trust to be honored.” That conviction runs through several further principles — on who makes stories (“the richness of the stories we tell depends on the diversity of those who create them”), on the conditions under which they are made (“freedom of creation is a condition of the vitality and diversity of the moving image”), and on those who face “political, economic or social pressures that threaten their ability to create and to be heard,” for whom the declaration backs international networks of solidarity. An industry that excludes women or operates in unsafe conditions, it states, must become “exemplary in the exercise” of its power to shape representations.

On economics, the declaration is equally explicit. “A powerful engine of economic growth” is how it describes the audiovisual industry – one that “drives investment across a broad range of businesses, creates jobs, cultivates a highly skilled workforce, fosters innovation.” Distributors and others who profit from exploiting works carry “both a responsibility and a direct interest in the next generation of creation,” it states, calling for public support to enable early-stage risk-taking and for conditions that allow creators to develop their work over time. “International co-production diversifies risk, enriches works and binds our ecosystems together,” it adds, with a commitment to deepen cooperation between established and emerging markets “so that the diversity of the world’s stories finds its way onto the world’s screens.” The commercial case for breadth of output is put plainly: “The diversity of works, across budgets, languages, genres, formats and geographies, is not a constraint on competitiveness; it is its foundation.”

Three of the 15 principles address technology. “Artificial intelligence can strengthen creativity, innovation and the circulation of works – provided it becomes a driver of creation,” the declaration states, adding that “human creation should always remain at the heart and foundation of works.” On discoverability, it flags a risk no multilateral document has previously named – the rise of agentic AI – warning of “the possible advent of a world in which access to works would increasingly be mediated by automated agents.” On piracy: “When creation is not rewarded, it cannot be renewed.”

The remaining principles address the physical and cultural infrastructure the industry depends on. “Diversity needs cinemas in order to thrive; cinemas need diversity in order to fulfill their cultural, economic and social role,” the declaration states on theatrical exhibition. On heritage, it warns of “the critical period for the conservation of physical archives, whose elements degrade inexorably over time,” calling for investment and solidarity so that “every country can pass its memory on, alive and visible, to future generations.” On education: “Just as previous centuries pursued universal literacy in the written word, the age of images demands an equally ambitious commitment to image literacy,” with cinema identified as “one of the last places where individual screens are switched off and where we learn, again, to watch together.” A final principle commits signatories to developing “best practices, flexible standards, and practical tools for the design and implementation of sustainable production, distribution and exhibition.”

The signatories committed to remain collectively engaged and to review progress together.

title: Inside the Restoration of Indian Cult Classic ‘English, August,’ Heading to Venice as Relevant as Ever (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Dev Benegal’s “English, August” almost didn’t survive to be restored. Its original camera negative had melted. The dupe was gone too. All that was left were two surviving 35mm prints – and, it turned out, a box of DAT tapes nobody expected to matter three decades later. “It’s really sad that when I saw the […]
content:
Dev Benegal‘s “English, August” almost didn’t survive to be restored. Its original camera negative had melted. The dupe was gone too. All that was left were two surviving 35mm prints – and, it turned out, a box of DAT tapes nobody expected to matter three decades later.

“It’s really sad that when I saw the original camera negative, it had melted. It was in terrible condition,” says Shivendra Singh Dungarpur, founder of the Film Heritage Foundation (FHF), the organization that took on the restoration. FHF was left to rebuild the film from whatever prints remained.

What remained were two 35mm release prints: one Benegal had personally kept and donated to FHF, the other preserved by the NFDC-National Film Archive of India, the government body that houses India’s official film archive. “There was no other material, so we had to look at both these materials, do the comparison and use these particular prints,” Dungarpur says. Both prints, he says, were in decent condition – a stroke of luck given how little else of the film had survived.

Popular on Variety

Released in 1994, “English, August” follows Agastya Sen, a young, Westernized trainee nicknamed “August,” sent to a remote provincial town for a year of civil-service training in India’s elite administrative cadre. Adrift among Bob Dylan records, Marcus Aurelius and a bureaucracy he can barely stomach, Agastya finds himself a stranger in a country that is technically his own. The film is adapted from Upamanyu Chatterjee’s 1988 novel of the same name, a book that became a defining portrait of a certain post-colonial, urban Indian generation.

Benegal says the screenplay only became the film in the editing room. “This is a film which was truly written on the editing table. I am a firm believer that’s where movies are actually written,” he says. “While we were editing, Upamanyu asked me, ‘Why did we even write a screenplay? We are writing the film right here.'”

The soundtrack turned out to be the restoration’s unlikely triumph. Benegal recalls the constraints under which the film was originally mixed. “Vikram Joglekar had recorded the sound in digital. Ignoring industry advice not to do that!” he says. “In 1994 we did not have the money to create a stereo mix. Those were days of the License Raj, where we had to secure special permission to import six reels of Kodak Optical Sound Negative. Even after that we only had outdated equipment to make a flat mono mix.” What survived instead was a set of DAT tapes Benegal had quietly kept for thirty years. “Back in 1994, DATs were the cutting-edge digital recording medium, and I kept them in my personal archive purely out of my obsession with audio – never imagining they would save the film three decades later when the original 35mm sound negatives vanished,” he says. “Going back to those tapes with Vikram Joglekar was like opening a time capsule.” Dungarpur confirms the tapes gave FHF something restorers rarely get. “We went back to the studio, and Vikram Joglekar, who was the sound recordist, brought back Satish P.M., the sound engineer, to work on restoring these tracks,” he says. “We had the unmixes, so it was great.”

Color grading brought its own rhythm to the process. Dungarpur says the palette was set by cinematographer Anoop Jotwani, who tested a single reel before the rest of the film followed his lead, with Benegal weighing in throughout from New York as the restoration work itself took place at L’Immagine Ritrovata, the film lab in Bologna, Italy. “You had Dev Benegal working almost daily on it. He did the English subtitles. We were talking daily about the look of the film, the way it was restored in Bologna, the grains and the color tone,” Dungarpur says. “There was a constant flow between Bologna and Dev Benegal, who was sitting in New York. He actually booked a suite to look at the grading, to look at the colors, to hear the sound.” Rahul Bose, who made his feature debut as the film’s lead, also came in to see part of the process, Dungarpur says.

Benegal is unequivocal about why Bose was right for that role. “Rahul Bose understood that Agastya wasn’t someone the audience needed to like; he needed to be truthful,” Benegal says. “He wasn’t trying to perform alienation – he simply inhabited the character with remarkable honesty. He also had the confidence to do very little. That’s much harder than it sounds.”

Not everything about the soundtrack could be fully reconstructed. Benegal says the production had gone to unusual lengths at the time to license its music. “Back in the day the producing team worked tirelessly to license and pay for music rights – something virtually unheard of then in India,” he says. One piece of paperwork never made it. “The paperwork documenting the Miles Davis’ “‘Round Midnight” clearance was lost in a torrential monsoon flood,” he says. The gap has created its own folklore among fans, he adds: “Some people have made a mix tape in their minds, from the box of tapes Agastya carried with him to Madna. Those tracks were never actually part of the original theatrical mix. Memory has a curious way of creating its own version of a film.”

For Dungarpur, the restoration answered a demand that had been building for years. “There was a great demand by people who wanted, were looking for, something to watch it back on the big screen and to see a restoration of this,” he says of “English, August.” “There are many people coming from around the world” eager to see the film again, he adds, calling it one of the independently produced films FHF exists to bring back “into a different time” for new audiences – including at Venice where the restoration premieres. It’s also FHF’s third consecutive year premiering a restoration at the festival, following Girish Kasaravalli’s “Ghatashraddha” in 2024 and Bimal Roy’s “Do Bigha Zamin” in 2025.

Watching “English, August” again more than 32 years after making it, Benegal finds the film’s portrait of isolation has only sharpened. “What feels familiar is the uncertainty,” he says. “India in the early 1990s was beginning to open up economically and culturally, but the old structures still shaped everyday life. There was a generation caught between inherited institutions and emerging freedoms. That sense of being in transition still resonates.” What has changed entirely, he says, is the texture of being alone. “The film unfolds in an India before mobile phones, social media and constant connectivity. Agastya is left alone with his thoughts… In 1994, if you were exiled to a small district town, you were genuinely off the grid. Agastya’s isolation was spatial and physical; today, isolation is algorithmic.”

Benegal argues the character’s alienation was never really about the West. “Agastya isn’t alienated because he listens to rock and jazz or reads Marcus Aurelius. He’s alienated because he’s searching for authenticity in a role that feels imposed upon him. That’s a condition that transcends both geography and time,” he says. He sees that same restlessness in a different uniform today: “The modern Agastyas aren’t just urban civil servants reading Marcus Aurelius in small towns – they are scrolling through curated, globalized lives on their phones from anywhere. The absurdity hasn’t disappeared; it’s just been upgraded to high-speed internet.”

The film’s satire of Indian bureaucracy has aged in a similar direction, according to Benegal. “Three decades later, the language of bureaucracy may have been digitized, but the core absurdities – the performance of power and the gap between official intent and ground reality – remain unchanged,” he says. “If anything, the satire feels almost prescient today.”

Benegal is candid that the film could not be made the same way now. “‘English, August’ succeeded precisely because it fit into zero existing boxes – it rejected that one prescribed way of making films,” he says. The five languages spoken across the film famously baffled censors at the time: “English, August has five languages, and that stumped the Indian censors who insisted, ‘a film can only have one language.'” Distribution came down to one gamble. “I have to give a huge shout out to Sunder Kimat Rai, who was country head of 20th Century Fox at that time, who took the gamble to distribute the film. He said, ‘the demographics match.’ I had no idea what ‘demographics’ even meant,” Benegal says. He doubts that kind of bet would be made today. “While we have streaming platforms and festival infrastructure, we also have hyper-calculated algorithms. Everything gets filtered through target demographics, pitch decks, and comparative commercial comps. The tools to shoot and edit are democratized, but the willingness of financiers and distributors to take a gamble on pure, unclassifiable tone is far rarer.”

Asked what a 20-year-old watching the film today might see that 1994 audiences couldn’t, Benegal points to something less generational than it first appears. “I hope they watch it as a portrait of someone asking timeless questions: Who am I? What kind of life do I want? What happens when the expectations of society don’t align with your inner life?” he says. “A young audience today may recognise mental and emotional states that weren’t discussed as openly in 1994. Agastya’s uncertainty may feel less like aimlessness and more like an honest search for meaning.”

Benegal is already looking past the restoration to his next project. “I’m working on ‘A Love Supreme’ a contemporary re-imagining of the epic Shakuntala – a story of a resilient, enigmatic woman whose path defies societal norms to become an autonomous woman,” he says. “But, the impulse remains the same as it was in 1994 – finding the humor, absurdity, and humanity in spaces where people feel out of place.”

title: The Talk Of Telluride: Secret Screening Of Elizabeth Holmes Documentary ‘You Can See Everything’
summary: Telluride chief Julie Huntsinger took a significant risk programming a documentary as the festival’s sneak premiere this year, given that nonfiction can’t claim the broad appeal of fiction. Indeed, just as she prepared to reveal the chosen film someone in the Werner Herzog Theater shouted “Digger!”, apparently hoping it would be the Tom Cruise-starring feature […]
content:
Telluride chief Julie Huntsinger took a significant risk programming a documentary as the festival’s sneak premiere this year, given that nonfiction can’t claim the broad appeal of fiction. Indeed, just as she prepared to reveal the chosen film someone in the Werner Herzog Theater shouted “Digger!”, apparently hoping it would be the Tom Cruise-starring feature from director Alejandro Iñárritu. That person may have been disappointed, but judging from reaction, the selection of the documentary You Can See Everything has turned into a triumph.

More than 24 hours after the premiere of the Nathan Fielder–Lance Oppenheim film, everyone in Telluride is still talking about it (well, everyone still in town; plenty headed to the airport Monday). One festival regular told me he’d got a message from someone in Lake Charles, LA wanting to know if he’d been one of the lucky few to get into the screening. The news has spread fast and far.

Walking near Colorado Avenue Monday afternoon, I spotted a publicist who had advance knowledge that You Can See Everything would be the super-secret special film. We proceeded to get into a 10-minute discussion of the film’s two principal characters – the enigmatic and unblinking Elizabeth Holmes, founder of the notorious Silicon Valley blood-testing startup Theranos, and her romantic partner, Billy Evans, father of her two young children. Is he out of his mind (as one important figure in the film exclaims)? Is she on the level or a preternaturally gifted manipulator trying to pull a Jedi mind trick on Fielder? Those kinds of vigorous debates have been going on from the moment the crowd spilled out of the Herzog into the Telluride night air.

Watch on Deadline

READ: ‘You Can See Everything’ Review: Shocking Elizabeth Holmes Documentary With Nathan Fielder Is Like No Other You Have Ever Seen – Telluride Film Festival

At an afterparty at La Marmotte (French for marmot, a stout ground-dwelling squirrel. I mention this because that’s the kind of weird detail I think Fielder would seize on), the directors held court as enthusiast after enthusiast heaped praise on them in between slurps of cocktails and bites of molten mushroom croquettes and seared tuna cubes. I spoke with Fielder and he seemed a bit dazed by the ardent reception for his film. He’s been working in intense secrecy on the project since before Holmes began her prison term in 2023 after her conviction for defrauding investors (and her acquittal, she repeats several times in the film, of defrauding patients). To emerge from that edit cave into the spotlight of public reaction must be disorienting. Fielder didn’t even know where the film would play next – whether distributor A24 would take it to another festival or proceed straight to theatrical release next month.

Two-time Oscar winner Emma Stone hung out at the afterparty too (can we say she Marmotted? Is that a verb?). She moderated the Q&A after the world premiere and acquitted herself admirably (as people were leaving the theater a veteran journalist went up to Emma and congratulated her on her performance as moderator, helpfully noting that actors typically don’t excel at that).

Nathan Fielder at the Deadline Contenders Television 2024 Portrait Studio held at the Directors Guild of America April 14, 2024 in Los Angeles. Deadline

The nearly three-hour long film drew continuous laughter, frequently triggered by hilarious reaction shots of Fielder, the Canadian comedian and co-director, who is seen on camera throughout attempting to process what Holmes and Evans are pushing. “Liz,” as she goes by in the film, suffered catastrophic reputational damage from the implosion of Theranos, not to mention a skewering she received in Alex Gibney’s documentary The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley and the devastating portrayal by actress Amanda Seyfried in the fictionalized Hulu series The Dropout. Aware of that and wishing to revive Theranos in a new form, the couple invited Fielder to observe their every move for the 30-some days before she had to report to federal prison in Texas.

Elizabeth Holmes Associated Press

In the glory days of Theranos, Holmes — her big blue eyes and blond hair set to advantage in black turtleneck sweaters — had reeled in powerful backers like Larry Ellison, Rupert Murdoch, Henry Kissinger, and George Shultz. Shedding the turtleneck in favor of a cozier sweater and rumpled coiffure for the documentary, she locks eyes with Fielder perhaps thinking she could work her magic on him. But he proves resistant, relentlessly probing whether Holmes knew she had oversold what her blood testing machines could do.

Former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes alongside her boyfriend Billy Evans, leaves a hearing at the Robert E. Peckham U.S. Courthouse on March 17, 2023 in San Jose, California. Philip Pacheco/Getty Images

Evans emerges as a troubling presence who may be exerting undue control over Holmes, in a possible recapitulation of her relationship with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, the Svengali-like president of Theranos and Holmes’s former romantic partner (he’s serving a federal prison term as well, of 12 years). Billy boy is eager to have the film crew record him pumping iron, and later, while showering at home – clearly aware a camera was on him – he proudly displays his, uh, manhood. Well into the film he gets into a discussion with the film team where he proclaims his prowess at love-making. And they call Donald Trump a narcissist. Questions arise about who’s controlling Holmes’s X/Twitter feed while she’s behind bars, just one of example of ways in which Billy appears to veer toward colonizing his beloved.

The motives of Holmes and Evans remain resolutely opaque; during the Q&A the directors said the film crew would often debate what they had witnessed of the couple after a day’s shooting, but no one could agree on a common interpretation. You Can See Everything, then, qualifies an arch title. What does it serve to “see everything” when you’re mired in muck?

(In the teaser below, you can see one of those delicious reaction shots of Fielder as Holmes assures him of her utter honesty).

title: Elon Musk’s Ex Ashley St. Clair on Rejecting a $40 Million NDA and Participating in ‘Musk’ Doc: ‘I Hope the Risk in Trying to Fight Back Helps a Little Bit’
summary: Elon Musk’s ex Ashley St. Clair spoke about her decision to reject a $40 million non-disclosure agreement after the influencer gave birth last year to Musk’s 13th child. By turning down the alleged payday, St. Clair was able to sit for an interview in “Musk,” a new documentary from Alex Gibney that seeks to make […]
content:
Elon Musk‘s ex Ashley St. Clair spoke about her decision to reject a $40 million non-disclosure agreement after the influencer gave birth last year to Musk’s 13th child. By turning down the alleged payday, St. Clair was able to sit for an interview in “Musk,” a new documentary from Alex Gibney that seeks to make sense of the controversial billionaire who has outsized influence on the world in which we live.

“When you are offered something like that, it creates a debate about what your speech means and how valuable that is,” St. Claire said at a Venice Film Festival press conference for “Musk,” which premieres on Tuesday. “Why do they want to offer me this amount of money to not speak?”

St. Claire participated in the doc to “set the example for my kids that we should never take being materially comfortable that we’re speaking the truth,” she said. St. Clair gained prominence as a right-wing political commentator who advocated for conservative and anti-trans politics. She is now expressing her regret for platforming those beliefs, which she chalked up to her youth and confidants at the time.

Popular on Variety

“I got involved with Republican politics when I was 18 after I met Charlie Kirk, and there was an air of ignorance,” said St. Clair, who is now 28. “But that ignorance does not excuse any role in that. I hope the risk that I’m taking now is speaking out and trying to fight back at least helps a little bit.”

Gibney, an Oscar-winning documentarian, has investigated corrupt corporations (“Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room”), sexual abuse coverups in the Catholic Church (“Mea Maxima Culpa: Silence in the House of God”), Scientology (“Going Clear: Scientology and the Prison of Disbelief”) and alleged Russian interference in the 2016 U.S. presidential election (“Agents of Chaos”). Gibney began working on a film about the tech titan and world’s richest man, with an estimated net worth of $900 billion through ventures including SpaceX and Tesla, back in 2023.

“The thing that struck me most, particularly early on, there was a tremendous sense of fear of talking — both among people who were his critics, colleagues and friends,” saidGibney said. “I talked to many, many, many people. Many declined to speak.” Gibney and St. Clair were joined at the press conference by another interview subject, tech journalist Zoë Schiffer.

“Musk,” which premieres at the festival on Tuesday, is nearly four hours long — and Gibney joked he didn’t set out to make such a long movie.

“We intended to make a shorter film before Musk became wrapped in the career of Donald Trump and the United States,” Gibney said, adding the first thing he did was reach out to Musk, who declined to be interviewed.

“Musk” promises to reframe all we know about him, “revealing that the so-called ‘visionary genius’ is little more than the 21st-century reincarnation of a confidence man,” according to the synopsis. Musk himself has said that perceived reality may be nothing more than a simulation, and Gibney argues “even his most heralded accomplishments are rife with illusion and misdirection.” Musk’s recent ventures include buying Twitter (and renaming the social media platform X) and starting xAI and its chatbot Grok. Although Musk didn’t participate in Gibney’s doc, he long ago called the film a “hit piece.”

Gibney called Musk a “very dangerous” man and expressed a deep concern about Musk’s unwillingness to show concern about other people.

“I would say he has a very difficult time with empathy, especially cognitive empathy, which is putting himself in the shoes of others,” Gibney said. “He seems incapable of doing that.”

Added St. Clair, “He makes a conscious choice to not put himself on other people’s shoes. It is a deliberate rejection of empathy.”

title: Levan Koguashvili Brings ’90s Georgia to Venice With Comedic Drama ‘Guria’

content:
Levan Koguashvili‘s “Guria” will world premiere in Venice’s Spotlight section on Sept. 9. The black-and-white tragicomedy, set in the western Georgian Guria region, follows Zuriko, a 45-year-old widower and farmer as he struggles to find love, as well as a fair price on hazelnuts.

“Guria” is a co-production between Georgia‘s Kino Iberica, Switzerland’s Cineworx, Luxembourg’s Tarantula and Bulgaria’s ArtFest, with support reaching further afield, including Turkey’s Ministry of Culture and Tourism, Norway’s SoRFond Film Fund and Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea Fund.

It’s the director’s fourth feature, following “Street Days” (2010), winner of a Tiger Award at Rotterdam; “Blind Dates” (2013), which scooped the Special Jury Award at Abu Dhabi, and “Brighton 4th” (2021), which took prizes at Tribeca and Cottbus. “Guria” was written by Koguashvili with Boris Frumin, a former professor and longtime collaborator.

Popular on Variety

Variety spoke with Koguashvili in Venice about “Guria” ahead of the film’s premiere.

This project is a seven-country co-production with global financing. Can you discuss how Guria came to interest so many parties in telling a Georgian story?

Koguashvili: Basically, the idea of bringing in so many parties came from financing. We had to look for many co-producers. In our case, you get a little bit of money from different places. Of course, it’s harder to manage a production when so many people are involved, but on the other hand, it makes for a very international crew. You have a sound guy from Switzerland, an editor from Luxembourg… it’s fun. I was really grateful that people got interested in this crazy story about friendship and love in Guria and found support in different countries. And Saudi Arabia came in at the very last moment. We were still raising money for some pickup shoots, and we brought the film to the Red Sea industry park and showed 20 minutes. We won a couple of awards there, and that’s how the Saudi co-producers came on board. It was a really great help, at the very last moment.

Can you talk about co-writing the film? What did that collaboration look like, and what did each of you bring to the story?

Koguashvili: Boris was my professor at NYU’s graduate program, and we ended up becoming friends and working together after school. There’s a an age difference (he’s almost 80 now), but we started collaborating during my first film there, and it’s kept going ever since. The way it works: I bring the material, Georgian scenes, life situations, characters, protagonists, and we discuss what to do with it, how to connect the story. What matters most is having strong scenes. You need a handful of very strong, cinematic scenes, and the rest can be good around them. So I lean hard on that. Boris is great at organizing and constructing material. He’s very much a teacher in that sense, about the logic of story development, and that’s what I learned from him. I loved his classes, in terms of how he approaches structure.

What about Georgia and Guria in the ’90s make it the time and place to anchor this story? What has changed about that world?

Koguashvili: I like Georgian provinces very much because they still have an authentic feeling. Big cities look alike everywhere now, but the provinces have their own flavor, and Guria especially has a very strong character. So it was already somewhere in my mind. Then I happened to read a book, “Gurian Diaries.” It was melancholic, about the poverty and the humor of that time, but there wasn’t really a story in it, just a guy remembering his childhood. I liked the atmosphere, so I called the author and asked if he had a concrete story. He didn’t, but he suggested we go to Guria together and see what we’d find. I spent maybe two or three months there. Once I felt I had enough material, I took everything to Boris, and in about three days we had the shape of a story, a plot.

Your work tends to straddle this line of hardship and comedy. What draws you to that place, finding light in the darkness?

Koguashvili: Several things, maybe, but mostly, this is how I see life. I don’t see even tragic moments as complete tragedy; life is always full of dimensions. By introducing irony and humor, you don’t make a tragic story less tragic. It just gets a different feeling, it becomes more human, and it’s easier to digest. It also gives the story a kind of lightness and lyricism, which I love. I believe tragedy and drama have to be told with some comedy in them. You try to find levity or humor even in the darkest, most dramatic situation. It’s also a way of working against cliché: when you think of the ’90s in a post-Soviet country, you picture a very dark movie, right? But I think that’s become a cliché too, and working against it is its own challenge. Also, Georgian character isn’t simple. Georgian life in that period was extremely difficult, but there was also a kind of absurdity to it, even a charm. So many things, but usually the films I love have that quality. They’re all comedies about tragedies. It’s a very tragic story, but the telling of it is full of comedy.

How did you come to use singing and song as such an important narrative tool in Guria? Can you talk about the songs the characters sing through the film?

Koguashvili: Georgia has a very strong tradition of folk singing, and Georgian singing is polyphonic. Usually there are three voices, but depending on the region, some songs have five, six, sometimes seven parts. It’s very complex, almost like Stravinsky, in a way. If you listen closely, it’s an absolute improvisation, done by people with no formal musical education, just peasants improvising, but creating enormously original music. Singing is also very much part of Georgian culture more broadly, of the Georgian dinners we call supra, when people gather around the table. I grew up in a family where we had those dinners often, 20 or 30 people coming to the house, drinking wine, and singing. So for Guria, I met a very interesting composer, the head of a folk center who works with traditional folk musicians. I told him I wanted to do something in the Georgian tradition but approached differently, not polyphonic, but a single voice, because a single voice felt more intimate to me. He’s from Guria himself, so he understood what I meant.

title: ‘Elite’ Star Ester Expósito Circles ‘Stink Eye,’ an Iberseries Co-Production & Financing Forum Title (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Spanish actor Ester Expósito (“Elite”) is circling the upcoming feature “Stink Eye” (“Malmirada”) and has signed a letter of intent to topline the feature debut of Colombian director-writer Cristina Sánchez Salamanca, who first caught the film world’s eye with her short “Bebé” at the 2022 Tribeca Festival. “Stink Eye” is among the projects participating at […]
content:
Spanish actor Ester Expósito (“Elite”) is circling the upcoming feature “Stink Eye” (“Malmirada”) and has signed a letter of intent to topline the feature debut of Colombian director-writer Cristina Sánchez Salamanca, who first caught the film world’s eye with her short “Bebé” at the 2022 Tribeca Festival.

“Stink Eye” is among the projects participating at Madrid’s Iberseries Co-Production and Financing Forum which has also snagged Goya-nominated cinematographer Gris Jordana, whose credits include Netflix’s “La Bola Negra” (Cannes 2026 Best Director winner and a strong contender to represent Spain at the Oscars), “La Mesías” and “Liberty” (“Libertad”).

The drama revolves around 13-year-old Nina whose life is upended when her father leaves her mother for Belén, a striking model-influencer, which would be role played by Expósito, who has a massive following on social media herself, with 24.7 million followers on Instagram alone.

Popular on Variety

The scandal leaves her mother grappling with her mental and physical health which forces Nina to move in with her father and his new wife. To improve her social status among the horny teens she wants to impress, she creates a black market of her stepmother’s stolen underwear, discovering her own identity and sexuality in the process.

As Nina longs to fill the maternal void in her life, she finds herself growing unexpectedly close to her stepmother. The closer Nina gets to Belén, the more conflicted she feels about her real mother.

Sánchez Salamanca drew from her own childhood experience to write the story: “When I was seven, my father left my mother for Miss Universe. Or well, the first runner-up. This woman was beautiful, poised, charming, intelligent and oozed sex. How can you find your own place in life when such a huge shadow is cast upon you?”

“The most exciting aspect of this project is having the magnetic Ester Expósito on board to play such an important figure in my own coming of age. I can’t think of anyone better to deconstruct the perfect woman and show something much more interesting that lies beneath. This isn’t a coming-of-age story. It’s closer to dark comedy body horror – but here, the horror lies in growing up as a 13-year-old girl in a world that validates women’s existence through the eyes of others.”

As a director and screenwriter, Sánchez’s work explores the fragility and darkness of the human condition. Alienation, the body, duality, identity and the shadow are recurring themes, rooted in her experience of navigating the world around her. In “Bebé,” she captured the angst of childhood amid the fractures of a broken family, while her vision for “The Tour ‘23,” a series of short documentaries commissioned by Victoria’s Secret, explored the chaotic experience of moving through Bogotá in a woman’s body.

“Stink Eye” is produced by Continente Pictures, led by Sánchez and her producing partner Duván Duque Vargas, along with Spain’s Ringo Media, run by Mireia Graell (“Matria”) and France’s Dibona Films, led by Jérémy Zelnik (“The Spectacle,” Cannes 2025).

Duque Vargas and Paola Pérez Nieto serve as producers.

Both of Continente Pictures’ debut features “Stink Eye” and “Name and Surname” have participated in such development programs as the Torino Film Lab, the ECAM Forum and Sørfond’s Pitching Forum, winning a host of awards at Colombia’s Bogota Audiovisual Market (BAM) as well as Ventana Sur and Guadalajara.

title: Andy Serkis Unleashes Imagination with Venice Immersive Breakout ‘Nevatars’
summary: Premiering out of Venice Immersive, “Nevatars” has long been a passion project for director Andy Serkis. It took root when Serkis and partner Jonathan Cavendish co-founded The Imaginarium, a production studio built on Serkis’ deep expertise in performance capture. They had the hardware, the knowledge — and, it turns out, had been sitting on the […]
content:
Premiering out of Venice Immersive, “Nevatars” has long been a passion project for director Andy Serkis.

It took root when Serkis and partner Jonathan Cavendish co-founded The Imaginarium, a production studio built on Serkis’ deep expertise in performance capture. They had the hardware, the knowledge — and, it turns out, had been sitting on the story all along.

“The idea came from experience,” Serkis explains. “What happens to all the incredible concept art for characters that never get used? These characters are given thought and spirit and a life of their own, and then they end up in a folder called ‘old assets,’ right next to one called ‘new projects.’ It was born from those digital rejects, hoping to be noticed.”

“Nevatars”

The Imaginarium team had kicked the idea around since 2011, but it gained real momentum when Google’s immersive production division, 100 Zeroes, approached the duo looking for stories suited to the format. “Nevatars” was the perfect fit.

Popular on Variety

Working with co-director Josh Nelson Youssef — himself founder of immersive storytelling outfit Boona — Serkis and co. centered the story around a young aspiring artist, unduly ashamed of her earlier creations.

“We wanted a young spirit,” Serkis explains. “Someone whose mind is free, but who gets quashed by the modern commercial-art world, forced into an algorithmic existence. It’s a parable about holding on to your initial creative instinct. She starts out making wonderfully chaotic, personal work, but risks losing that to become an artist who just fits in. When she finally makes something to please everyone, it feels generic — and nobody wants that.”

Of course, the 30-minute XR experience plays out as a narrative adventure, part chase and part escape story, following both the young artist and her rag-tag group of design rejects as they try to break free from the desktop trash bin. The voice cast includes Daisy Ridley, Josh Gad, Kathleen Turner, Steve Zahn, Kelly Marie Tran and Serkis himself.

“Nevatars”

“The story deals with human, accessible themes like perfectionism and self-doubt,” says Boona’s Matthew O’Rourke. “But we also wanted to chart a new path. We used a cinematic viewport, where things move in and out of the frame, familiar like a traditional movie while really taking advantage of what immersive can do. There are moments that feel like a stunning animated film, and then it comes alive in ways that are still untraditional for the medium.”

The project was initially designed for the Android XR platform, so it came as a happy surprise this past April when “Nevatars” was tapped as one of the first titles to launch on the XREAL Aura — Google-powered AR smart glasses being positioned as a potential game-changer for their portability and light weight. The glasses’ voice-activation capability opened up new storytelling tools, and gave the experience itself a new dimension.

“It’s fully interactive,” O’Rourke says. “There are moments where you’re touching and moving things, which gives you a sense of agency that blends seamlessly with the film itself. The fidelity of the visuals is stunning, too, especially for something that sits on your face like a pair of glasses.”

The Imaginarium’s Phil Robertson describes the effect as something closer to augmentation than escapism. “You get coherent, moving, funny storytelling, but it’s mind-boggling in the sense that it surrounds you without shutting you off from the world behind a pair of goggles,” he says. “You’re part of the world, but with these things happening around — and inside — your head.”

“Nevatars”

As one of only two Aura-supported projects showcased this year, “Nevatars” has been a major draw on Venice’s Immersive island — much to the filmmakers’ delight.

“It’s been amazing to watch people experience it for the first time,” Serkis says. “It’s a bit like ‘Minority Report,’ moving screens around in the world in front of you with your hands. You’re in a world within your world: comfortable in your own environment, with another one right there to step into and explore.”

Looking ahead, Serkis and Cavendish hope to keep exploring “Nevatars” as cross-media IP, all while further entrenching themselves in the immersive space.

“Andy has this unique ability to imagine new storytelling universes,” Cavendish says. “He thinks in 4D while the rest of us think in 2D. This is just the beginning.”

title: France TV Exports Plummet Amid Ad Decline, Broadcaster Budget Cuts, ‘Deteriorating Economic Environment’
summary: The French National Film Board (CNC) and Unifrance on Tuesday offered a sobering assessment of France’s TV content exports in 2025, citing “a deteriorating economic environment and numerous uncertainties” that contributed to a sharp 21.6% drop in the international sales of French audiovisual programs to €164.3 million ($190.8 million) — the lowest level in a […]
content:
The French National Film Board (CNC) and Unifrance on Tuesday offered a sobering assessment of France’s TV content exports in 2025, citing “a deteriorating economic environment and numerous uncertainties” that contributed to a sharp 21.6% drop in the international sales of French audiovisual programs to €164.3 million ($190.8 million) — the lowest level in a decade.

The report, presented at the Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre, noted the sharp contrast with the previous year, stressing that 2024 exports actually rose 3% year-on-year to reach €209.6 million — their second highest level in 30 years — “a year that had remained at an excellent level, with export activity proving resilient despite the international economic environment.”

In 2025, fiction remained the leading export genre with a 33.4% total share, making it the most exported genre for the fourth consecutive year. Nevertheless, it suffered a double-digit decline for the first time since 2018: €54.9 million in 2025, down 27% year-on-year. (In 2018, fiction fell 22.5%.)

Popular on Variety

Documentary overtook animation for the first time with 26.2% of international sales, above the past 10-year average of 21.2%. The sales decline for documentary fare was more moderate at just 2.7% to €43.1 million, close to the decade average of €41.1 million.

Animation, despite its success in recent years, fell to an all-time low at 19.6%. After five strong years, from 2016 to 2020, animation was the first genre hit by contracting international demand, according to the report, and the downward trend continued in 2025 with a massive 30.3% drop to €32.2 million.

Taking a closer look at fiction, sales remained concentrated around light crime and lighter-toned procedurals. Among the top sellers were “Bright Minds,” about a neurodivergent police records archivist with an extraordinary memory who helps a troubled police inspector solve complex crimes; “Deadly Tropics,” which follows a mismatched duo of female detectives as they solve local murder cases on the Caribbean island of Martinique; and “Alexandra Ehle,” about a brilliant and eccentric forensic pathologist in Bordeaux.

In general, sales saw reduced genre diversity in favor of a more standardized offering despite some strong examples to the contrary, including “Samber,” the true-crime miniseries about a serial rapist who stalked women along the Sambre River for three decades until he was finally arrested; and World War I steampunk sci-fi actioner “The Sentinels.”

The decline of animation, meanwhile, was exacerbated by the court-ordered liquidation of once leading companies Cyber Group and TeamTO (the latter was acquired in 2024 by U.S.-based Riva Studios). In addition, sales for animation were down in every region except North America, which was up 5.9%, and Africa, plus 38.7%, both of which remained at low levels, however.

“Buyers increasingly favor established IP,” the reported noted, pointing out that the global market “has at times become saturated, with production continuing even as international demand slowed.”

Documentary, on the other hand, has proved more resilient.

European TV broadcasters remain the main buyers of French documentaries, with more than half of sales going to Western Europe. However, while French productions are internationally recognized, export barriers are multiplying, according to the report, including a global shift towards local preference. Editorial strategies are refocusing on locally relevant themes, which are less suited to export.

Nevertheless, priority is given to event documentaries with high-impact subject matter, exceptional access and/or exclusivity.

Leading titles included “Machu Picchu: Secrets of the Lost City of the Incas,” sold by Kwanza; “1939-1945: and the World Changes,” from ZED; and Terranoa’s “Extraordinary Clouds.”

Belgium remained the leading export territory for French content despite sales falling 18.8% year-on-year to €20.2 million. Documentary fare was the leading genre for the second consecutive year in the country, making up 39.2% of sales, ahead of fiction with 35.5%.

The U.S. returned to the top three, rising to second place in 2025 (after ranking sixth the previous year) with €10.1 million in sales, up 31%.

Italy was again in third place despite sales falling 26.1% to €9.3 million.

Overall, the CNC and Unifrance annual report found an economic environment marked by a “decline in the TV advertising market, budget cuts at many public broadcasters and fewer program commissions worldwide.”

It added: “Buyers remain highly risk-averse: tighter editorial and budget trade-offs, rationalized investment — especially among SVOD services, which buy fewer multi-territory rights and favor a ‘local for local’ strategy — longer decision-making processes, and priority for recognizable, high-potential programs already proven in other markets.”

title: Alex Gibney Encountered “Tremendous Sense Of Fear Of Talking” As He Researched Bombshell Doc ‘Musk’- Venice
summary: Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney told a Venice Film Festival press conference on Tuesday that he came up against a “tremendous sense of fear” as he canvassed for interviewees his new bombshell documentary Musk about controversial tech tycoon Elon Musk. “There was a tremendous sense of fear of talking, really almost existential fear, both among people […]
content:
Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney told a Venice Film Festival press conference on Tuesday that he came up against a “tremendous sense of fear” as he canvassed for interviewees his new bombshell documentary Musk about controversial tech tycoon Elon Musk.

“There was a tremendous sense of fear of talking, really almost existential fear, both among people who were his critics, people who were his business colleagues and people who are his friends,” he said. “I talked to you know many, many, many, many people who, except for some of the brave people here with me here, declined to speak.”

Gibney was joined at the press conference by Musk interviewees Ashley St. Clair, Elon Musk’s ex-partner and the mother of one of his children, and journalist and writer Zoë Schiffer, author of the 2024 book ‘Extremely Hardcore: Inside Elon Musk’s Twitter’.

Watch on Deadline

Asked why the had agreed to participate in the film, St. Clair brought up a previously reported $40M NDA offer she received from Musk after their relationship ended.

“When you’re offered something like that, it really causes a debate in your head about what your speech means and how valuable that is, and why do they want to offer me this amount of money to not speak?,” she said.

“And I believe Alex spoke to it a little bit about Elon’s unreality, and he does complicated relationships generally, but his most complicated relationship is with the truth. And so, I think most importantly, I want to set the example for my kids that you should never take being materially comfortable over speaking the truth.”

Overnight the production released a first trailer giving a taste of the film, with soundbites describing Musk as “chaotic”, “capricious” , “manifestly cruel”, “a nuke” and “a “fascist”

Musk had yet to respond to the trailer by the time the press conference kicked off at 12.30pm CET (3am PT), having pre-emptively fired off a post on X on about the Gibney and the documentary last week.

His social posts over the past 24 hour have focused instead on showing support for the victory of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in elections Germany’s eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt over the weekend.

Musk is Oscar-winning director’ latest exploration into the corrupting influence of power, and follows documentaries such as Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, Steve Jobs: TheMan in the Machine, The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, and We Steal Secrets: The Story of WikiLeaks.

title: Sherri Shepherd Heading To Broadway As The Genie In Disney’s ‘Aladdin’
summary: Talk show host Sherri Shepherd will make a rare Broadway appearance as the Genie in Disney’s Aladdin when she begins a limited run in the musical on Friday, October 16. Shepherd, who gave her first and do-date-only Broadway performance in 2014 as the Evil Stepmother in Rodgers + Hammerstein’s Cinderella, will play in Aladdin during […]
content:
Talk show host Sherri Shepherd will make a rare Broadway appearance as the Genie in Disney’s Aladdin when she begins a limited run in the musical on Friday, October 16.

Shepherd, who gave her first and do-date-only Broadway performance in 2014 as the Evil Stepmother in Rodgers + Hammerstein’s Cinderella, will play in Aladdin during the lucrative holiday season with her final performance set for Sunday, January 3, 2027.

The former View host was expected to return as a guest on today’s season premiere of the ABC talk show.

“Joining Aladdin on Broadway is an absolute dream come true,” Shepherd said in a statement, “and an incredible honor. The Genie is such an iconic character, and I’m beyond excited to bring my own energy, humor, heart, and a little bit of magic to this role. I hope audiences see themselves in this Genie and leave the theater feeling so much joy and inspired to believe in the impossible. To step on that stage as the first woman to ever play the Genie is something I don’t take lightly. I’m ready to rub the lamp, unleash some magic, and have the time of my life on Broadway.”

Watch on Deadline

Shepherd was a co-host of The View for seven years and has hosted Dish Nation, The Newlywed Game, and Best Ever Trivia Show, among others. Her other television credits include 30 Rock, Friends, Sex Lives of College Girls and others. She’s appeared in such films as Precious, Ride Along 2, and Beauty Shop. Her upcoming Lifetime film, Angel in the Rubble, premieres September 12.

Her stage credits include the Off Broadway shows Love, Loss, and What I Wore, and Joy Behar’s My First Ex-Husband. She continues to tour as a stand-up comedian.

“Throughout her career, Sherri has represented delight, wit, and loving good humor, making her the perfect entertainer to play the life force that is the Genie,” said Disney Theatrical Group’s Andrew Flatt (Managing Director) and Anne Quart (Executive Producer).

Aladdin opened on Broadway at the New Amsterdam Theatre on March 20, 2014 and remains among Broadway’s most popular attractions.

title: Harry & Meghan Briefing War Breaks Out Within Days Of UK Return; Couple “Surprised” By King Charles Edict
summary: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have only been back in the UK for a matter of days, but they have already resumed hostilities with Buckingham Palace. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are said to be “surprised” that King Charles III communicated his desire for them to remain non-working members of the royal family after […]
content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have only been back in the UK for a matter of days, but they have already resumed hostilities with Buckingham Palace.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are said to be “surprised” that King Charles III communicated his desire for them to remain non-working members of the royal family after they initially left the UK in 2020.

In a letter sent on behalf of the King on Monday, senior Palace official Lord Chamberlain said: “It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family.”

In a coordinated briefing to UK media on Tuesday, a person close to Harry and Meghan said the couple “were a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance.” Royal sources told BBC News that Prince Harry and Markle were made aware of the letter before it was made public.

Watch on Deadline

Deadline has contacted a spokesperson for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

The Lord Chamberlain’s letter continued: “Any specific questions from official and state organizations about the courtesies which should be extended to the Duke and Duchess, and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace.”

On Prince Harry and Markle’s security arrangements, the letter added: “Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities.”

Deadline reported on Monday that BBC News’ coverage of Harry and Markle‘s decision to move back to the UK prompted viewer complaints.

The BBC revealed that audience members contacted the UK broadcaster to raise concerns that it was dedicating “too much” airtime to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. The BBC did not disclose how many complaints it received from disgruntled viewers, but rejected the concerns in a notice published on its website.

“We believe our approach to this story was proportionate, offering legitimate analysis of the different implications,” the BBC said.
