content:
EXCLUSIVE: Here’s your first footage from Casey Affleck‘s Venice Film Festival Competition drama, Company, starring Nick Nolte, Ben Mendelsohn, Adelaide Clemens, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, and Caylee Cowan.

The film also introduces Affleck’s son Atticus (who features in the opening footage of the clip above) for the first time on screen and marks the second feature for his son Indiana.

Described as “a meditation on grief, vengeance, forgiveness, and the quiet acts of compassion that can heal even the deepest wounds”, the gothic drama is set over a single night in 1975 when a wintry holiday gathering is interrupted by a mysterious woman who recounts a tale from decades before.

The full synopsis reads: “On a winter night in 1975, a mysterious woman named Evelyn arrives uninvited at a holiday gathering and tells the story of Tom, an aging hermit who rescues a stranded actress during a Colorado blizzard in 1953. To pass the night, the actress recounts an older tale of a farming couple who take in a troubled young drifter as a series of grisly murders spreads fear across the frontier.”

Watch on Deadline

Oscar winner Affleck co-wrote the script with Ron Hansen. Producers include Steven Schneider and Roy Lee via Spooky Features, Catherine Caylee Cowan, Dan Lawler, Affleck, Sean Patrick O’Reilly, K. Asher Levin, Enzo Marc, and Anthony Katagas. Executive producers include Ben Ross via Image Nation Studios, Rami Yasin for Spooky Pictures, Ronnie Exley and Jeremy Ross via Rabbits Black, Ron McLeod, Dr. Terence Chan, Brian Meng, and Maria Breese for 3:33 Creative Productions, and Jonathan Miller.

It has been seven years since Affleck’s sophomore directorial outing, Light Of My Life.

title: BBC Breakout Comedy ‘Small Prophets’ Renewed For Season 2 After Stellar Ratings & Apple TV Pickup
summary: The Homunculi spirits are set to commune once more. The BBC has renewed Small Prophets for a second season after the comedy became a breakout hit for the British broadcaster, drawing up to 9.2 million viewers. Apple TV acquired worldwide rights to Season 1 last month. Created by Mackenzie Crook, star of the UK version […]
content:
The Homunculi spirits are set to commune once more.

The BBC has renewed Small Prophets for a second season after the comedy became a breakout hit for the British broadcaster, drawing up to 9.2 million viewers. Apple TV acquired worldwide rights to Season 1 last month.

Created by Mackenzie Crook, star of the UK version of The Office, the show will be promoted from BBC One to BBC Two for Season 2, which will premiere in 2027.

The series stars Pearce Quigley as Manchester resident Michael Sleep, who is still adjusting to life without his partner, Clea, who mysteriously disappeared seven years earlier.

Watch on Deadline

While working in a DIY store, he hatches a plan with his father, Brian (Michael Palin), to create some Homunculi, magical prophesying spirits, in his garden shed.

Along the way, Michael develops an unlikely friendship with Kacey (Lauren Patel), while navigating the demands of his boss Gordon (Crook) and the watchful eyes of nosy neighbours Bev (Sophie Willan) and Clive (Jon Pointing).

Emma Lawson, BBC interim director of comedy, said: “Mackenzie has created a world packed with wonder, magic and unforgettable characters which feels completely unlike anything else on television and we can’t wait to see where the story takes us next.”

Small Prophets is a Treasure Trove Productions and Channel X North production. It is written, created and directed by Crook. The executive producers are Crook and Lisa Thomas for Treasure Trove, and Alan Marke and Jim Reid for Channel X North. Gill Isles is the producer. Sphere Abacus is the international distributor.

Crook said: “The prophets have foretold that series two will be happening next year and, as we know, they are compelled to speak the truth.”

title: ‘Littermates’ Sets Theatrical Release Via Alamo Exclusives; Comic Dystopian Film Also Sets Fantastic Fest Screening (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson’s indie feature “Littermates” is headed to the big screen. The comic dystopian feature is set to open at over 30 Alamo Drafthouse locations on Nov. 6 via Alamo Exclusives. The film will also have a special presentation screening at Fantastic Fest on Sept. 20, with a conversation with the filmmakers […]
content:
Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson’s indie feature “Littermates” is headed to the big screen. The comic dystopian feature is set to open at over 30 Alamo Drafthouse locations on Nov. 6 via Alamo Exclusives. The film will also have a special presentation screening at Fantastic Fest on Sept. 20, with a conversation with the filmmakers and cast to follow.

The film, which was produced in just 15 days, stars Joey Bader, Kaylee McGregor, Oliver Woolf and Jack Redmayne. Tinkham wrote the script, and the film was produced by Woolf, Woloson, Tinkham and McGregor. Woloson was also the cinematographer and editor, and the film has an original score by Noa Margalit. “Littermates” was produced by That’s The Fish, and Haley Nicole Johnson serves as executive producer.

Per the official synopsis: “Set against the backdrop of a mysterious war, ‘Littermates’ follows two disoriented survivors who take refuge at an isolated cottage in the English countryside. Liam and Mel arrive bloodied, speechless and unable to fully understand what has happened to them. They are taken in by Chester, an enigmatic caretaker who feeds them, teaches them to speak again and establishes a carefully controlled domestic order where good behavior earns “nifties,” tokens that can be exchanged for small comforts including karaoke, hot tub time, dance parties and favorite meals. As explosions, gunfire, sirens and karaoke fill the air, their makeshift family begins to fracture — exposing the fear, loyalty and unanswered questions holding it together.”

Popular on Variety

“We made ‘Littermates’ to explore the strange, primal and often trivial relationship between siblings. At its heart, the film is an unconventional coming-of-age story set against a dystopian backdrop,” directors Scott Tinkham and Michael Woloson said in a statement. “We always imagined the film as something to experience with a crowd, so introducing it at Fantastic Fest and then bringing it to audiences around the country through Alamo Exclusives feels like the perfect way to start this next chapter.”

“Littermates” is the second film from Alamo Exclusives, following the documentary “Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt.”

“’Littermates’ is exactly the kind of discovery Alamo Exclusives exists to champion. It’s funny, audacious, visually confident and nearly impossible to fit inside a conventional box,” Michael Kustermann, CEO of Alamo Drafthouse Cinema, said in a statement. “Through deadpan social absurdity and unnerving family dynamics, Scott and Michael have created a strange little world that is entirely their own. I can’t wait to introduce it to the Fantastic Fest fiends before bringing it to Alamo Drafthouse theaters nationwide.”

“Some of the most important voices in genre cinema emerge from its scrappiest edges, where limitation becomes a point of view,” Lisa Dreyer, director of Fantastic Fest and film innovation, also said in a statement. “’Littermates’ is funny, unnerving, formally exacting and completely confident in its own strange wavelength … exactly the kind of discovery Fantastic Fest exists to champion and Alamo Exclusives was built to carry beyond the festival circuit. Fans of Yorgos Lanthimos will love this one!”

title: The New Chris Rock: The Comedy Icon on Directing ‘Misty Green’ and Not Returning to the Oscars Unless He’s Nominated
summary: Chris Rock isn’t exactly who you remember him to be. He likes to take his time. “What am I trying to say?” he asks himself repeatedly in conversation, pausing to truly consider that question before continuing to speak. And he doesn’t speak at all on an empty stomach. “I don’t want to say something mean […]
content:
Chris Rock isn’t exactly who you remember him to be.

He likes to take his time. “What am I trying to say?” he asks himself repeatedly in conversation, pausing to truly consider that question before continuing to speak. And he doesn’t speak at all on an empty stomach. “I don’t want to say something mean and get canceled,” Rock says more than once while reaching for a bite of a pastrami sandwich. Sure, it’s just a joke. But he’s also a celebrity whose friends over the years have included Dave Chappelle and Kanye West. He’s seen firsthand what can happen when you don’t eat your pastrami.

Thea Traff for Variety

That isn’t to say he’s shed the opinionated, incendiary persona that caught Eddie Murphy’s eye at a New York comedy club one night when Rock was just 19, leading to his being cast in Murphy’s “Beverly Hills Cop II” (1987) and later “Saturday Night Live” (1990-93). Rock was one of the few celebrities to publicly predict Donald Trump would win the 2016 election, and speaking about the president today, Rock says, “I’m not a fan. But it’s weird when somebody gets one thing right, and the one thing almost clears them of all their other sins. The news is fake. He got that right.”

Still, Rock has formed a habit of making concessions to his least generous interpreters before anyone has even criticized him. “People have their reasons, and nobody’s wrong,” he says after remarking that it’s difficult to find actresses interested in roles that involve nudity. Referencing some Black actors’ grievances about the prevalence of Brits and nepo babies in Hollywood — a position he disagrees with and satirizes in his upcoming film “Misty Green” — he says, “They’re valid. I’m not going to dismiss anyone.”

On one hand, that caution feels surprising coming from the man behind “Bring the Pain,” the outrageous 1996 HBO stand-up special that transformed him overnight from an “SNL” has-been who couldn’t get an agent into a global superstar being offered blank checks. Rock went on a lengthy tirade during that hour-long set about a cultural tension he famously referred to as “Black people versus n—-s,” which stoked significant controversy, but not before it brought the house down. And if you thought the recorded version was uncouth, you should have seen him workshop it on tour. “In Oakland one night, I remember dying a death. People wanted to fight, because I didn’t have it right yet,” he recalls. “You gotta go over the line to find the line. That’s what people don’t understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at a club, it’s like, ‘Dude, that’s what the club’s for.’”

On the other hand, Rock is 61. He doesn’t spend much time at the club anymore. “We’re all different people at different points in our lives, and I think I got everything I could out of the last guy — whoever I was then,” he says. “Now I’m this director guy.”

Rock is gearing up for the Toronto International Film Festival premiere of “Misty Green,” his first directorial effort in 12 years, which will hit theaters via A24 in October. Rosalind Eleazar of “Slow Horses” gives a breathtaking performance as the title character, a once-famous actress with a nearly empty bank account who can no longer maintain the ocean views and Equinox membership she’s accustomed to after her sugar daddy dies. The film follows a week of Misty’s life as she vents to her only friend (Anna Kendrick) and rubs elbows with former colleagues (Rock and Adam Driver) while desperately hunting for a gig that will pay enough to cover both her cushy Santa Monica lifestyle and the care of her mentally ill brother, Jordan, played by Daniel Kaluuya in a heartrending return to the big screen.

But as her agent (Topher Grace) reminds her, it’s not particularly desirable to work with Misty Green. “The last time I cast you, you punched this bitch in the face,” Rock’s character says to Misty. (There’s a stunning real-world resonance in this moment that Rock, in his first sit-down interview since Will Smith slapped him at the Oscars in 2022, claims he never noticed. More on that later.)

Rock began his directing career with 2003’s “Head of State” and 2007’s “I Think I Love My Wife.” Both were negatively reviewed; neither succeeded at the box office. By the 2014 release of his thoughtful rom-dramedy “Top Five,” though, Rock had matured as an artist, casting himself as a comedian and recovering addict who spends a day verbally sparring with a reporter and fellow AA attendee (Rosario Dawson). Critics loved it, and the film was moderately profitable.

“Misty Green” is what Rock calls a “tiny” movie — the budget came out to roughly $5 million, he says, less than any of his previous films. But it’s also the most important moment of his career since “Bring the Pain.”

Thea Traff for Variety

That’s in large part because, aside from “Selective Outrage,” the 2023 Netflix special that marked his first time addressing the Smith incident in detail, “Misty Green” is Rock’s first major project since being diagnosed in 2020 with nonverbal learning disorder. “It’s a kind of ADHD-ish, Asperger-y thing,” he says.

Thanks to extensive therapy, “I have a level of concentration and empathy that I just did not have back then,” he says. “I was so good at telling jokes that I didn’t have to face a lot of things. My comedic gifts put me in a position where I didn’t have to grow up. So I’m better equipped to make this kind of movie now.”

Rock returns to his mantra: “I’m a different guy. I’m trying to be, anyway.”

But don’t worry. He’s still making jokes. “We’ll see what happens,” Rock continues. “I’m saying I’m a writer-director guy, then I’ll get an offer for some show on CBS where I’m Mandy Patinkin’s neighbor — ‘Hey, I brought back your wrench!’ — making 80 grand a week.”

What inspired you to write “Misty Green”?

Have you ever read “Breakfast at Tiffany’s”? The drug use. She uses the N-word several times. Like, she’s racist. They should have made that movie. And I like “Frances Ha.” I love “Vicky Cristina Barcelona.” You’re not allowed to say Woody [Allen], so I’m trying to get around it — who makes those types of movies anymore?

I stole from a bunch of movies. The biggest was “Legally Blonde.” Reese Witherspoon is as funny in “Legally Blonde” as Jim Carrey is in “Dumb and Dumber.” The key is that she’s smart. If you only watched the trailer, you would think we’re gonna follow some ditzy girl, but when they make her smart, it elevates it to this whole other thing. So I knew Misty had to be great. You can’t just be a fuck-up. And I didn’t have the money to do it, but I was really going for a “Magnolia” thing. The movie is about Misty Green, but a lot of it’s about L.A. L.A. has got very wonky priorities. There’s a real estate office on the same street as The Ivy on Robertson, and in the window, there are houses for $30-$40 million. In the window. But there’s a homeless guy sleeping right outside. The movie is about that crazy dichotomy.

Tell me about your relationship to L.A.

It’s weird. I just bought a place there [assumes a snobbish affect] so I winter in L.A. I love parts of it. I always say: The average movie studio, like Paramount, what’s in Paramount? There’s cameras, sound equipment. But what are you gonna do with that? Can you really steal that stuff? There’s more value at the average Home Depot than at Paramount, but Paramount’s got armed guards. Why? Because they have dreams in there. And people will do anything to get to their dreams.

L.A. is a complicated place, man. Fame’s a complicated thing. I’ve seen the switch in my lifetime. It used to be that everybody wanted to be great — a great singer, great actor, great comedian. Now it’s just fame, and the greatness is almost assumed. I mean, you’re always gonna be outed at some point if you don’t have the goods. But L.A. is the mecca of that. It can be beautiful. It’s got the best weather in the world. But it also attracts an underbelly that people want to pretend doesn’t exist.

Thea Traff for Variety

Since Misty was relatively popular before her fall from grace, the obvious choice would have been to cast a more famous actress. How did you become aware of Rosalind Eleazar?

Oh, we had other people that I will never name in a million years. It’s a hard part to cast. Some of it was money. Some of it was because we shot in the summer, and people have vacations and shit. Also, there’s a little bit of nudity in the movie, but there was definitely more in the script. Mikey Madison won the Oscar for “Anora,” and you would still have a hard time casting that role today. People have their reasons, and nobody’s wrong.

We just auditioned Rosalind. We were gonna do a Zoom, but she didn’t want to — she flew herself in from London, knowing good and well it would only be 40 minutes. She blew us away. She wasn’t famous, so we kept trying to figure out reasons to not cast her. Different actresses — a singer or two — were attached at different times. But she was just the best one, by a lot.

And as a director, when you’re talking with a celebrity, they’re talking about themselves: “How am I gonna look?” But with Rosalind, it was all character, all the time. I basically didn’t meet Rosalind until we were done with the movie. I was dealing with Misty the whole time.

How did the rest of your cast come together?

Adam really liked “Top Five,” so he would call me periodically. I was like, “Dude, I did ‘Top Five’ 10 years ago.” But every six to eight months, I get a call from Adam Driver. “What are you working on?” I’m sure he’s got a long list of directors that he’s checking with, so when he gets down to the R’s, he calls me. And this time I happened to be working on something.

Similar with Anna Kendrick. It was “Top Five” love, and I loved her movie [“Woman of the Hour”]. She’s a great director. And there’s something about her [dating] Black men [onscreen] that’s kinda like, “Hmm! OK …”

Daniel was kind of retired. We hung out when I was on tour with Chappelle. I had to beg him. He was the only one I had to beg. Everybody else was like, “I can’t wait to do this movie!” Daniel, I had to go to his hotel. I definitely tap-danced. It was worth it.

Why was he hesitant?

Well, we had no money. People want to get paid! This is a good time — all these streaming services and diversity and whatever. Everybody’s getting paid on some level. But this movie was like …

You were paying scale?

Kind of. And people don’t say yes to scale right away. Like, “OK, I guess I’ll go home with you.” But he knew Rosalind because they’re both Brits. He had seen her do theater. He was the only person that really knew how good Rosalind was. That’s what got him excited, more than anything.

There’s a joke in the movie about Brits “taking” roles from Black American actors. Did you write that before or after casting two Brits as American siblings?

Before. I’ve been in those rooms where people complain about nepo babies and Brits, and it’s been the same complaints for the last 30 years. “We need our own distribution.” Whatever. They’re valid. I’m not going to dismiss anyone. But these movies play all over the world. They’re not just ours. And I don’t know a lot of better actors than Daniel Kaluuya.

Thea Traff for Variety

What was your thought process for the role you play?

I got to a point where — I sound like Olivia Wilde — I decided at the last minute to act in the movie. I was really thinking about doing a movie that I just directed. It was a self-imposed “Fuck being on camera.” I was actually imagining Donald Glover. He’s really hard to get. But I love him. We’re talking about another thing.

You mentioned that you “got everything” you could out of who you were earlier in your career, and that you’re now a “director guy.” Who’s that? What’s he about?

I like directing and writing a lot. I like the discipline, how contained it is. When you’re acting, if that’s your main hustle, it’s a lot of campaigning. You’re on the campaign trail [looking for work]. When you’re a writer-director, your script does all the work. So as I get older and less vain, I’m like, “Do I really feel like coloring my hair? Do I really feel like not having carbs for six months?” Spike [Lee] used to be in all the movies, and then one day he wasn’t. Clint Eastwood used to be in all the movies, and then one day he wasn’t. [Ben] Stiller too. Stiller is really the guy I look at, like, “How do I gracefully become this other thing?”

I always say: If only smart people get your jokes, they’re not that smart. All your idols were pop stars. Everybody we think is a genius was a pop star. Miles Davis was a pop star. They played “Kind of Blue” on FM radio in the middle of the afternoon after Kool & the Gang — that’s how pop Miles Davis was. Bob Marley’s a pop artist. Louis Armstrong was as pop as Harry Styles.

And you’re looking to become a pop star?

Not in the sense that I want to make a Marvel movie or something, but you can make a great piece of art that everybody gets. Chris Nolan’s last two movies are the most popular art movies ever made. “Oppenheimer,” in the hands of somebody else, would have been a little movie. But in his hands, it’s fucking … “The Odyssey” is like, what the fuck? And the last “Joker” — not “Joker 2” but “Joker 1” — is a freaking art movie. That’s what I’m aspiring to do.

Several characters in “Misty Green” also aspire to make great art that’s broadly popular, but they all compromise. Industry pressures, family problems and finances force them to accept careers and lifestyles they did not want. Where did that theme come from?

It’s part of being a grown-up. We live in this world of no settling, but it’s like, “Dude, everybody settles.” Not only do we settle — we learn to fall in love with settling. One of my favorite song lyrics is by Garth Brooks: “Thank God for unanswered prayers.” We all hit an age where you’re like, “Oh shit, I gotta stop. This bullshit has to stop.” I did a joke 100 years ago where I said, “I want to find God before God finds me.” That’s what everybody in the movie is trying to do. “Let me find God, because when God knocks on my door, it’s not going to be good news.”

What has that process looked like in your life?

I’ve been lucky. I’ve made some money. I’m not swimming in it. I’m not on jets all the time. I don’t own a boat. But I always tell people: Your monthly nut — that’s your religion. You think you’re Catholic? How much are your monthly bills? Because if you can keep your monthly low enough, you can say no to things. I don’t own a car. Yeah, I have a place in New York and L.A., but I don’t even have a doorman. I live on a normal block in both places. You can ring my bell. It doesn’t say “Rock” on the bell, but you can ring my bell. And I do this purposely, so I don’t have to do things I don’t want to do. There’s meetings I don’t have to take because I keep my expenses down. Holly Robinson’s mom, the great Dolores Robinson, was a talent manager, and she used to say, “You have to spend income, not if-come.” That’s the problem with most people in Hollywood. They’re spending if-come. If-come will ruin your life.

It’s been 12 years since you last directed a movie.

I can’t believe they let me direct a movie. I kept expecting to see Donald Glover on the set, like, “Hey, what are you doing here?”

Were you truly worried you wouldn’t be able to make “Misty Green”?

Unless you’re a Leo DiCaprio, box-office-guaranteed guy, every movie is a miracle. A movie is a loan you don’t have to pay back. That’s a weird gamble, because with most gambles, they get your house. I’ve been lucky enough to be in the right place at the right time. Some of it is my work speaking for me. Some of it is just being a nice guy. Being a decent hang will get you more work than you would imagine.

Did it feel that miraculous to you when you directed “Head of State” 23 years ago?

Me and Chappelle always joke that that was back when I was Drake. Back when I was Harry Styles. Man, I was so hot. Like, what the fuck, dude? I got money to do “Good Hair.” I did “Pootie Tang.” I was literally doing whatever I wanted. So in retrospect, “Head of State” is not even remotely ambitious enough for the juice I had at the time. If I knew what I know now, I wouldn’t have starred in “Head of State.” I would have written it for Denzel [Washington]. I didn’t have a real sense of my own power at the time.

At what point did that change?

You have your career, and you have your life. And they intertwine from time to time. Not everybody makes it. Some people are just dead, who you loved. And there’s people who didn’t make smart decisions, who now don’t get to express themselves, which is really not cool. Everybody doesn’t get to make the movie they wrote. So I don’t take it for granted. And I always say: The worst thing that can happen to an artist is not that you’re washed up. The worst thing that can happen is that you’re not washed up, and no one wants to hear you. That you’re actually still good, and you’ve fucking worn out your welcome. I’ve seen it happen to other people where — I’m not gonna say who — but things just got so complicated.

Chris Rock on location for ” Misty Green” Merrick Morton/A24

“Bring the Pain” is when you truly became a celebrity. What has changed about your experience of fame from then to now?

It used to just be about getting free stuff. And how you’re basically on the third date with anybody you date. They’re like, “I know you!” You’re at least on the second date. You skip a date just by being famous.

Part of this is just getting diagnosed [with NVLD], but when people come up to me, it used to scare me. Now, I realize that you’re making somebody’s day. I try to ask them at least one question. “Where are you from?” As simple as that. And they’re like, “Oh, shit! I had a conversation with him!” I’ve learned to accept this is who I am. It’s like basketball. If you’re seven feet tall, you can’t get mad at people asking if you play.

I try not to think about fame, but it could be a lot worse — you could be infamous. So I accept it. It helps me get work.

Your first two movies struggled at the box office. “Top Five” did better, but we live in a different world now. Is there more pressure on you this time around?

I would love to have a box office hit. I would love for the people that helped me make this movie to get their money back. I’m dropping names today — Warren Beatty told me a long time ago, “The only measure of success is: Does it get you another job?” So I hope this movie does very well, because I hope people continue to show faith in me. I hope Adam Driver calls me six months from now, like, “What are you working on, dude?” I hope Michael B. Jordan calls me up. Part of it is about making something that does well, but it’s also got to be really good. Because all these movies end up in the exact same place, and you don’t know which ones made money. At some point, when you’re going through your Apple TV looking for a movie, the hits and the misses are right next to each other. Isn’t that weird?

So you’re playing the long game.

I always play the long game. I’m not looking for Michael B. Jordan numbers here. I’m realistic. But hopefully, it makes enough money that somebody at A24 calls me up and goes, “What do you want to do next?” That’s all I care about.

It seems like “Misty Green” will become part of the awards conversation.

You’re not gonna hear me say that. No one’s ever talked about anything I’ve made like that before. You’re the first person. You. Right now.

Rosalind Eleazar is already in Variety’s predictions.

I’ll say this: 100 years ago, when we were doing “New Jack City,” we rehearsed for a week before Wesley [Snipes] got there. It’s me, Ice-T, Al Payne, Vanessa Williams, Bill Nunn. We’re rehearsing, and we’re fine. Then Wesley comes. None of us knew Wesley. At the table read, Wesley sits at the head of the table and puts on the Nino Brown hat. He starts reading, and — I’m not lying to you — within 10 pages, we realize we’re in a motherfucking classic. We were looking at him like we weren’t in the fucking movie. Like, “Oh my God.”

And I say that to say: By the end of the first week of filming, I’m looking at Rosalind like, “Oh, shit, she is throwing the fuck down.” To the point that I had to elevate my own work. Like, “Shit! I got scenes with her next week!” The only other time I’ve had that feeling was with Wesley. Like, “Oh, a star is born.”

What was it like to direct her?

The thing about her — about all the great actresses, because I went through this with Rosario too, and she should have gotten nominated — all great actors are just really smart. Her script notes were impeccable. So anything false: “Get rid of that.” We would argue back and forth, and 90% of the time, she was right.

So it’s not about directing her. It’s about protecting her. It’s about keeping things truthful around her. You ever have a friend, and they lie, and even though you don’t know what they’re lying about, you just know there’s a lie being told? Because when you know somebody, they speak in a rhythm. And lies are spoken at a different rhythm than the truth. Scenes are like that — what’s the rhythm? So directing her was just beautiful music. She was always on key.

Directing is 80% casting. It really is. I can say the same things for Daniel and Adam and Anna. And Topher Grace is great. Topher actually read two parts at a table read I had three years ago. This guy’s got “Spider-Man” money. He don’t need to be at my fucking table read. But he smelled a decent script, and he got in early.

You made “Head of State” and “I Think I Love My Wife” at the height of your stand-up fame. Back then, did you see yourself wanting to make something like “Misty Green”?

I didn’t go to college. I got a GED. I wasn’t that sophisticated. Like, I played Pookie in “New Jack City.” I had just done this dramatic role, and I remember my agent telling me about [Julian] Schnabel’s “Basquiat,” but I didn’t know who Basquiat was. I wasn’t sophisticated enough to do “Misty Green” back when I did “Head of State.” I just wasn’t. Getting treatment [for NVLD] has changed my life. I’ve gone from reading three books a year to 23.

But hey, we’re all working on ourselves. I don’t want to be one of those people bragging about their therapy. I crawled in there like everybody else. Nobody struts into therapy. You crawl in there on your knees, soaked from crying.

But there was a turning point in your work before you started therapy. “Top Five” was a big jump in 2014, and you did a Broadway play in 2011. When did you start to see yourself as an artist and filmmaker instead of just a comedian?

Hey, being a comedian is the hardest one of those. It’s the only one they don’t have a school for. But you’re right. I did the play — boy, there’s nothing like doing a play. I wish I could do another play. Plays are fucking magical. It’s some of the best writing in the world.

I’m really into what I’m not already seeing. Before there was Spike Lee, there was not a Black guy like Spike Lee. It just didn’t exist. And before Denzel — I mean, Sidney Poitier did some great work, but he was never the bad guy. Denzel has done a fucking roller-coaster ride of parts. And what would Richard [Pryor] have done if he was sober? Richard did a lot of great work — my favorite is actually “Blue Collar” — but there was more there. He got sick, and there was the drugs and the fire, but there was a lot more there. So I don’t know. I’m trying to be a guy I haven’t seen, or at least that I haven’t seen as a Black guy.

You’ve explored substance abuse a lot in your work. Your question about what a sober Pryor could have achieved feels present in both “Top Five” and “Misty Green.”

I mean, my brother drank himself to death. I’ve lost a lot of friends to substance abuse. Here’s the crazy thing: In most instances, the ones who died are better than the ones who haven’t quite reached their potential because of their substance abuse. There’s something sadder about a person coming in fourth place than a person dying, actually. Because you know they could have come in first if it wasn’t for substances.

It’s been a part of my life since I was in my late teens. The crack epidemic in America, especially in Bed-Stuy, was insane, so that really implanted into my brain. There was nothing like my neighborhood when crack was big, man. The things I’ve seen, I wish I could have not seen them. Users aren’t the only abusers, as Jay-Z famously said.

So substance abuse has been really, really, really big in my life. But I’ve been very fortunate. I like drugs, but they soothe me; they don’t move me. Like, “We’re gonna do some coke? I’ll do some coke.” But I wouldn’t cross the street to do some coke. I’m not like, “Oh, my friend is uptown, he’s got stuff, we’re gonna get in a cab for half an hour” — no, no, no. I’m going to bed. Now, even with drinking, you get a certain age and these hangovers are bad, dude. Like, I love the morning. I love being up at 7 a.m. and walking and listening to a podcast or whatever the hell, attacking the day.

What’s your next goal after this movie?

I’m trying to write a book. A series of essays, like all the [James] Baldwin books. The title is “When the Homeless Know Your Name.” Because when they ask you for money, it’s one thing. When they ask me for money, they know I have it — it’s a whole ‘nother thing. AIso, I came to this realization that being an author is the highest form of art. Half the world’s at war over stuff in books. No one’s getting killed over a freaking miniseries. Nobody’s getting killed over “Love Island.” But you put some shit in a book 1,000 years ago, and people would get their heads chopped off. Books are powerful.

I’ve been reading. I read the Baldwin biography, that big 700-page thing. I read the Elon [Musk] one recently. They had nothing in common, but they both knew they had a place in history while they were doing it, not after the fact. That’s something. That’s something.

You were in the Lorne Michaels documentary earlier this year. What sticks with you about your time at “Saturday Night Live”?

It’s the best doc ever where you don’t learn one thing about the guy. The most interesting people in the world — who do not tell you about him. But I met Lorne Michaels and haven’t been broke a day since. That is my guy.

Chris Farley and me and Adam [Sandler] and David Spade shared an office. We would go, “Oh, let’s make a McDonald’s run.” “Carolyn Bessette’s here tonight! You gonna talk to her?” “No, you talk to her.” Then she came in with JFK. “Oh, that’s what she’s going for.” It was a magical time. All you remember are the friendships. I didn’t go to college, but those would have been the years I was in college.

You mentioned that you think your hosting career is over. Have you been asked to host the Oscars again?

When people answer those questions, they’re being disrespectful to the people that got the gig. They have great hosts. Conan O’Brien is amazing. Nikki Glaser is amazing on the Golden Globes. I’m not going to say never, but my time might have passed, honestly.

How has it felt to think about returning to the Oscars for the first time since 2022?

I’m not getting nominated. The only way I’ll go back is if I’m nominated, and I’m not getting nominated. And that’s OK. We’ll deal with that if it happens. Like, let’s manage expectations.

But you know that all eyes are on you when it comes to the Oscars. And you made a movie about a woman who smacks her colleague, where you play a character that has to decide whether to forgive her.

Oh. Yeah. You know, I never even thought about it like that.

No?

No. This is literally the first time I — that she got connected to — yeah.

It’s been four years since Will Smith slapped you. How do you feel about it all now?

Hey, man. You know, to answer your question a little bit, I wish nothing would have happened. And also, I don’t want to say anything that takes any attention away from Rosalind and how good she is in this movie. It’s a crazy world. We walk by homeless people. There’s all sorts of shit going on right now. Me having a bad day is not the biggest — it’s not that important.

Is that what you’re saying with all of the juxtaposition in “Misty Green”? That hard things have happened to you in this business, but they don’t matter in the end?

A long time ago, I went to a comedy club on a freaking whim. I got onstage and did about five minutes, and the owner of the club said, “You should come back.” If he didn’t say that, I probably wouldn’t have come again. That one night changed the whole trajectory of not just me, but my whole family.

So, you know. What am I trying to say? Showbiz has been very, very good to me. In a world where we have trillionaires, I don’t have that much money. But my dad got sick when I was poor, and my mother got sick when I had some money. Dad’s dead. My mom’s doing great. You know what I mean? It’s literally that simple. So I’m good. I’m really good.

content:
Grammy-winning artist FKA Twigs has begun principal photography as the legendary entertainer and activist Josephine Baker.

Production on “Josephine Baker” has kicked off in France and will run through Nov. 13, with additional shooting in Sofia, Bulgaria.

The film is directed and co-written by Maïmouna Doucouré, the César- and Sundance-winning filmmaker behind “Cuties” and “Hawa,” working from a script developed with co-writer Olivier Lorelle. Studiocanal and Bien ou Bien Productions are producing, with CPB Films and Leyland Films serving as associated producers. The project carries the official blessing of Baker’s sons Jean-Claude Bouillon Baker and Brian Bouillon Baker, along with the Rainbow tribe.

Joining FKA Twigs in the ensemble are Aunjanue Ellis-Taylor (“King Richard,” “Origin”), Giuseppe Maggio (“Mrs. Playmen,” “Being Maria”), Grégory Montel (“Call My Agent!,” “Barking Dogs”), Benjamin Millepied (“Black Swan,” “Dune: Part Two”), Féodor Atkine (“Dog 51,” “Out of Love”), Alex Lutz (“Strangers by Night,” “Connemara”) and Harmony Riley.

Popular on Variety

The film traces Baker’s arc from a childhood marked by racial segregation in the United States to her breakthrough as one of the most celebrated stage and screen performers of 1920s Paris, through her service with the French Resistance during the Second World War, and into her 1951 return to America – where she confronted a country still shaped by the injustices she had fled decades earlier.

FKA Twigs brings a cross-disciplinary background to the role. A singer-songwriter, dancer-choreographer and visual artist, she broke into film with Alma Har’el’s “Honey Boy” and has since appeared in Rupert Sanders’ “The Crow” and David Lowery’s A24 feature “Mother Mary,” opposite Anne Hathaway and Michaela Coel.

Doucouré’s short film “Mother(S)” won some 70 international prizes, among them the Sundance Film Festival International Award and the 2017 César for best short film. Her debut feature “Cuties” took the directing award in the World Cinema Dramatic competition at Sundance before reaching Netflix audiences globally.

Studiocanal will handle theatrical distribution across its own territory footprint – the U.K., France, Germany, Italy, Benelux, Poland, Australia and New Zealand – and is managing worldwide sales.

content:
Altman2 Entertainment, Vital Signs Entertainment and Galaxie Productions have released the trailer for “The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World,” a new documentary about the history and cultural impact of the iconic sci-fi franchise.

The film’s official logline reads, “Drawing on exclusive interviews, never-before-seen archival material and first-hand accounts from the people who built the franchise as well as celebrity superfans, ‘The Sixty-Year Mission’ traces ‘Star Trek’ from its turbulent beginnings in the 1960s through its transformation into one of the most enduring and influential properties in entertainment history.”

The documentary features interviews with “Star Trek” legends like William Shatner, Walter Koenig and George Takei, as well as Rod Roddenberry, Simon Pegg, Jonathan Frakes, Brent Spiner, Gates McFadden, Ethan Peck, Christina Chong, Robert Picardo, Denise Crosby, Nana Visitor, Terry Farrell, Armin Shimerman and Rainn Wilson.

Popular on Variety

“’Star Trek’ has been celebrated countless times, but we wanted to make the film that goes beyond the mythology and asks why this unlikely television series survived, evolved, thrived and ultimately became an icon of popular culture,” said Mark A. Altman, writer and director of “The Sixty-Year Mission.” “The real story is full of extraordinary creative risks, battles, failures and breakthroughs. What emerged from all of that was something far bigger than a franchise. It became a cultural institution that has inspired millions of fans and defined a hopeful vision of the future for generations.”

Shatner serves as executive producer of “The Sixty-Year Mission,” alongside Altman, Michael S. Broder, Daren Dochterman, Ashley E. Miller, Alan Pao and Thomas P. Vitale. Altman2 Entertainment, Vital Signs Entertainment, Aaron Rattner and Galaxie Productions serve as producers.

Tickets are now on sale for “The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World,” which opens exclusively in Regal Cinemas on Oct. 8. Check out the trailer below.

title: India’s Gubbara Launches Distribution Arm as ‘Termite’ Heads to Toronto (EXCLUSIVE)
summary: India’s Gubbara Entertainment is launching a distribution arm, timed to the world premiere of its short film “Termite” at the Toronto Film Festival and a chapter of its Kashmir feature anthology “Muhabbat Se” at the inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir. The distribution push marks the next phase for Gubbara Entertainment, which is […]
content:
India’s Gubbara Entertainment is launching a distribution arm, timed to the world premiere of its short film “Termite” at the Toronto Film Festival and a chapter of its Kashmir feature anthology “Muhabbat Se” at the inaugural International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir.

The distribution push marks the next phase for Gubbara Entertainment, which is approaching its third anniversary. That effort dates to 2024, when the company set up a $1 million fund for script development at Cannes.

A chapter of the anthology will have its world premiere at the International Film Festival of Jammu and Kashmir on Sept. 8, ahead of a theatrical release in select cities via PVR starting Oct. 23. Among the anthology’s chapters is “Arifa,” directed by Rohin Raveendran.

Popular on Variety

Gubbara’s latest production, “Termite,” will have its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival. Kiterabbit Films and the Azim Premji Foundation partnered with Gubbara on the short, which comes from Academy Award-nominated filmmaker Shaunak Sen (“All That Breathes”), marking his move into fiction filmmaking.

“My ambition is to create and strengthen a pipeline. A slate is pointless unless it delivers. I want everything we create at Gubbara to reach an audience. That is how an independent production company becomes a sustainable creative business. Films languishing in hard drives is tragic,” said Dimpy Agrawal, founder of Gubbara Entertainment.

Agrawal came from a banking background before entering the industry, working at Phantom Studios, Dharma Production and Netflix ahead of founding Gubbara Entertainment in 2024. She has built the company’s strategy around financial sustainability, rigorous development, deep creator relationships and audience development through a bespoke distribution network.

“We are building capital around different stages of a project’s life cycle rather than waiting for studios or platforms to enter once a project is fully developed. Development is where we began but our financial strategy has now expanded to rights acquisition, release, and alternate distribution. I am creating infrastructure across these stages that is both scalable and can be replicated by other founders,” Agrawal said.

Gubbara has nine long-form titles in active development, has produced seven short documentaries, and has one fiction short and one anthology feature in post-production. The company has worked with six debutant filmmakers – Pearl Malik (“Delicate Darling”), Shaunak Sen (“Termite”), Nitin Baid (“Chashma”), Durgesh Singh (“Kashmir Willow”), Garima Sadhwani (“Khelne Chalogi?”) and Nandini Mahbubani (“Udd Chali Hoon”) – and five women filmmakers, including Archana Phadke and Parinaz Jal alongside Malik, Sadhwani and Mahbubani. Its long-form slate is set to roll out in 2027.

“I am not working with limitations of format or marketing buckets. Just because our long form slate rolls out in 2027 doesn’t mean I will not make short films. We run a short film fellowship. And I will continue to make them despite a robust feature and series slate. The features we are making have a pocket size the story demands. It will be hard to slot them and this is intentional,” Agrawal said.

Gubbara has focused on partnerships throughout its build-out, working with organizations including the Azim Premji Foundation as well as individual creators, and casting itself less as a conventional commissioning studio and more as an ongoing creative partner.

“I want the creators I work with to think of me first when they think about their next project. These are the kind of creative partnerships I nurture. The magic lies in finding the people who you can repeatedly create with,” Agrawal said.

The year ahead is pivotal for Gubbara, with collaborations involving streaming platforms, studios and major creators set to roll out as the company’s distribution strategy is tested.

“I believe in talking after the work is done. I am very proud of where we are at right now. I know where we want to be but I will always leave enough room for things I cannot apprehend right now. Some of our best has come out of being curious and intrepid. I am ready for the ride ahead,” Agrawal said.

title: Amazon MGM Snaps Up ‘Throttled’ Romance Based On Lauren Asher Book; ‘Off Campus’ Star Josh Heuston Leads Cast

content:
Amazon MGM Studios has taken worldwide rights to Throttled, a feature adaptation of Lauren Asher‘s motorsport racing romance novel, to star Josh Heuston of the hit romantic drama series, Off Campus.

The first book in Asher’s Dirty Air series, Throttled tells the story of an ambitious young woman who joins her brother on the racing circuit and falls into a forbidden, high-stakes romance with her brother’s ruthless teammate and fiercest racing rival, played by Heuston.

Nzingha Stewart is set to direct the streaming title from a script adapted by Melissa Osborne. Max Handelman and Elizabeth Banks of Brownstone Productions are producing along with Ethea Entertainment’s Jennifer Gibgot and Andrew Panay, as well as Garrett Grant. Alison Small of Brownstone Productions and author Asher are exec producing.

Virtually every member of this package has history with Amazon MGM. In addition to Heuston, this includes Stewart, who comes to the project after earning Emmy, DGA and PGA Award nominations for her work on the hit Prime Video series, Daisy Jones & the Six; screenwriter Osborne, who penned Prime Video’s My Fault: London; and producer Grant, who worked on The Man With the Bag, the Christmas action comedy coming to Prime Video December 2, which stars Arnold Schwarzenegger and Alan Ritchson.

Watch on Deadline

Most recently, Banks and her Brownstone set up a Prime Video series centered on the Karen Read trials, where Banks would play the lead role and exec produce. Ethea is coming off The Last Sunrise, Prime’s film adaptation of the Anna Todd romance novel, after producing the After films based on Todd’s books. Most recently, they set up House of Crowns, a romance series in early development at Amazon MGM, based on a forthcoming novel from Todd.

title: Hot-Button Play ‘Downstate’ Confirmed For Broadway, Leans Into Controversy
summary: Downstate, Bruce Norris’ controversial play about a group home housing convicted sex offenders, will, as expected, get a Broadway staging this fall, and far from shying away from its hot-button subject matter, the production, with Scott Rudin and Barry Diller producing, is leaning into the debate. content:
Downstate, Bruce Norris‘ controversial play about a group home housing convicted sex offenders, will, as expected, get a Broadway staging this fall, and far from shying away from its hot-button subject matter, the production, with Scott Rudin and Barry Diller producing, is leaning into the debate.

The producers confirmed the Broadway staging today – it’s set to begin previews Saturday, October 17, at the Booth Theatre ahead of a Sunday, November 15, opening night – and released a trailer that not only features the usual favorable critics’ quotes but also a notorious slam from right-wing politico Ted Cruz.

Watch the trailer above.

Cruz’s quote – “So now the corporate media is praising pedophillia” – was first made on X in the senator’s response to a favorable review given the play by the Washington Post when Downstate was staged Off Broadway in 2022. Another quote in the video comes from New York Post critic Johnny Oleksinski: “How can you miss the play that will thoroughly piss off half of America?”

Downstate, to be directed by Tony winner Joe Mantello, will play a limited 12-week engagement at the Booth Theater. It’s been generating controversy (and overwhelmingly favorable reviews) since its world premiere in 2018, followed by a 2019 UK staging at the National Theatre and the Off Broadway premiere at Playwrights Horizons in 2022.

Today’s announcement of the Broadway staging refers to Downstate as “one of the most fearless American plays of the modern era,” and the synopsis suggests why:

“In downstate Illinois, four men convicted of sex crimes against minors live together in a group home, their every movement governed by restrictions that continue to close in around them. The house’s fragile order begins to fracture as an accuser arrives to confront his abuser, bringing with him a storm of unspoken memories. Shockingly funny, savage and furiously political, Bruce Norris’s play pulls audiences into a world where punishment is unending, compassion itself can feel like a transgression, and forgiveness is always out of reach.”

Among the critics’ quotes included with the announcement in a quote from Peter Marks’ WaPo review that so angered Cruz: “Downstate is proof that you can love a play that turns you inside out.”

Also announced today was the cast: The Broadway staging of Downstate will feature Cassie Beck, K. Todd Freeman, Francis Guinan, Adrian Martinez, Al’Jaleel McGhee, Thomas Sadoski, Ivy Wolk and Liza Colón-Zayas.

The production reunites producer Rudin and his frequent collaborator Mantello: The two most recently scored with the Broadway revival of Arthur Miller’s Death of Salesman, the most Tony Award-winning show of the 2025-2026 season with six wins including Best Revival of a Play and Best Direction of a Play.

The creative team for Downstate will include scenic designer Scott Pask, costume designer Ann Roth, lighting designer Heather Gilbert and sound designer Mikaal Sulaiman.

title: As NFL Season Kicks Off, Here Are Five Things In The Mix For 2026
summary: The NFL is back – not that it ever really left. This week, the actual on-field action begins with […]
content:
The NFL is back – not that it ever really left.

The league that rules the media business, Madison Avenue and American culture has managed to turn once-obscure events like the combine in February, the draft in April and the schedule release in May into major events. This week, the actual on-field action begins with a novel kickoff to the regular season.

A rematch of last February’s Super Bowl will feature the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots in NBC’s season opener on Wednesday night. It’s the first time since 2012 the season has started on a Wednesday, one of the remaining rare days of the week that is usually devoid of NFL games. A one-off or a harbinger of future game creep? Read on.

The following night, the Los Angeles Rams will take on the San Francisco 49ers in Australia, the first visit to the continent by the NFL as it continues its international push.

Watch on Deadline

Is all of this empire building, with ratings, revenue and team valuations continuing to notch new records, ever going to hit the wall? Couldn’t the league be nearing its ceiling?

“I’ve learned never to doubt the NFL” Martin Blich, U.S. head of sports partnerships and investment for ad giant WPP Media, told Deadline in an interview.

“There’s always a point of saturation, but we haven’t gotten to the point of saturation,” agreed Mark Conrad, a professor of law and ethics at Fordham University’s business school. “The NFL is only about 20 games a season. It’s not basketball, it’s not baseball.”

While conquest seems to be assured, there still will be a number of intriguing elements this season. Here are five of the biggest:

1. Waiting All Day For Wednesday Night?

Along with the season opener, the new wrinkle for 2026 is a game on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Along with the recently created Black Friday window, the game will give the NFL presence over three days in a key holiday window.

With Black Friday and also Christmas Day games on Netflix only becoming a thing over the past couple of years, some have wondered if the NFL has a wandering eye. It planted games on Christmas opposite the long-established NBA slate. Could a Wednesday slot be next?

Hans Schroeder, EVP of media distribution for the NFL, splashed some cold water on that notion during a recent call with the media. “I don’t know if we’re looking at Wednesday night football as a night for regularly scheduled NFL games,” he said. Rather, the growth of Thanksgiving ratings in recent years shows “how core football, food and family” are over that holiday span, he added. Viewership trends “suggested to us that there’s an opportunity to make that bigger, and that Wednesday night of Thanksgiving, as people often are going back to… they’re traveling, they’re back in their hometowns, they’re together, they’re out, and this is a great intersection.”

WPP’s Blich said he is “excited to see” how the Wednesday opener resonates with viewers. He said it remains unclear whether “people are prepared for the Wednesday after Labor Day, versus the Thursday that everybody had been attuned to.”

2. Billion-Dollar Rights Fight

Due to a “change of control” provision in the NFL’s 11-year deals with its current media partners, the league is understood to have the option to revisit those deals. That could mean billions of additional dollars being coughed up by already cost-conscious traditional rightsholders like Fox, NBCUniversal and CBS/Paramount. The 2025 merger of Skydance and Paramount initially triggered the change-of-control clause, and the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery deal could do likewise.

Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch put an emphatic stake in the ground recently, declaring on the company’s quarterly earnings call that the company doesn’t plan to alter its timetable. Asked about Murdoch’s comments, Schroeder deflected, as did CBS Sports President David Berson at a recent media preview day in New York.

“That’s really a question for them,” Schroeder said.

“I’m not going to speak to Fox’s comments, obviously,” Berson said. “We have an incredible relationship with the NFL. We talk to them daily on a whole variety of topics. We have lots of intersecting business with them. … We continue to have discussions with them. Nothing to share at this point.”

Berson highlighted the reach of CBS, which has been the No. 1 broadcast network in 17 of last 18 years. He also noted the 11-year duration of the current contract, which will expire in 2032.

“There’s plenty of runway here,” he said, and “no specific timing constraints.”

Schroeder and his league colleagues were pressed by reporters about their approach to rights negotiations, especially given the challenging state of traditional media compared with Big Tech.

“We’re always talking to our partners,” Schroeder said We’re always talking about what we can do better, both in what’s right in front of us and what’s longer term. So, I don’t think anything’s changed on our end. We’re always going to look at opportunities to sort of make sure we have the right model.”

Repeatedly emphasizing the league talking point that 87% of games are available on free, over-the-air broadcast, he said reach would always be important. And yet, six decades after games first lit up on TV, league officials “continue to engage the marketplace, evaluate the marketplace, and continue to talk to our partners and the market more broadly,” Schroeder added. “We’re always going to look for whether those are incremental opportunities” – either with pure-play streamers like Netflix or with additional inventory going to traditional broadcasters.

3. Global Ambitions

The Australia game extends a long push of the NFL to expand globally. In recent seasons, it has widened the scope from an initial slate in the UK to include Mexico, Brazil, Ireland, Spain and Germany.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said over the summer that he expected the league to soon play games in Japan. Schroeder noted “a long history of football in Japan” spanning decades. He called the country “a great market with, you know, a great understanding and love of football already.”

With UK games closing in on two decades as a fixture on the NFL schedule, there has been growing speculation about an NFL franchise potentially being set up outside of the U.S. NFL execs aren’t willing to go there yet, but Schroeder said putting on games in international markets “really energizes a weekend, and you see the strength of football in some of these markets when it all comes together. I think there’s more and more interest from cities around the world about hosting NFL games.”

4. Advertisers Move The Chains

With all but a handful of the top 100 Nielsen-rated programs in a typical year being NFL games, demand from advertisers remains robust.

Blich said the upfront sales process was “really strong.” Over the last five years, he added, “If you’re not placing ads in the upfront, you’re at risk of not having access.” The robust interest helped propel Disney to an early sellout of Super Bowl inventory. ABC will air its first Super Bowl in 20 years next February, with the game simultaneously airing on ESPN for the first time.

Despite boom times in many respect, measurement remains a contentious issue. Nielsen, as ever, remains in the crosshairs as it looks to strike a balance among linear, streaming and out-of-home.

Paul Ballew, the NFL’s chief data and analytics officer, said the league is trying to “make sense” of recent changes at Nielsen, which has expanded its counting of out-of-home viewing. “They’ve rushed in terms of a number of fixes into the market, we don’t have enough impact data to fully assess, we’re still trying to make sense of it, still trying to make sense of some of the logic behind some of the methodological changes.”

Initially, he said, updated Nielsen methodology “looks like a negative for sports. On the other side, co-viewing, or partial co-viewing implementation is a positive.

“So we’re going to have to continue to spend some time pulling this apart and making sense of it. … It’s adding into the amount of homework we have to do. … We do think it’s a misstep on Nielsen’s part, to go do this, the way they’re doing it. And it continues to accelerate our pressure point to pursue ongoing measurement improvements, because it’s so critically important to us, and to everybody else in this space.

Berson of CBS sees the recent changes as largely positive. “We’re pleased that the viewership metrics are finally capturing what we think is the accurate audience,” he said.

5. Stream On, You Crazy Streamer

The big question on many fans’ minds heading into the season is about streaming. Will games keep migrating away from traditional TV and toward Big Tech? YouTube’s acquisition of Sunday Ticket rights and Amazon’s successful takeover of Thursday nights are bringing significant benefits to the league and those stakeholders, but some fans remain wary.

The tension begs a number of questions. What would the biggest sports programming in the U.S. look like if even more of it goes to streaming? Would the league consider a form of equity partnership akin to its 10% stake in ESPN in order to keep broadcasters as primary partners?

“We want to be on the platform screens where our fans are spending their time,” Schroeder said.

Broadcast television, he added, “continues to be the core and the foundation of everything we do.”

At the same time, “we know our fans are there” on streaming platforms. “And we’re going to be selective and judicious with where and how we go onto those platforms.”

title: AMC Global Media Settles Breach Of Contract Suit With ‘Walking Dead’ Creator, Producers
summary: AMC Global Networks said Tuesday it has entered a settlement agreement worth $120 million with The Walking Dead creator Robert Kirkman and franchise producers for a breach of contract lawsuit dating from 2022. The case was set to go to trial in October. The agreement calls for AMC to pay a total of $120 million […]
content:
AMC Global Networks said Tuesday it has entered a settlement agreement worth $120 million with The Walking Dead creator Robert Kirkman and franchise producers for a breach of contract lawsuit dating from 2022.

The case was set to go to trial in October.

The agreement calls for AMC to pay a total of $120 million starting with a cash payment of $85 million by September 18, and $35 million no later than January 31, 2027, the company said in an SEC filing. The latter amount will be treated as an advance against modified adjusted gross receipts participation amounts that will accrue to the plaintiffs under contractual arrangements relating to The Walking Dead and Fear The Walking Dead.

Plaintiffs, who also include Glen Mazzara, David Alpert, Gale Anne Hurd and Charles Eglee, will continue to receive “ordinary course” participation on a go forward basis, offset by the advance.

Watch on Deadline

As a result of the settlement, AMC will take a one-time charge of $85 million for the September quarter.

A federal judge in California in 2024 rejected AMC’s motion to have the case dismissed.

The Walking Dead defined AMC for yearswith the original series show running for 12 seasons through 2022 and Fear The Walking Dead wrapping in 2023 following by an army of spinoffs including The Walking Dead: Dead City, Daryl Dixon and TWD: The Ones Who Live.

title: ‘Dexter: Resurrection’ Sets Season 2 Premiere Date & Drops Teaser Trailer
summary: Showtime’s Dexter: Resurrection will premiere its second season on October 30 on Paramount+, with serial killers and ghosts aplenty to help kick off the Halloween holiday. A new teaser (above) also dropped, showing the titular Dexter Morgan (Michael C. Hall) at the optometrist getting his vision exam. While testing his vision, Dexter sees words and […]
content:
Showtime‘s Dexter: Resurrection will premiere its second season on October 30 on Paramount+, with serial killers and ghosts aplenty to help kick off the Halloween holiday.

A new teaser (above) also dropped, showing the titular Dexter Morgan (Michael C. Hall) at the optometrist getting his vision exam. While testing his vision, Dexter sees words and numbers appear, including the Season 2 premiere date, as well as the words “He’s Back” and “He’s Sharper Than Ever,” after showing him playing with his knives.

Dexter is rocking a new pair of glasses; the frames are smoky black, and they look very typical of a serial killer. I don’t know what I would expect from him style-wise, but I guess a pair of Ray-Ban Aviator glasses might’ve been way too cool, making him stand out.

Last week, production on Season 2 headed to the most private spot in New York City—Times Square! One day, Hall was shooting scenes with Uma Thurman, who returns this season as Charley, and the next day with David Zayas, who plays the beloved OG Angel Batista. Seeing Zayas on set as Batista was quite a surprise to the fandom because the character was murdered by Leon Prater (Peter Dinklage) in Season 1.

Watch on Deadline

But hey, this is a show that deals with ghosts and spirits all the time. James Remar has played Dexter’s deceased dad, Harry, since the original series. Dexter’s brother Brian Moser died in the original series, but Christian Camargo reprised the role in Dexter: Resurrection‘s first season. John Lithgow has returned a few times as the Trinity Killer, who died in the original series as well. The list is pretty endless. One thing I did confirm last week: Batista is definitely dead.

The October 30th premiere date is nearly a month after the franchise’s official 20th anniversary. The mothership series Dexter premiered on October 1, 2006.

From showrunner and executive producer Clyde Phillips, the second season of Dexter: Resurrection finds Dexter Morgan (Hall) caught between two killers — one (Brian Cox) with decades of notoriety and a lifetime of kills behind him, and the other a fresh young face (Dan Stevens) terrorizing New York in ways no one has ever seen. Meanwhile, Dexter battles a new and unexpected enemy: a mid-life crisis. Harrison (Jack Alcott) continues his own pursuit of justice as father and son face their darkest chapter yet.

A slew of previously released first-look photos of the new season, released by Showtime, reveal that Harrison has joined the family business in law enforcement. He is now an officer with the NYPD.

The official cast list and who they will play can be found below.

The new serial killers: Brian Cox as The New York Ripper; Dan Stevens as The Five Borough Killer; and Gabriel Luna as Ray Ballard, who operates under the name The Sleepy-Eyed Stranger. Krysten Ritter is also coming back to the show; in what capacity is as yet unknown. There’s plenty of speculation about her character, Mia LaPierre, aka Lady Vengeance, still being alive, but she could also return as a ghost.

Franchise star Desmond Harrington, who first appeared briefly in Season 1 of Dexter: Resurrection, was upped to series regular for Season 2, so expect to see a lot more Joey Quinn. The cast will also include newcomer Bokeem Woodbine as Capt. Mixon and Nona Parker Johnson as Fiona Mixon, and returning cast Ntare Guma Mbaho Mwine, Kadia Saraf, Dominic Fumusa, and James Remar.

These are the names that have been released officially, but if Season 1 is anything to go by, Season 2 should bring about some surprises.
